That’s the way the story is put together, how the overcoat is made, and so on. But story, that’s what the plot is about, and if that’s what the plot is about, how can we avoid calling it content? Well, it’s very interesting. In the first place, notice that sometimes story can be the dominant in obviously formal terms. I think of that story that all of you have probably read in school, The Things They Carried by Tim O’Brien. It’s a list of the contents of the knapsack of a soldier during the Vietnam War, just a list of the contents. Of course, all these items in the knapsack are evocative and what they do is they suggest a plot. By the end of the story, in other words, there is implied a plot. It’s just the opposite of the usual relationship between plot and story. Ordinarily, a plot constructs something which is implied–that is to say, that which happens, that which we can talk about in paraphrase or as a subject matter outside the text–but here in O’Brien’s story, you’re given the subject matter. The subject matter itself becomes the dominant device, and it implies in your imagination a way to construct it, but the way to construct it is not the dominant. The way to construct it is something that’s up to you. What’s the dominant in the text is just the stuff, the stuff in his knapsack listed with as little implication as possible. So that’s an instance of the way in which you can see the relationship between plot and story as a relationship of devices, even though it’s awfully tempting to say, “Oh, the story’s just the content and the plot’s the form”–but no. The formalists don’t want to keep that distinction for the reasons that I have been trying to develop.

在文学史发展的特定时期，任何一种修辞手法都可能占据主导地位。任何修辞手法都可能成为主导。在朗费罗的《海华沙之歌》中，韵律就是修辞手法。你肯定知道是怎么回事。而在丁尼生的诗歌中，音韵才是修辞手法，“低语的幽静”——哦，我今天完全记不住。我把它和济慈的一句诗混淆了，而且我还要再说说济慈。我只想告诉你，丁尼生认为英语中最美的两个词是“地窖门”，而听觉之美是他创作诗歌时最为关注的。所以我们可以说，丁尼生诗歌中，如同许多维多利亚时代的诗歌——当然也包括斯温伯恩的诗歌——中，主导的修辞手法是音韵；而在济慈的诗歌中，我们可以说主导的修辞手法是意象，他尤其强调联觉，以及各种感官如何在意象的唤起中融合。

Any device can be the dominant at a given moment in the development of literary history. Any device can be the dominant. In Hiawatha, Longfellow’s Hiawatha, meter is the device. You know how it goes. Well, in Tennyson sound is the device, “the murmurous haunt”–oh, I have no memory at all today. I’m mixing it up with a line of Keats, and I’m going to say something else about Keats. I’ll just tell you that Tennyson thought the two most beautiful words in the English language were “cellar door” and that audible beauty was his preoccupation in the making of poetry. So we can say that the dominant device in Tennyson’s poetry, as in much Victorian poetry–certainly Swinburne’s–is sound, and in Keats we can say that the dominant device is imagery, with his famous emphasis on synesthesia and the way in which the various senses merge in the evocation of images.

换句话说，学院派和象征主义者当然痴迷于意象，但这并不意味着俄国形式主义者就不能处理意象。在某些诗人的作品中，意象，或者说意象模式，无疑可以被视为主导手法。例如，济慈的作品可能就是如此。在格特鲁德·斯坦的作品中，主导手法无疑是重复。而在华兹华斯、乔伊斯或伍尔夫的作品中，主导手法或许并非形式。想想那种感觉：华兹华斯的无韵诗似乎就这么消失在了散文之中。我认为这种说法并不完全正确，但正如马修·阿诺德所说，人们普遍认为华兹华斯没有风格。在华兹华斯、乔伊斯或伍尔夫的作品中，主导手法是意识的内在性——也就是说，我们称之为意识流或思想内省的方式——这也是你在艾肯鲍姆的文章中会遇到的另一个词——驱动着文本中发生的一切。换句话说，文学的各个方面（被理解为“文学性”）都可以成为主导因素。

In other words, of course the academicians and the Symbolists were obsessed with imagery, but that’s not to say that a Russian formalist can’t deal with imagery. In a certain poet, the image, the image patterns, can certainly be recognized as the dominant device. That would probably be the case, for example, with Keats. In Gertrude Stein, the dominant is repetition undoubtedly. In Wordsworth or Joyce or Woolf, the dominant is perhaps not formal. Think of the feeling that Wordsworth’s blank verse just kind of disappears into prose. I don’t think that’s quite true, but there’s a general feeling that, as Matthew Arnold said, Wordsworth has no style. In Wordsworth or Joyce or Woolf, the dominant is the interiority of consciousness–that is, the way in which what we call stream of consciousness or the inwardness of thought motivates–this is another word that you encounter in Eikhenbaum’s essay–motivates everything else that goes on in the text. In other words, an enormous variety of aspects of literature, understood as “literariness,” can become the dominant.

一旦我们开始讨论“主导地位”之类的概念，我们也会意识到主导地位的消逝。例如，某一代人奉为圭臬的东西——这里我引用艾肯鲍姆的一段话——比如陀思妥耶夫斯基之前的犯罪小说手法，就变得至关重要。他主要指的是《罪与罚》，但陀思妥耶夫斯基的其他作品也同样如此。因此，廉价侦探小说的手法实际上成为了主流文学形式的驱动主导力量，但随后它们又会走向衰落，被其他主导力量所取代。换句话说，一旦你开始思考主导地位的消逝，你也就同时在思考文学史了。

Now as soon as we start talking about things like the dominant, we are also aware of the evanescence of dominance. What is culinary in one generation–and here I’m alluding to a passage quoted by Eikhenbaum–for example, the devices of crime fiction prior to the work of Dostoyevsky, become absolutely central. He’s thinking primarily of Crime and Punishment, but this is true of other works of Dostoyevsky as well, so that the devices of the dime-store detective novel actually then become the motivating dominant of a mainstream literary form, but then they in turn run their course and are replaced by some other dominant. In other words, once you start thinking about the evanescence of dominance, you’re also thinking about literary history.

第七章 文学作为史学

Chapter 7. The Literary as Historiography

对俄国形式主义者最不实的指责之一——这也是托洛茨基等人提出的众多指责之一——是他们忽视历史，而新批评家也经常受到同样的指责。他们根本没有忽视历史。几乎从一开始，尤其是在二十年代，他们就将注意力转向文学史学的问题，并就此发表了一些相当振奋人心的言论。在您第12页的文本中，左侧栏——我将继续用这些印章编号来指代您泰科复印中心文本的左侧——我们发现艾肯鲍姆引用了民族志批评家维谢洛夫斯基和维克托·什克洛夫斯基之间的一段意见交流：

One of the most false charges–and it was a charge leveled by Trotsky among many others against the Russian formalists–is that they ignore history, the same charge so often leveled against the New Critics. They don’t at all ignore history. Almost from the beginning, but increasingly during the twenties, they turned their attention to the problems of literary historiography, and they said some rather bracing things about it. In your text on page 012, the left-hand column–I’ll keep referring to those stamped numbers, the left-hand side of your Tyco [copy center] text–we find Eikhenbaum evoking an exchange of opinion between the ethnographic critic Veselovsky and Victor Shklovsky:

什克洛夫斯基（艾肯鲍姆在书中三分之一处写道）接触到了维谢洛夫斯基的公式，这个公式大致基于民族志原则，即“新形式的目的是表达新内容[换句话说，新内容指的是那些迫使文学技巧改变的社会、历史和环境力量]……这就是‘民族志’立场。这就是所使用的词语。它显然也是唯物主义或社会立场。历史创造文学；而且不仅仅是文学史，社会史也创造文学。”什克洛夫斯基对此持不同意见，他决定提出一个完全不同的观点。

He [Shklovsky] [Eikhenbaum says, a third of the way down] had encountered Veselovsky’s formula, a formula broadly based on the ethnographic principle that “the purpose of new form is to express new content [new content, in other words, being those social and historical and environmental forces that oblige literary techniques to change]… That’s the”ethnographic” position. That’s the word used. It is obviously also the materialist, or, social position. History produces literature; and not just literary history, but social history, produces literature. Shklovsky disagreed and he decided to advance a completely different point of view.

艺术作品的产生源于其他作品的背景，并通过与它们的关联而形成。艺术作品的形式是由它与其他艺术作品以及先前存在的形式之间的关系所定义的……不仅是戏仿（顺便一提，戏仿在俄罗斯形式主义思想中是一个非常非常宽泛的概念，某种程度上仅仅意味着改变——也就是说，一个文本不可避免地会借鉴另一个文本，以发展自身的技巧和重点，并寻求一种新的主​​导地位），而且任何类型的艺术作品都是与某种形式平行且对立地产生的。新形式的目的不是为了表达新的内容，而是为了改变一种已经失去其审美特质的旧形式（也就是说，失去了其陌生化的力量，失去了其将电影从我们眼前带走的力量）。现在——当你思考这个问题时，你会对自己说，这一切都非常振奋人心，非常大胆，但维谢洛夫斯基是对的。[笑]我们知道文学是由历史力量产生的。新形式的出现仅仅是为了取代一个在美学上不再可行的旧形式，这是什么意思？这又是如何发生的呢？你知道，如果你要谈论变革，就必须诉诸社会力量。在我看来，这似乎确实是我们倾向于得出的自然结论。正因如此，我才给你看了你那份纸上的非凡段落（为了反驳这个结论），即廷亚诺夫1927年所著《论文学演变》的结尾部分，换句话说，这篇文章也是对托洛茨基《文学与革命》的回应。廷亚诺夫是这样说的：

The work of art arises from a background of other works and through association with them. The form of a work of art is defined by its relation to other works of art to forms existing prior to it… Not only parody [parody, by the way, is a very, very broad term in Russian formalist thought, in a way simply meaning change–that is to say, the way in which one text inevitably riffs on another text in elaborating its own devices and emphases and in search of a new kind of dominance], but also any kind of work of art is created parallel to and opposed to some kind of form. The purpose of new form is not to express new content, but to change an old form which has lost its aesthetic quality [that is to say, lost its power to defamiliarize, lost its power to take the film away from our eyes]. Now this–as you think about it, you say to yourself, That’s all very bracing and daring but Veselovsky is right. [laughs] We know literature is produced by historical forces. What does it mean, a new form comes about only to replace an old form which has ceased to be aesthetically viable? How does that happen? You know, you’ve got to appeal to social forces if you’re going to talk about change. That really does seem to me to be the spontaneous conclusion we are inclined to draw. That’s why I gave you (to offset this conclusion) the extraordinary passage on your sheet, the end of Tynjanov’s “On Literary Evolution,” written also 1927, written also, in other words, in response to Trotsky’s Literature and Revolution. This is what Tynjanov says:

在形式主义史学中，主要社会因素的首要意义丝毫没有被忽视。[换句话说，我们并非只是在玩游戏。我们也理解所谓“社会功能”的重要性。]相反，它必须通过文学演化问题得到充分阐明。这与建立主要社会因素的直接影响形成鲜明对比[接下来是这段话最令人惊叹之处，我认为这确实非同凡响]，后者用文学作品的修改（即变形）研究取代了对文学演化的研究。你明白其中的区别。在自然选择中，某些事情会发生。会发生突变。新的基因出现并成为显性基因，不再是隐性或潜在基因，生物体因此而改变。这就是演化，但生物体的变化是在一个背景下发生的——你知道，生物体的变化是剧烈的。拇指的出现，紧接着就发生了巨大的地震，拥有拇指的人从地球上消失了——也就是说，人类很可能就此灭绝。这就是形式的改变。在我看来，这是一个非凡的区别。任何时期都会自发地出现催生社会主义现实主义的冲动，但如果有人从天而降告诉你，如果你要写作，就必须写社会主义现实主义，那就是一种改变。这是对文学史学理解框架内自然演进的改变。

In formalist historiography, the prime significance of major social factors is not at all discarded. [In other words, we’re not just playing a game here. We, too, understand the relevance of what we call “the society function.”] Rather it must be elucidated in its full extent through the problem of the evolution of literature. This is in contrast to the establishment of the direct influence of major social factors [and here comes the amazing part of this utterance, which I think is truly remarkable] which replaces the study of evolution of literature with the study of the modification of literary works, that is to say their deformation. You see the distinction. In natural selection, certain things happen. There is mutation. New genes emerge as dominant, no longer recessive or latent, and organisms change. That’s evolution, but organisms change against a backdrop–you know, organisms are changing like crazy. In comes the prehensile thumb, and the next thing you know you get a colossal earthquake, and the possessor of the prehensile thumb disappears from the earth–which is to say, very possibly the human species will never develop. That’s the modification of a form. It strikes me that it’s a remarkable distinction. You will get in any period spontaneously the sorts of impulses that bring about socialist realism, but if you have a ukase from above telling you that if you’re going to write, it has to be socialist realism, that’s a modification. That is the modification of what would and does evolve in and of itself within an understanding of literary historiography.

在我看来，这种区分很有说服力。或许唯一可以反对的地方在于，很多时候，坚持这种区分得不偿失。如果我们说“哦，社会因素与此无关”，那我们就会陷入冗长繁琐的解释和回避显而易见的事实的怪圈（笑），所以我们还不如干脆——不放弃这种区分，因为我认为始终牢记这一点非常重要。从达尔文主义的角度来看，牢记这一点至关重要，而这正是廷亚诺夫所坚持的。这就是为什么他将自己的文章命名为“论文学演化”，而不是文学“革命”，而是文学“演化”。我认为，即使在实践中，我们发现几乎不可能，甚至在很多情况下，坚持这种区分可能是在浪费时间，但我们仍然应该牢记这种区分。然而，仔细想想，这确实是一种存在的区别，值得存在，也值得在我们思考文学史写作的各种方式时被记住。

The distinction, it seems to me, is compelling. The only objection to be made to it perhaps indeed is that much of the time, it’s just more trouble than it’s worth to enforce it. It would drive us into such baroque circumlocutions and avoidances of the obvious to say, “Oh, social factors have nothing to do with this,” [laughs] that we might as well just sort of–not give the distinction up, because I think it’s very important always to have it in the back of our minds. It’s important in Darwinian terms to have it in the back of our minds, and that’s what Tynjanov is insisting on. That’s why he calls his essay “On Literary Evolution,” not literary “revolution” but literary “evolution.” I think it’s terribly important to keep the distinction in the back of our minds even if we find it, in practical terms, well nigh impossible and possibly even in many contexts a waste of time to be perpetually enforcing it. It is nevertheless a distinction that does exist, once you think about it, that deserves to exist and deserves to be remembered when we think about the variety of ways in which literary history can be written.

我就先讲到这里吧，时间到了。我觉得还有一些话要说，当然，俄国形式主义可能受到的批判也需要尽快回顾一下。下次我们再讨论索绪尔之前，先把这些都讲清楚。

Now I’m going to stop there. Time’s up. There is a little more to say, I think, and certainly the possible ways in which Russian formalism is subject to critique need quickly to be passed in review. We’ll do all this next time before we get into Saussure.

第八讲——符号学与结构主义

Lecture 8 - Semiotics and Structuralism

第一章 什么是符号学？

Chapter 1. What is Semiology?

保罗·弗莱教授：所以，至少理论上，我会在黑板上指点。我想今天我会比平时更多地指黑板。我平时用粉笔做的“PPT”功能今天不太一样，因为我对一些图表方面的内容也很感兴趣，正如我所说，我会指着它们讲解。

Professor Paul Fry: So I’m going to be pointing to the board, at least in theory. I suppose I expect to be pointing to the board a little bit more today than ordinarily. The usual function of my [chalk] equivalent of Power Point isn’t quite the same today because I’m taking an interest in some of these diagrammatic matters as well and, as I say, I will be pointing to them.

好的。首先，我要推迟讲解一个你们可能已经很关心的问题，虽然这个问题在这次讲座中也会多次提及——那就是俄国形式主义者和索绪尔的符号学概念之间相互影响的完整关系——直到下周我们讨论罗曼·雅各布森的论文《语言学与诗学》时才会展开。我认为，雅各布森本人也参与了这两个运动，届时这两个运动之间的关系会更加清晰，也更加自然，比我现在试图概述它们之间的联系要容易得多。所以，这是我们系列讲座中一个需要推迟到下周讲解的内容，从上一讲开始就一直延续到下周。

All right. So to begin I’m actually going to postpone something that you’re probably already wondering about, although it will come into this lecture on a couple of occasions–that is to say, the full relationship in terms of the influence of both movements–between the Russian formalists and Saussure’s notion of semiology and semiotics–until next week when we discuss Roman Jakobson’s essay, “Linguistics and Poetics,” where I think the relationship between the two movements in which he himself was involved will become clearer and will come into focus more naturally than if I tried to outline what the connection between the two movements is now. So that is an aspect of our sequence of lectures, beginning with the last one, that will be postponed until next week.

符号学本身并非一种文学理论。正如我们下周将从雅各布森那里了解到的，文学——或者他称之为文学研究的“诗学”——可以被理解为符号学的一个分支，但符号学本身并非一种文学理论。换句话说，或许会让你感到沮丧，你今天读到的内容本身并不能告诉你任何关于文学的信息。这并非本课程中最后一次出现这种情况，但我们的任务当然是揭示我们所读文本（即使它们与文学研究没有直接关联）对文学的意义。索绪尔和符号学这门学科的重要意义在于它对几乎所有后续文学理论形式都产生了巨大的影响。这正是我们需要牢记的。符号学最终演变成了所谓的“结构主义”，我们将在下周探讨它。反过来，它又将其术语、问题体系和思维框架传承给了解构主义、拉康精神分析、法国马克思主义以及关于种族、殖民和性别的二元理论——换句话说，传承给了我们接下来将在本课程大纲中学习的大量内容。因此，尽管我们今天阅读的内容本身并非文学理论，但它对我们即将学习的许多文学理论发展却具有至关重要的塑造作用。

Now semiotics is not in itself a literary theory. As we’ll learn from Jakobson next week, literature can be understood–or what he calls the study of literature, “poetics”–can be understood as a subfield of semiotics, but semiotics is not in itself a literary theory. In other words, perhaps to your frustration, what you read today has nothing at all, in and of itself, to tell you about literature. This isn’t the last time this will happen during the course of the syllabus, but then of course, our job is to bring out the implications for literature of texts that we read that don’t have any direct bearing on literary study. The important thing about Saussure and the discipline of semiotics is the incredible influence that it has had on virtually every form of subsequent literary theory. That’s what we need to keep in mind. Semiotics evolves into what is called “structuralism,” which we’ll be considering next week. That in turn, as it were, bequeaths its terminology and its set of issues and frameworks for thinking to deconstruction, to Lacanian psychoanalysis, to French Marxism, and to binary theories of race, colonization and gender–in other words, to a great deal that we will be studying subsequently on this syllabus. So while again, what we read for today is not in itself literary theory, it is nevertheless crucially formative for a great many of the developments in literary theory that we’ll be studying.

现在，我想就此打住，谈一些轶事或推测——我一直觉得这非常有趣，忍不住要分享——在我们这个领域——批评史、文学理论——有很多被认为是奠基之作的文本，但奇怪的是，就像福柯所指出的那样，它们实际上并没有作者。我们知道，亚里士多德的《诗学》实际上并非亚里士多德所著，而是他的学生整理的讲义汇编。这正是中世纪阿拉伯学术黄金时代围绕《诗学》展开激烈争论的原因之一。我们发现的那个时期的手稿中，到处都是学者们互相指责的旁注，他们说：“不，不，不。不可能是那样。”换句话说，从某种意义上说，它是一部充满争议的文本，并非亚里士多德所著，但它同时也是一部奠基之作。亚里士多德被认为是“批评之父”，然而，福柯也称他为“话语性的奠基人”。

Now as an anecdotal or conjectural aside–I’ve always found this so fascinating I can never resist talking about it–there are various texts in our field–the history of criticism, literary theory–texts that are considered foundational but which curiously enough, a la Foucault, don’t actually have an author. Aristotle’s Poetics we know actually not to have been one of the texts written by Aristotle but rather to be a compendium of lecture notes put together by his students. This is one of the reasons why in the golden age of Arabic scholarship in the Middle Ages, there was so much dispute about thePoetics. The manuscripts we find from this period are full of marginal notes where the scholars are chiding each other and saying, “No, no, no. It can’t be that way.” In other words, in a way it’s a disputed text and it is not written by Aristotle, but it’s also a foundational text. Aristotle is considered the “father of criticism,” and yet he is also what Foucault would call a “founder of discursivity.”

奇怪的是，索绪尔的情况也完全一样。正如我刚才提到的，他可以被视为某种文学理论的奠基人。索绪尔的《普通语言学教程》并非索绪尔本人所著，而是他的学生们在他1906年至1911年间的一系列讲座中整理的讲义汇编，后由他的两位语言学家弟子汇编成书。令人费解的是，这部著作竟然也具有同样的奠基作用。前往日内瓦研究索绪尔档案的学者们各有各的目的。其中一些人对索绪尔抱有成见，希望通过了解他那些并未在正文中提及的观点来否定他。有些人像索绪尔一样，觉得需要把他从排字工手中拯救出来[笑]，而另一些人则怀着崇拜的态度，希望档案能够为他们提供充分的证据，证明我们称之为《普通语言学教程》的文本的完整性；因此，从某种意义上说，鉴于索绪尔档案与我们拥有的实际文本之间存在着不稳定的关系，对索绪尔档案的研究就像一张地图，如果有人研究它，就可以将其与二十世纪文学理论的思考史联系起来。

Well, the odd thing is it’s exactly the same with Saussure, who can be considered the father or patriarch of a certain kind of literary theory as I have just indicated. Saussure’s Course in General Linguistics is not something written by Saussure but is a compendium of lecture notes written by his students in a series of lectures that he gave from 1906 to 1911 and then gathered together in book form by two of his disciples who were linguists. Now it’s odd that this text does have the same formative function. Scholars who go to Geneva go for a variety of reasons when they look at the Saussure archive. Some of them are predisposed to dislike Saussure and to hope that they can somehow discredit him by learning more about things that he thought that aren’t actually in the text. Others like Saussure and feel that he needs to be rescued [laughs] from his compositors, and yet others go in an attitude of worship and hope that the archive will yield to them full confirmation of the integrity of the text we call the Course in General Linguistics; so that in a way, the study of the Saussure archive, given the volatile relationship of that archive with the actual text that we have, is a kind of map that, if one were to study it, one could associate with the history of thinking about literary theory in the twentieth century.

这其实无关紧要。我只是觉得很有意思，两位无可争议的[笑]我们所研究领域话语建构的奠基人，实际上严格来说并非作者[笑]，这在某种程度上印证了我们一开始阅读的那篇论文中福柯的观点。好了，就此打住。我们得努力弄清楚索绪尔的意图。让我们继续深入探讨吧。

This is really all neither here nor there. I just find it interesting that two people who are incontestably [laughs] founders of discursivity in the field that we study are in fact not strictly speaking authors, [laughs] somehow or another confirming the insight of Foucault in the essay that we began by reading. Anyway, enough of that. We have to try to figure out what Saussure is up to. Let’s move on to begin to do so.

什么是符号学？它是对现存的、约定俗成的交流系统的研究。所有这些系统我们都可以称之为“语言”，而“语言”——也就是我们彼此交谈时使用的词语——就是其中之一。其他系统，例如哑剧演员使用的手势、信号灯、铁路信号灯以及红绿黄三色交通信号灯——都是符号系统。换句话说，它们都是我们赖以生存的交流方式，其可理解性使我们能够与周围的世界互动。符号学已经扩展到思维的方方面面。存在达尔文符号学，它用符号学的术语来理解物种之间的关系。换句话说，几乎所有可以想象的事物都可以被理解为一种由符号系统构成的语言——我们稍后会谈到符号——但在此之前，重要的是要理解符号学究竟是什么。这就是它的本质。

What is semiology? It’s the study of existing, conventional, communicative systems. All of these systems we can call “languages,” and “language”–that is to say, the words that we use when we speak to each other–is one of those systems. Other systems: the gestures that mimes use, semaphores, railroad semaphores and a stoplight–red, green, yellow–are all semiotic systems. In other words, all of them are modes of communication with which we function, the intelligibility of which allows us to negotiate the world around us. Semiotics has expanded into every imaginable aspect of thought. There is a Darwinian semiotics, understanding the relationships among species in semiotic terms. There is, in other words, a semiotics of virtually every imaginable thing understood as a language made up of a system of signs–signs we’ll be getting to in a minute–but in the meantime, it’s important to understand what semiology actually is. That’s what it is.

哦，我正想问你们呢。昨晚我通过邮件发给你们的那些材料，有多少人没带？好的。我们这里有，会分发给大家。我们大概有二十五份，所以如果不需要就别拿了。

Oh, I meant to ask you. How many of you did not bring the passages that I sent to you by e-mail last night? All right. We have them here and they’ll be passed around. We have about twenty-five copies, so don’t take one if you don’t need it.

第二章 “语言”与“言语”，“所指”与“能指”

Chapter 2. “Langue” and “Parole,” “Signified” and “Signifier”

接下来我要讲的是纸上的第二段文字，我认为这段文字能阐明这些系统的本质。“语言，”索绪尔说，“并非说话者的产物。”他这里当然指的是人类语言。“它是被个体被动吸收的产物。”这究竟意味着什么呢？人类语言并非我的语言——也就是说，它并非源于我，换句话说，它并非我的私人语言——这当然意味着某种损失，因为这意味着当我说话，当我在言语中使用语言时，我使用的东西并非完全属于我自己。它是约定俗成的——也就是说，它属于我们所有人的公共领域，而这其中或许蕴含着某种浪漫主义式的失落。如果语言在某种意义上属于我自己，那该有多好啊？

I am going to be turning to the second passage on the sheet in which something about the nature of these systems, I think, can be made clear. “Language,” says Saussure, “is not a function of the speaker.” Here of course he is talking about human language. “It is a product that is passively assimilated by the individual.” Now what does this mean? The fact that human language is not my language–that is to say, the fact that it doesn’t originate in me, the fact that it’s not, in other words, my private language–suggests, of course, a certain loss because it means that when I speak, when I use language in speech, I’m using something that is not strictly my own. It’s conventional–that is to say, it belongs in the public sphere to all of us, and there’s perhaps a certain sort of Romantic loss in that. Wouldn’t it be nice if language in some sense were my own?

但语言之所以能成为索绪尔希望研究的科学对象，其不可思议的益处在于——这显然是他与形式主义者的共同之处——如果语言不是私人的，如果它不是我个人的，如果它不是我可以随心所欲创造的东西，换句话说，如果它是约定俗成的，属于我们所有人，那么这恰恰是它具有交际功能的原因。换句话说，它是一个符号系统，我们可以利用它，我们之所以能将其识别为符号，正是因为它们存在于我们之间，是我们可以共享的。这正是索绪尔作为语言学家和符号学家所关注的对象。

But the incredible gain which makes language something like the object of science that Saussure is hoping to secure–this is one of the things, obviously, that he has in common with the formalists–the incredible gain is that if language is not private, if it’s not my own, if it’s not something that I can make up as I go along, and if, in other words, it is conventional, belonging to all of us, then that’s precisely what allows it to be communicative. It is a system of signs, in other words, that we can make use of, that we recognize as signs precisely because they exist among us as something that can be shared in common. This then is the object of Saussure’s attention as a linguist and as a semiotician.

这个想法的隐含意思是，语言是我们使用的东西。最直接、最简洁的说法是：我不会说语言。语言作为一种整体而存在，可以说——这一点在我们今天不时会再次提及的这些概念中也会反复出现——可以说，语言作为一种整体是虚拟的。你们还记得弗洛伊德说过，我们必须从意识的异常行为中推断出无意识。潜意识中必然存在某种东西，所以我们称之为“无意识”，并尝试描述它。语言，或者索绪尔所说的“langue”，也是如此。我们所做的就是说话，当我们说话时，当然，我们会说我们“使用”语言，但我们仍然需要知道语言是什么，我们需要理解语言和言语之间的关系。

Now what’s implied in this idea is that language is something that we use. The best way to say it and the quickest way to say it is that I don’t speak language. Language as something that exists as an aggregate all at once, arguably–and this is something that’s going to come up again and again as we come back to these coordinates that we’ll be touching on from time to time today also–arguably, language as an aggregate is something virtual. You remember that Freud said we have to infer the unconscious from the erratic behavior of consciousness. There’s got to be something back there, so we’re going to call it “the unconscious” and we’re going to try to describe it. It is very much the same with language, or “langue” as Saussure calls it. What we do is speak, and when we speak, of course, we say correctly that we “use” language, but we still need to know what language is and we need to understand the relationship between language and speech.

现在我们可以把语言理解为词汇库、词典中所包含的一切，以及某种理想化或完全系统化的语法和句法规则体系中所包含的一切的集合体，但实际上并不存在这样的集合体。换句话说，它存在，它就在那里，等待语言学家们通过实验和推测来构建；但作为一种在空间上同时存在的复合体，语言在某种意义上，就像弗洛伊德的无意识一样，是我们从言语中推断出来的。言语就是我们的行为。言语是我们挪用、运用和使用语言的方式，索绪尔称之为“言语”（parole）。言语是空间中一系列可能性在时间中的展开，而这一系列可能性正是索绪尔所说的“语言”（langue）。

Now we can understand language as a kind of aggregate of everything that’s in the lexicon, in the dictionary, together with everything that would be in some sort of ideal or utterly systematized set of rules of grammar and syntax, but there is no real aggregate of that kind. In other words, it exists, it’s there to be put together partly as a matter of experiment and partly as a matter of conjecture by the linguists; but as a composite thing existing in a spatial simultaneity, synchronically, language is something that in a very real sense, as is the case with Freud’s unconscious, we infer from speech. Now speech is what we do. Speech is the way in which we appropriate, deploy and make use of language, and Saussure calls that “parole.” Parole is the unfolding in time of a set of possibilities given in space, that set of possibilities being what Saussure calls “langue.”

语言是一套符号系统。什么是符号？索绪尔著名的图示足以说明一切。[指向黑板] 线上代表概念，线下代表声音意象。换句话说，我想到某件事，而我对这件事的思考就对应着一个我事先准备好的声音意象。这可以理解为想到“树”这个概念——这就是为什么它要加引号，因为我讲拉丁语——并且知道与“树”这个概念对应的声音意象是“arbor”（树），对吧？我就可以想到[笑]类似的东西[画一棵树]，某种程度上与它相似的东西。同样地——我仍然讲拉丁语——它对应的声音意象是“arbor”。我今天可能不会再谈到这个了，但是在这个问号里（在符号图旁边的黑板上，所指的树写在能指的凉亭上面，两者都没有加引号），就藏着解构的秘密，好吗？——只是[笑声]让你保持警惕，忐忑不安。

Now language is a system of signs. What is a sign? Saussure’s famous diagrams make it clear enough. [Gestures to board.] We have above the line a concept and we have below the line a sound image. In other words, I think of something and that thinking of something corresponds to a sound image that I have ready to hand for it. That can be understood in terms of thinking of the concept “tree”–that’s why this is in quotation marks, I speak Latin–and knowing that the sound image correlative to the concept tree is “arbor,” right, I can think of [laughs] something like that [drawing of a tree], something in some way resembling that. By the same token–I still speak Latin–the sound image corresponding to it is “arbor.” I may or may not get back to this today, but in this question mark [on the board next to a sign diagram in which the signified tree is written over the signifier arbor, neither of them in quotation marks] is the secret of deconstruction, all right?– just [laughter] to keep you poised and on tenterhooks.

与此同时，索绪尔对线上下这种关系的处理方式是，他认为概念与声音意象之间存在一种任意的关系。他将概念称为“所指”，将声音意象称为“能指”。换句话说，一个符号在某种意义上是由两个方面构成的：所指与能指之间的关系。我们必须将它们放在一起思考。它们不可分割。它们之间的关系是必要的，但正如我们稍后将看到的，它是任意的，每个符号都是如此。我们组合符号的方式是，将这些概念与声音意象之间的二元关系组合起来，并按照展开的顺序进行调整。这就是我们说话的方式。这就是我们造句的方式。

In the meantime, what Saussure is doing with this relationship above and below the line is, he is saying that there is anarbitrary relationship between the concept and the sound image. The concept he calls a “signified” and the sound image he calls a “signifier.” A sign, in other words, is made up of two sides in, as it were, a thought moment: a relationship between that which is signified and that which signifies it. It’s to be understood that we have to think of them together. They’re not divisible. Their relationship is necessary but, as we’ll see in a minute, arbitrary, and each sign is like that. The way in which we put signs together is to take these bundles, these binary relationships between a concept and a sound image, and adjust them in an unfolding sequence. That’s how we speak. That’s how we make a sentence.

好的。所以，从某种意义上说，能指，比如我发出的声音，指代一个概念，并且由此推断——一种非常有力、必然的推断——它指代的并非一个具体的事物，这种观点本身并不新颖。词语指代概念而非事物的观点，早在约翰·洛克的《人类理解论》中就已经得到了充分阐述，此后也或多或少地被人们所接受，正如我所说，这本身就是一个约定俗成的思想，索绪尔只是对其进行了调整和运用。但是，索绪尔的创新之处，以及符号学作为一门科学的真正基础，在于他接下来对符号提出的两个观点。首先，正如我所说，能指与所指之间的关系是任意的。他要说的第二点是，我们区分不同符号的方式——无论是研究语言的整体性（其中符号群彼此关联），还是研究言语行为（其中符号按顺序并列出现）——我们理解符号意义的方式都是差异性的。因此，索绪尔关于所指与能指关系的思考的新颖之处在于，他认为这种关系中所涉及的符号既是任意的，又是差异性的。

All right. So in a way the idea that a signifier, a sound that I make, arbor, refers to a concept and by implication, by a very powerful and strong and necessary implication, not to a thing–is not in itself new. The idea that a word signifies an idea and not an object is already fully developed in John Locke’s Essay on Human Understanding and is more or less commonly agreed on ever afterwards and is, as I say, in itself a conventional thought that Saussure adapts and makes use of. But what is new in Saussure and what really is foundational in semiotics as a science is two things that Saussure then goes on to say about the sign. The first thing he has to say is that the signified-signifier relationship, as I said, is arbitrary. And the second thing he has to say is that the way in which we know one sign from another–either studying language in the aggregate, whereby clusters of signs exist in associational relation to each other, or studying it in speech acts, in speech, whereby signs exist next to each other in a sequence–the way in which we understand what a sign means is differential. So that what’s new in Saussure’s thinking about the relationship between signified and signifier is that the sign tied up in this relationship is both arbitrary and differential.

第三章 正面知识与负面知识：任意性和差异性

Chapter 3. Positive and Negative Knowledge: Arbitrary and Differential

好的。这是对一些基本概念的初步介绍。我想回到语言和言语的区别，并请大家阅读第一段文字——现在你们每个人都拿到了——因为和俄国形式主义者一样，索绪尔主要关注的是阐明他所说的“符号学”的含义，从而将符号学确立为一门科学。就像俄国形式主义者——某种程度上也像新批评派——谈论他们的“学院派”同行一样，索绪尔对语言学研究中的混乱和缺乏系统性感到困扰。以下是他在第一段文字中的观点：

Okay. This is a first walk through some essential ideas. I want to go back to the distinction between language and speech and refer you to the first passage which–now all of you have it–is on your sheet, because like the Russian formalists, Saussure is chiefly concerned in outlining what he means by “semiology” to establish the semiological project as a science. Like the Russian formalists–and in a way like the New Critics–talking about their “academic” colleagues, Saussure is vexed by the messiness and lack of system in the study of linguistics. This is what he says in this first passage. He says:

如果我们同时从多个角度研究言语，语言学的研究对象在我们看来就像是一团杂乱无章、互不相关的异质事物。这就是言语。[指向黑板上坐标系的横轴。] 我是一名语言学家，那我做什么呢？我研究言语，研究各种言语，如果我这样做，并且不断地从各种角度思考它，那么各种各样的框架就会争相吸引我的注意力。索绪尔继续说道：

If we study speech from several viewpoints simultaneously, the object of linguistics appears to us as a confused mass of heterogeneous and unrelated things. This is speech. [Gestures towards the horizontal axis of the coordinates on the board.] I’m a linguist and so what do I do? I study speech, I study speeches, and if I do so, and if I keep thinking about it in a variety of ways, all sorts of frameworks jostle for attention. Saussure continues:

这种方法为心理学、人类学、规范语法、语文学等诸多学科打开了大门，这些学科虽然与语言学不同，但都声称，鉴于语言学方法的缺陷，言语是它们的研究对象之一。在我看来，解决上述所有难题只有一个办法。从一开始（这真是一个奇特的混合比喻），我们就必须脚踏实地地站在语言的根基上，并将语言作为所有其他言语表现形式的规范。就好像他试图压制语言一样。（笑）“待在那儿，待在那儿。”我们脚踏实地地站在语言的根基上，这样我们才能将其理解为一个系统，一个可以被精确地、差异化地理解的事物，一个可以通过语言组织符号的各种方式来理解的事物。

This procedure opens the door to several sciences, psychology, anthropology, normative grammar, philology and so on which are distinct from linguistics but which claim speech in view of the faulty method of linguistics as one of their objects. As I see it, there is only one solution to all the foregoing difficulties. From the very outset [and this is [laughs] a really peculiar mixed metaphor] we must put both feet on the ground of language and use language as the norm of all the other manifestations of speech. It’s as if he’s trying to hold language down. [laughs] “Stay there. Stay there.” We put both feet on the ground of language so that we have it intelligible to us as a system, as something that can be understood, precisely, differentially, that can be understood in the variety of ways in which language organizes signs.

我们不妨停下来思考一下语言中符号的各种含义，所有这些含义都与选择某个符号进入句子的方式有关。以“船”这个词为例。“船”的发音与某些其他词语非常接近。为了避免口误，我们就不一一列举了，但这确实是一个词组。这只是语言中“船”这个符号排列方式的一种联想矩阵或网络，但“船”还有很多同义词：“bark”（小船）、“boat”（船）、“bateau”（平底船）、“sailboat”（帆船）等等。它们也聚集在一起：“steamship”（轮船）、“ocean liner”（远洋客轮），换句话说，这些词发音完全不同，但在同义词上却很接近。它们就是这样聚集在一起的。此外，“船”还与某些事物相对应，因此它也会与“train”（火车）、“car”（汽车）、“truck”（卡车）、“mule”（骡子）等交通工具建立联系，对吧？通过所有这些方式，“船”在语言中以联想的方式聚集在一起，使其可以被选择，可以被选择用于我们说话时试图构建的特定语义语境中。

It might be worth pausing over the variety of ways in which we can think of signs in language, all of which have to do with the way in which a given sign might be chosen to go into a speech sentence. Take the word “ship.” “Ship” is very closely related in sound to certain other words. We won’t specify them for fear of a Freudian slip, but that is one cluster. That is one associational matrix or network that one can think of in the arrangement of that sign in language, but there are also synonyms for “ship”: “bark,”boat,” “bateau,” a great many other synonyms–“sailboat,” whatever. They, too, exist in a cluster: “steamship,” “ocean liner,” in other words, words that don’t sound at all the same, but are contiguous in synonymity. They cluster in that way. And then furthermore “ship” is also the opposite of certain things, so that it would also enter into a relationship with “train,” “car,” “truck,” “mule,” modes of transportation, right? In all of these ways, “ship” is clustered associationally in language in ways that make it available to be chosen, available to be chosen as appropriate for a certain semantic context that we try to develop when we speak.

这就是语言中符号的运作方式。这只是任何特定符号运作方式的冰山一角。顺便说一句，我刚才的描述过于简化，假设语言的基本单位是词。语言学家们知道，情况并非总是如此。语言学家可以从不同的抽象层次研究语言。有时基本单位是短语，有时是音素——也就是单个声音单位——或者，如果研究语言作为一种书写系统，那么基本单位可能是音节。它可以是图形或听觉上理解的字母，语言学研究中基本单位选择的多样性意味着我们需要一个专门的词来指代这个单位，这个词通常被称为“语素”。换句话说，无论你如何理解语言的系统化和理解，以及作为基本构成单位的“词”（虽然我刚才用了这个词，但它可能不是最受欢迎的选择之一[笑]），统称都是“词素”。因此，你也可以将符号的关联性理解为词素性的。

So that’s the way a sign works in language. This is the tip of the iceberg for any given sign. By the way, in what I’m saying, I oversimplify by supposing that the basic unit of language is a word. The linguists know that that’s not at all necessarily the case. Linguists can work at different levels of abstraction with language. Sometimes the basic unit is the phrase, but some other times the basic unit is the phoneme–that is to say, the single sound unit–or if one’s studying language as a system of writing it might be the syllable. It could be the letter understood either graphically or audibly, and the variety of ways in which one can choose a basic unit in the study of linguistics means that you need a special word for that unit, which is characteristically “the tagmeme.” In other words, whatever you are thinking of as your systematizing, your understanding, of language, and as the basic constituent unit–“the word” being probably one of the less popular choices, [laughs] even though that’s the one I’ve just used–the blanket term for that is “the tagmeme.” So you can understand the associational nature of signs also as tagmemic.

当然，由于存在一定的语义收益，比如说，即使你谈论的是一个音素——尤其因为，正如索绪尔所说，我稍后会再谈到，在语言拟声词容易产生误导的现象中，某个声音可能具有某些内涵，这意味着该声音可能聚集在一个联想网络中。但根据所选单元的不同，联想网络也会有所不同。

Then of course, since there is a certain amount of semantic payoff, let’s say, even when you’re talking about a phoneme–especially because, as Saussure will say, and as I’ll get back to, in the misleading onomatopoetic drift of language, perhaps a certain sound has certain connotations, meaning the sound may cluster in an associational network. But depending on the unit chosen, the associational networks will differ.

但无论在哪个层面，它们仍然会以矩阵的形式存在。换句话说，我们又如何才能在语言中感受到系统性呢？我说话时，很可能不会随便选择一个词。E·E·卡明斯大胆地尝试了这一原则，并引起了语言学家的注意，尤其是一位名叫戴尔·海姆斯的语言学家。卡明斯写出了像“He danced his did”这样的句子，其中“did”显然不是一个你会认为会以任何方式参与相关联想的词。“He danced his did”：这在任何意义上都是一次失误，正如一种语言学派所称，然而与此同时，卡明斯却对我们嗤之以鼻，故意使用这个词，几乎就像是在对符号学进行批判，但同时符号学或许也拥有反驳的方法和手段。只需要一点创造力就能注意到，“d”音或“duh”音重复了“d”音，“danced”中的“duh”音也是如此，而且他的意识会受到各种组合压力，从而选择“did”而不是其他一些看似无关的词。

But at any level they will still exist as a matrix. In other words, how else could we have any sense of systematicity in language? It is always probably the case that when I speak I won’t choose just any word. e. e. cummings actually boldly experimented with this principle and he attracted the attention of the linguists, particularly a linguist named Dell Hymes. e. e. cummings wrote sentences like “He danced his did” where “did” is obviously not a word you would have supposed to be in any way involved in a relevant associational cluster. “He danced his did”: that is in every sense a misfire, as one school of thinking about language would call it, and yet at the same time, cummings thumbs his nose at us and deliberately uses that word almost as though he were issuing a critique of semiotics but at the same time such that semiotics would probably have available to it its ways and means of refutation. A certain amount of ingenuity is all that’s required to notice that the “d” sound or “duh” reiterates the “d,” the “duh” sound in “danced,” and that there are all sorts of combinatory pressures on his consciousness to choose “did” as opposed to some other seemingly irrelevant word.

所以无论如何，即便有这些极端例子，你仍然可以理解语言，即便它千变万化，仍然是联想性的，它将可用的符号以某种方式聚集在一起，使它们比其他条件相同时更容易被选择。总之，语言是一个符号系统。这些符号既是任意的，又是差异性的。

So in any case, you can still, even with these egregious examples, understand language even in its infinite variety nevertheless as associational and as clustering its available signs in ways that make them more readily to hand for choice than they might be, all other things being equal. Well, in any case, so language is a system of signs. The signs are both arbitrary and differential.

那么，这意味着什么呢？这或许是我们受所谓“文学理论”及其相关思考（即关于感知本质的思考）影响而学到的第二件事。如果符号既是任意的又是差异性的——也就是说，如果不存在自然符号，不存在由自然、由事物本身的本质以及与事物相关的词语本质所联系的东西——如果正如索绪尔所说，在边界的一侧，我们看到一头牛说“ochs”，而在边界的另一侧，我们看到一头牛说“boeuf”，如果我们跨越一片相当大的水域，看到一头牛说“cow”，那么显然，事物与符号之间的关系——能指与所指之间的关系——就不存在了。所以，符号是任意的，而且也是差异性的。我必须能够区分我在任何交流序列中使用的所有符号。我该如何做到这一点呢？通过引入并非其他符号的符号。符号与自然界之间没有任何自然联系，符号与其他符号之间也没有任何自然联系。我并不肯定地了解我用来与你交流的语言单位。我否定地了解它。我了解它仅仅是因为它不是其他任何事物。它与最接近的事物之间，无论通过相似还是差异，都不可能存在同一性关系。它不是其他事物，但总的来说，符号的意义就在于它不是其他任何事物。即使是同音异义词也是如此。即使是看似相同的符号也是如此，因为每个符号都有其使用价值，并且只有在特定的语境中才能被理解为它所代表的含义。

Now what does this mean? This is actually the second thing, maybe, that we learn under the influence of what we call “literary theory” and the thinking that surrounds it about the nature of perception. If the sign is both arbitrary and differential–that is to say, if there is no such thing as a natural sign, something that is linked by nature, by the nature of the thing and the word together with the thing–if on one side of the border, as Saussure puts it, we look at a cow and say, “ochs,” and if on the other side of the border we look at a cow and say, “boeuf,” and if we cross a considerable body of water and we look at a cow and say “cow,” plainly the relationship between the thing and the sign–the matrix signifier, signified–just doesn’t exist. So signs are arbitrary– and they’re also differential. I have to be able to distinguish between all the signs I use in any communicative sequence. How do I do it? By putting in signs which are not other signs. The sign is not linked to the natural world by any natural means, and the sign is not linked to other signs by any natural means. I don’t know a unit of language– which I use to communicate with you– positively. I know it negatively. I know it only because it is not everything else. Its direct relationship with the thing that’s most closely adjacent to it somehow either through similarity or dissimilarity can never be a relationship of identity. It’s not that other thing, but, generally speaking, the point about a sign is that it’s not any other thing. This is true even in homonyms. This is true even of seemingly identical signs, because each has its use value and is only intelligible as that which it exists to mean in a certain context.

所以，我只能在与他人沟通、被他人理解的情况下才能知道我所知道的，这是否定性的。我无法仅仅因为那是某种符号就知道它。我无法肯定地知道它。我接下来要举个例子，希望能够阐明我的意思；在此之前，我们先来看索绪尔的几段文字，或许能说明这一点。今天我发的这份纸上没有（笑），但在我昨晚发的电子版里，有第五段文字，这段文字实际上是索绪尔在你文章中两个不同部分的表述的组合。第一段在第844页。这有可能吗？（笑）我希望是这样。不，这不对。正确的是第845页，左下角那一栏，索绪尔在那里说：

So it is always the case that I can only know what I know if it’s a question of being communicated with, having something rendered intelligible for me, negatively. I can’t know it because it just is that sign. I don’t know it positively. I’m about to give an example of this which I hope will flesh out what I’m trying to get across; in the meantime, let’s look at a couple of passages in Saussure that may make the point. Now not on the version of the sheet that I passed out today [laughs] but on the version that I sent electronically last night, there is a fifth passage, and that passage is actually a combination of formulations by Saussure that are in two separate parts of your text. The first one is on page 844. Can this possibly be correct? I [laughs] hope it can. No, it is not correct. It’s page 845, the lower left-hand column where Saussure says:

语言是一个由相互依存的术语构成的系统，其中每个术语的价值完全取决于其他术语的同时存在，正如下图所示……换句话说，一个术语的价值——我说一句话，我发出一个声音——这个声音的价值只能通过其语境来确定。我只能通过它与周围一切事物之间的差异来了解它。

Language is a system of interdependent terms in which the value of each term results solely from the simultaneous presence of the others as in the diagram, [just below it]… In other words, the value of a term–I say something, I utter a sound–the value of that sound cannot be determined except by its context. I can’t know it except by the way in which it differs from everything that surrounds it.

他接着说——这段话在第 847 页左侧栏中间偏下的位置：

He goes on to say–this is on page 847 about halfway down the left-hand column:

……归根结底，语言的任何片段都不可能基于任何其他因素，只能基于它与其他部分的不一致。任意性和差异性是两个相互关联的特质。此外，在第846页右侧栏中间位置还有一段话：“……概念纯粹是差异性的，它们并非由其积极的内涵定义，而是由它们与系统中其他术语的消极关系定义。” 这或许很难凭直觉接受。我们在感知周围世界时，会感觉自己了解事物的本质和属性。我看着某样东西，就知道它是什么，却忘记了，我或许只是因为身处特定的语境才知道它是什么，而在这个语境中，它实际上并非与它相关的其他事物。

… [A] segment of language can never in the final analysis be based on anything except its noncoincidence with the rest. Arbitrary and differential are two correlative qualities. And then again another passage on page 846, the right-hand column halfway down: “… [C]oncepts are purely differential and defined not by their positive content but negatively by their relations with other terms of the system.” Now probably this is hard to accept intuitively. We feel as we process the world around us that we know things for and as what they are. I look at something and I know what it is, forgetting that possibly I only know what it is because of a context in which indeed it is not those other things that are linked to it.

第四章 示例：红灯

Chapter 4. Example: the Red Stoplight

现在我想举个例子。我可以用任何例子，但我打算用一个显然可以在各种符号系统间转换的例子。它本身是一种语言，但正如我们马上会看到的，它也属于其他类型的符号系统。我想用红灯的例子。红绿灯可能是我们拥有的最简单的符号系统之一——它只有三个（或者说，可以说只有三个）彼此明显不同的变量：红、黄、绿——我们对红灯有两种理解方式。如果我们认为我们的认知是肯定的，那么我们会说“红灯”意味着“停止”。我们会自然而然地说“红灯”意味着“停止”。

Now I want to take an example. I could use any example but I’m going to use something which plainly does move around among various semiotic systems. It’s a piece of language but it also belongs to other sorts of semiotic systems as we’ll immediately see. I want to use the example of the red light. Now in a stoplight, which is probably just about the simplest semiotic system that we have–it only has three, one is tempted to say, variables plainly differing from each other: red, yellow and green–we have two ways of thinking about the red light. If we think that our knowledge is positive, we say “red” in a red light means stop. It comes spontaneously to us to say “red light” means “stop.”

如果我们只能依据这套符号系统，那就很难对这种思维方式提出质疑，因为我们会说“黄灯”代表“停止”，“绿灯”代表“通行”。这三种灯光及其各自的颜色确实代表着这些积极的含义。每个人都知道这一点，而且我肯定不会在接近十字路口时，看到红灯亮起时心里想着——我不会对自己说，“哦，不是黄灯，也不是绿灯。”[笑声] 我的思维方式并非如此。好吧，但它仍然是红灯，对吧？我们的假设是，红灯具有积极意义，因为它代表着某种特定的含义。我们说，它意味着“停止”。那么，假设红灯出现在驯鹿的鼻子上，或者像驯鹿的鼻子一样。在这种情况下，红灯就成了一个灯塔，意味着“前进”、“通行”、“跟我来”、“管他呢”。对吧？ [笑] 我们得赶紧把这些礼物分发出去。时间紧迫。我们飞奔而去——说不定会出事故，谁知道呢？[笑]——我们被红灯的含义所驱使，红灯的意思是“通行”，对吧？

Now if all we have to go on is just this semiotic system, it’s going to be kind of hard to put up resistance to that sort of thinking because by the same token we’ll say “yellow” means “pause,” “green” means “go.” These three lights with their respective colors just do positively mean these things. Everybody knows it, and I’m certainly not thinking when I approach an intersection that when the red light goes on–I’m not saying to myself, “Oh, not yellow, not green.” [laughter] My mind just doesn’t work that way. All right, but still it’s a red light, right, and our hypothesis is that the red light has positive value in the sense that it means a certain thing. It means, we say, “stop.” Well, suppose the red light appeared on or as the nose of a reindeer. In that case the red light would be a beacon which means “forward,” “go,” “follow me,” “damn the torpedoes.” Right? [laughs] We’ve got to get these presents distributed. No time to waste. And we race off–perhaps risking an accident, who knows? [laughs] –we race off under the compulsion of the meaning of the red light, which is “go,” right?

顺便提一下，有个轶事，真假我始终无法考证。据说在中国文化大革命期间，毛泽东夫人非常反对红灯表示“停止”，因为红色当然是进步的颜色。它应该意味着“前进”，并且背后蕴藏着一切。但毋庸置疑，她的想法从未付诸实施，因为（笑）如果今天红灯表示“停止”，明天红灯表示“前进”，那可能会出现一些问题。顺便说一句，这说明符号系统中的一切都是约定俗成的，对吧？我的意思是，意识到红灯最终可能表示“前进”本身，就意味着积极意义的缺失——我接下来还会举更多例子。这是约定俗成的。无论在差异系统中遵循何种约定俗成，正是这些约定俗成使得符号能够被理解。

Now by the way, there’s an anecdote, the truth of which I’ve never been able to ascertain, that during the cultural revolution in China, Madame Mao very much disapproved of the fact that red lights meant “stop” because red is, of course, the color of progress. It ought to mean “to go forward” with everything behind it, but needless to say her thoughts on the subject were never implemented because [laughs] if one day red light means “stop” and the next day red light means “go,” there might be a few problems. This, by the way, is a way of showing the fact that everything which appears in a semiotic system is conventional, right? I mean, there is an emptying out of positive meaning in the very awareness that, after all, the red light could mean “go”–I’m about to go on and give more examples. It’s conventional. Whatever the convention is within a system of differences, that’s what makes the sign intelligible.

好的。再举几个例子：街门上方的红灯。嗯，它的意思不是“停”。而是“进去”、“进来”，对吧？当然，它与街门上方的白灯存在符号学上的关联，白灯的意思是“这是我家；如果你愿意，可以按门铃，但我更希望你待在外面”。这盏灯很可能是为了防止窃贼进入而亮的，所以意思是“停”，对吧？换句话说，在这个符号学体系中，红灯是可以理解的。现在说说礼堂门上的灯——当然，我们刚才已经注意到那个灯了，它并不是一个好例子。我希望它上面写的不是“出口”，但它确实写的是“出口”，因为这有点削弱了我的论点，但很多礼堂门上都挂着红灯。显然，它的意思不是像街门上的红灯那样的“进来”。它的意思是“出去”，对吧？ “这是出口，这是你离开这里的路”，而不是“这是你进来的路”。红灯有很多种含义，既不是“停”，也不是“走”，但我们目前似乎只局限于红灯与交通或交通中断相关的那些情况。在每一种新的系统中，你都会发现，它总是根据它所不代表的含义而获得新的含义。

All right. Just some other examples: a red light over a street door. Well, that doesn’t mean “stop.” That means “go in,” “come in,” right? And of course it exists in a semiotic relationship to a white light over a street door which means “this is my house; if you wish you can ring the bell but I’d just as soon you stayed out.” This light is probably on to keep burglars away and so: “stop,” right? The red light is intelligible, in other words, within that semiotic system. Now over an auditorium door–and of course we’ve already been gazing at that light back there, and it’s not a good example. I wish it didn’t say “exit,” but it does say “exit,” because that kind of weakens my point, but over many auditorium doors a red light just hangs there. Obviously, it doesn’t mean “come in” in the sense of the red light over a street door. It means “go out,” right? “This is the way out. This is the way you get out of here,” not “This is the way you get in here.” There are a lot of ways in which a red light means neither “stop” nor “go,” but we are sort of confining ourselves so far to the ways in which a red light has something to do with locomotion or the lack thereof. In each new system, you can see it takes on a new meaning always with respect to whatever it is not.

好的，我们可以继续。在情人节彩灯上，它表示“不要停，继续走”。换句话说，它的功能在于否定自身在另一个符号系统中的含义，在这个例子中，这个符号系统是交通信号灯。在救护车或警车上——诚然，如今很多这类车辆的警示灯都是蓝色的，但我们假设，按照传统，它们仍然是红色的——它们的意思是“让开”或“停车”，对吧？换句话说，它们可能与交通信号灯的符号学意义存在某种遥远的联系，这或许就是救护车和警车选择红色警示灯的原因：因为红色警示灯会让人联想到“停车”。但在这个例子中，同样重要的“让开”概念使“停车”的含义变得复杂，因为“让开”并不一定意味着停车，而是加速朝另一个方向行驶。

Well, we can continue. On a light-up valentine it means “don’t stop, go.” It has the function, in other words, of negating its own meaning in another semiotic system, in this case the semiotic system of the stoplight. On an ambulance or a police car–admittedly, many of these lights are blue these days but let’s suppose that, tradition prevailing, that they are still red–they mean “get out of the way” or “stop,” right? In other words, they probably bear a distant relation to the semiotics of the stoplight, and that’s probably why red was chosen for ambulances and police cars: because they put into your head the notion of “stop.” But it’s a notion that’s complicated in this case by the equally imperative notion “get out of the way,” which doesn’t at all necessarily entail stopping but rather accelerating in a different direction.

所有这些都让情况变得有些复杂，但同时，我认为你也能看到这些符号系统之间存在联系。就颜色而言，这是一个比较薄弱的系统。以救护车和警车为例，问题更多在于亮度。正如我所说，人们往往会选择红色，但如果实验室实验表明，某种特定的蓝色气体比红色更容易侵入你的意识，那么选择红色作为颜色的随意性就不复存在了。正如我所说，这种不稳定性在交通信号灯的符号学中是绝对不存在的，因为交通信号灯的问题不在于颜色的亮度——尽管你也知道，这方面已经做过实验——而在于人们坚持认为颜色就是它本身。

All of that somewhat complicates the picture, but at the same time, I think you can see that there is a connection between those semiotic systems. It’s a weak system in terms of color. In the case of the ambulance and police car, it’s more a question of brightness. As I say, red tends to be chosen, but then if you get lab experiments showing that that particular color of gas blue is somehow or another sort of more invasive of your consciousness than red is, then you move away from the arbitrariness of the choice of red as a color. As I say, there’s a certain instability which could never apply in the semiotics of the stoplight because there it’s not so much a question of the brightness of the color–although that has been experimented with, as you know–but rather the insistence that the color is just that color.

最后——某种程度上，这或许是最有趣的地方，因为它迫使我们展现符号关系的复杂性：比如，回到基督教节日，圣诞树上的一盏红灯。我们首先想到的可能是：哦，啊哈，这没有任何意义，对吧？讨论红灯、绿灯、黄灯、白灯或蓝灯——或者圣诞树上的其他颜色——之间的负面关系毫无意义，因为它们都具有相同的价值。它们都很明亮，都很喜庆，都在说“圣诞快乐”，等等等等。那么，我们该如何理解它们呢？这里，一盏红灯似乎并不符合这种任意性和差异性的概念。

Then finally–and here is where, in a way, this is perhaps the most interesting thing because it forces us to show the complexity, to see the complexity, of semiotic relationships: a red light, just to return to the Christian holiday, a red light on a Christmas tree. Now our first thought is, Oh, aha, that has no meaning, right? It’s no use talking about the negative relationship between a red light and a green light and a yellow, white, or blue one–whatever the other colors on the Christmas tree are–because they all have the same value. They’re all bright, they’re all cheerful, they all say “Merry Christmas,” etc., etc., etc. So what are you supposed to do with that? Here you’ve got a red light which doesn’t seem to enter into this sense of the arbitrary and differential.

那是因为在符号系统中，它实际上并不是一个基本的构成单元，对吧？“明亮的灯光”才是基本的构成单元，而这些明亮灯光的种类——这关乎美学——却讽刺地被支配我们理解它们的共同能指“明亮的灯光”所中和——在这个例子中，它尤其指圣诞树上或装饰着其他具有类似价值的饰品。一旦你理解了这一点，一旦你理解了“圣诞树”的价值，而不是“红灯”（“红灯”或许是某些圣诞树的一部分），那么你就会发现你又回到了一个符号系统，而且是一个非常显而易见的系统，因为圣诞树不是烛台，也不是宽扎节的蜡烛。换句话说，圣诞树是一个符号，只有在特定的文化语境下才能被理解。我们当然会想，哦，我们知道那是什么，当然，我们可能确实知道，但我们误以为这就是理解它作为符号的关键，因为完全可以想象这样一种情况：有人可能不知道它是什么，这迫使我们即便熟悉它，也不得不问自己：“那么，它到底是什么？我们怎么知道它是什么？” 然后我们再次意识到，只有当我们理解了——在这种情况下，或许最好说是理解了——它出现的文化体系（被理解为符号过程）时，我们才能知道它是什么。

Well, that’s because it’s actually not a gross constituent unit in a semiotic system, right? “Bright lights” is the gross constituent unit and the variety of those bright lights, which is a matter of aesthetics, is, ironically enough, neutralized by the common signifier governing our understanding of them, which is “bright lights”–in this case, particularly on a tree or festooning another ornament that has some sort of comparable value. Once you get that, once you get the value, “Christmas tree,” as opposed to “red lights,” “red lights” being perhaps a part of some Christmas trees, then you see that you’re back in a semiotic system and a very obvious one, because a Christmas tree is a not-menorah, not-Kwanzaa candles. A Christmas tree, in other words, is a sign that can only be understood intelligibly in terms of a certain cultural understanding. We think of course, oh, we know what that is, and of course probably we do, but we’re misled in supposing that that’s the key to the understanding of it as a sign, because it’s very possible to imagine a circumstance in which someone wouldn’t know what it was, forcing us despite its familiarity to ask ourselves, “Well, what is it and how do we know what it is?” Then we realize once again that we can only know what it is if we come to understand–in this case, probably, it’s best to say a cultural system, understood as a semiosis, within which it appears.

所以，这最后一个版本的红灯引入了一些有趣的复杂情况，但我认为这些情况不应该让我们感到困惑。我认为它们实际上应该让我们更深入地了解我们如何将周围和我们自身内部的事物组织理解为符号系统。我们知道，我们已经从海德格尔和诠释学传统中了解到，我们把它们当作某种东西来认识，但问题在于我们如何认识它们。也就是说，我们并非肯定地认识它们。我的意思是，海德格尔提出了一个有趣的观点，即我们会自发地识别某些事物。但这对于符号学来说可能是一个危险点，因为它会让我们认为或假设我们肯定地认识事物——换句话说，我们并没有思考“我知道这是一个出口标志，我不知道它是一个带有红色标记的白色物体，但我知道它是一个出口标志”；但根据索绪尔的论证，如果我不知道它并非它所不是的所有事物，我就无法知道这一点。如果它代表所有它不是什么的事物，或者如果它与所有它以某种方式不是什么的事物完全相同，那么我将陷入非常困境，因为我将没有任何途径去具体地了解它。正因为我需要具体地了解它，才使得我需要从否定的角度去了解它。换句话说，我们现在从这个角度了解了我们如何感知事物的两件事，将它们结合起来非常有用：一是我们总是先于事物本身——在我们“仅仅拥有它们”之前——但同时，认为我们先于事物了解它们就意味着我们肯定地了解它们是误导性的；我们先于事物了解它们，但我们也否定地了解它们，否定其他事物。

So this last version of the red light introduces interesting complications which I don’t think should confuse us. I think they should actually show us a little bit more about how we can understand the organization of the things around us and within us as systems of signs. We know that we’ve already learned from Heidegger and the hermeneutic tradition that we know them as something, but it remained to show how we know them. That is to say, we don’t know them positively. I mean, Heidegger raises the interesting fact that we spontaneously recognize something. But that’s one of the things which could be dangerous for semiotics because it would make us think or assume that we know things positively–without thinking, in other words, “I know that that’s an exit sign, I don’t know that it’s a white thing with red marks on it, but I know that it’s an exit sign”; but I can’t know that, the Saussurian argument goes, without knowing that it is not all the things that it’s not. If it were all the things that it’s not, or if it were identical to all the things that somehow or another it’s not, then I would be in a very difficult situation because I wouldn’t have any means of knowing it in particular. The very fact that I need to know it in particular is what makes me need to know it negatively. In other words, we now know two things about how we perceive things from the standpoint of this subject matter, and it’s very useful to put them together, the fact that we always know things first–before we “just have them there before us”– but at the same time the fact that it’s misleading to think that our knowing them first means that we know them positively; we know them first but we also know them negatively, in negation of other things.

第五章 共时性与历时性

Chapter 5. Synchrony and Diachrony

好的。那么，让我再回到符号系统如何被理解这个话题上来，因为在这样的课程中，我们经常会遇到这样的情况：我们似乎在说，“哦，我们什么都不知道”，或者“我们不知道自己知道什么”，或者“我们怎么知道自己知道什么？”也许我们是在回避这类反问句，但实际上并非如此。我们今天讨论的是我们如何认知事物。对吧？如果我们认真对待符号学，它会为我们提供一种相当精密的方法来理解我们究竟是如何认知事物的，但它坚持认为，我们之所以认知事物，是因为它们的约定俗成性：也就是说，因为它们是存在于约定俗成体系中的约定俗成，只要我们能够识别它们——事物、符号——的存在，因为如果我们思考一个事物，我们就是在符号学中将这个事物视为一个符号。如果我们不知道这一点，如果我们无法识别它在某个系统中的存在——或者更确切地说，如果我们无法思考它属于哪个系统——那就等同于说我们真的不知道它是什么。我认为，我们思考得越多，就越会意识到，只有当我们知道它所属的系统时，我们才能真正了解它是什么，也就是说，只有当我们知道所有与它相关但又不属于它的事物时，我们才能真正了解它。对吧？

Okay. So let me just return once again to the way in which sign systems are intelligible because lots of- there are going to be lots of moments in a course like this in which what we seem to be saying is that, “Oh, we can’t know anything,” or “We don’t know what we know,” or “How do we know what we know?” Maybe we’re skirting rhetorical questions of that kind, but we’re really not. What we’re talking about today is how we do know things. Right? If we take semiotics seriously, it gives us a rather sophisticated means of understanding precisely how we know things, but it insists that we know things because of their conventional nature: that is to say, because they are conventions existing within a system of conventions insofar as we recognize them–things, signs–as existing, because if we’re thinking about a thing, we’re thinking about that thing as a sign in semiotics. If we don’t know that, if we don’t recognize its existence in a system–if we can’t think what system it belongs to, perhaps to put it in a better way–that’s tantamount to saying we really don’t know what it is. I think the more we think about it, the more we realize that we only know what it is if we know the system that it belongs to, which is to say, all of the things related to it which it is not. Right?

好的。所以，符号系统的可理解性在于它们的约定俗成性。这就是为什么没人能说：“哦，我不喜欢红灯是红色的。这在象征意义上是错误的。我们把红灯改成​​‘通行’的符号吧。” 而现在，随着生态运动的兴起，把绿灯改成“停止”的符号也很难，而且无论如何都会引发各种各样的问题。[笑] 对吧？但与此同时，你也看到了，我们不能把个人意志强加于约定俗成的系统之上，然后指望它发生改变。一个看似例外的情况是，有时个人确实可以通过运用自身的影响力和声望来改变我们谈论事物的方式。但这只是一个看似例外的情况。想想杰西·杰克逊是如何几乎凭借一己之力说服我们使用“非裔美国人”这个表达方式的，尽管这是一个冗长、多音节的表达，你可能会觉得它因为发音难而本能地被排斥，但事实并非如此。他成功说服了我们所有人说“非裔美国人”。你会对自己说：“啊哈！这就是一个例子，有人抓住了语言的衣领，以个人意志改变它，用个人意志对抗语言的传统规范。”

Okay. So the intelligibility of sign systems is their conventionality. That’s why it’s impossible for anybody to come along and say, “Oh, I don’t like the fact that the red light is red. It’s symbolically the wrong move. Let’s make the red light the symbol of ‘go.’” And now with the ecological movement it would be very difficult to make the green light the symbol of “stop,” and in any case all sorts of complications would arise. [laughs] Right? But in the meantime you see that we can’t mess with conventional systems by imposing the individuality of our will on them and expecting anything to change. A seeming exception is the fact that sometimes individuals can, through the exertion of their influence and prestige, actually change the way we speak about things. This is a seeming exception. Think about the way Jesse Jackson almost single-handedly convinced us that we should use the expression “African American” even though it’s a cumbersome, polysyllabic expression which you would think somehow or another would be intuitively rejected because it’s so hard to say, but it worked. He convinced us all to say “African American.” You say to yourself, “Ah ha! There is an example of somebody taking language by the scruff of the neck and changing it as an individual, exerting an individual will over against the conventional nature of language.”

符号学家对此的回答是，语言的改变绝不可能仅仅出于能动性或意志力，它必须得到默许。你需要使用语言惯例的社群默许这种用法的改变。记住，语言是共时存在的：它只存在于某个瞬间，存在于同时性的瞬间。我们研究语言是历时性的——也就是说，我们研究它的历史，研究它在时间中的演变。根据符号学家的观点——这里又与俄国形式主义者有所关联——这种演变并非研究语言如何从外部发生变化——也就是说，并非研究例如某个人如何站出来坚持改变某个符号；而是一系列共时性的切面。语言每时每刻都在变化，但如果我们想要理解语言，就必须尊重它的同时性。在这种情况下，我们将其理解为一系列横截面，而不是某种随时间自然发生的有机变化。在每个横截面上，人们要么愿意以某种方式使用某个符号，要么不愿意。关键在于：如果他们不愿意，符号的使用就无法奏效，这印证了个人行为本身无法改变任何事物的观点。

The semiotician’s answer to this is it never could have happened simply as an act of agency, as an act of will. It had to be acquiesced in. You needed the community that makes use of linguistic conventions to acquiesce in a change of use. Remember, language exists synchronically: it only exists in a moment, in a moment of simultaneity. We study language diachronically–that is to say, we study its history. We study its unfolding in time. Now this unfolding is not, according to the semioticians–and here’s another link with the Russian formalists–is not a question of studying the way in which language is changed from without–that is to say, studying the way in which, for example, an individual can rise up and insist on changing one of the signs; but rather a sequence of synchronic cross-sections. From moment to moment, language changes, but if we’re to understand it as language we have to honor its simultaneity. In that case, we understand it as a sequence of cross-sections rather than something that somehow organically changes through time. At each cross-section, people are either willing to use a certain sign in a certain way or they’re not. That’s the crucial thing: if they’re not willing, the use of the sign doesn’t work, which confirms the idea that nothing can be changed simply by individual agency in and of itself.

好的。我需要再谈谈共时性和历时性。下次我会讲，以后的几节课可能也会讲，因为我们会一直用到这些概念。我们会继续研究存在于空间中的事物（无论虚拟与否）以及在时间中展开的事物，以及它们彼此之间的关系，以此来理解这些塑造了后来许多文学理论的基本原则。谢谢。

All right. I need to come back to synchrony and diachrony. I’ll do so next time and probably in subsequent lectures because we’re going to keep using these coordinates. We’re going to keep using the things that exist in space, virtual or not, and the things that unfold in time in their relationship with each other as we continue to try to understand these basic principles which shape so much of subsequent literary theory. Thank you.

第九讲——语言学与文学

Lecture 9 - Linguistics and Literature

第一章 共时性与历时性

Chapter 1. Synchrony and Diachrony

保罗·弗莱教授：上次我讲课的时候，我误以为——我真应该养成看教学大纲的习惯——你们周四的课只读索绪尔。结果，我周末瞥了一眼教学大纲，发现你们还要读列维-斯特劳斯，所以我们今天得讲一些内容了。我想我们能做到。我想把对结构主义的批判留到周四课的开头，因为这能很好地引出我们接下来要讨论的德里达。我已经承诺过，对结构主义的批判其实就是解构。我希望周四能证明这一点；但我确实想先从两三个方面展开对结构主义的批判，所以我希望今天能尽快推进。

Professor Paul Fry: Last time I lectured under the illusion that–I really should get in the habit of looking at the syllabus–that all you had been assigned for Thursday’s lecture was the Saussure. Lo and behold, I did take a glance at the syllabus over the weekend and realized that you’d also been assigned the Levi-Strauss, so we have a little bit of ground to cover today. I think we can do it. I think I want to reserve something like a critique of structuralism for the beginning of Thursday’s lecture, because it segues very nicely into what we’ll have to say about Derrida. I already promised that somehow or another the critique of structuralism just was deconstruction. I hope to be able to demonstrate that on Thursday; but I do want to get up to the point of launching a critique of structuralism on two or three grounds, and so I hope to be able to move along fairly quickly today.

还有一个被忽略的内容，即便考虑到周四的讨论仅限于索绪尔，那就是对共时性和历时性之间关系的充分阐述，以及这一概念的关键重要性——不仅对符号学，而且对其在结构主义中的后续发展，以及与俄国形式主义者的关系而言，都至关重要。因为你们应该记得，在讨论功能时，那些致力于思考文学史和文学史学问题的形式主义者，非常重视这样一个观点：特定文本中的功能可以有两种不同的理解方式。一种是共时功能，即该功能与文本中所有其他功能之间的关系——换句话说，将其视为文本的一个方面；另一种是同一功能的自发功能，即该功能在文学史中持续存在和反复出现的方式，有时是主导性的，有时是潜在的或隐蔽的，但总是以某种形式存在。

Now another thing that got left out, even given the proviso that it was only about Saussure on Thursday, was an adequate account of the relationship between synchrony and diachrony and the pivotal importance of this concept, not only for semiotics but for its aftermath in structuralism, and also for its relation to the Russian formalists; because you remember that in talking about function, the formalists who undertook to think about literary history and the problems of literary historiography were very much engaged in the notion that a function in a given text could be understood in two different ways. There was the syn-function, which was the relationship between that function and all of the other functions in the text–in other words, viewed as an aspect of that text, but there was also of the same function its auto-function, which is the way in which it persists and recurs throughout the history of literature sometimes as the dominant, sometimes latent or recessive, but always in one form or another there.

在索绪尔的语言学中，共时性和历时性之间的关系也大致相同。要全面考察语言，就必须从共时性的角度考察它在特定时刻的发展。也就是说，如果你同时考虑语言的历史演变，就不能将其视为一个系统。你会注意到，雅各布森在对符号系统进行共时性分析时引入了时间因素，他认为必须同时考虑古老特征和创新特征，但只要从共时性的角度解读或分析，这些特征就仅仅被标记为古老或创新，而不会被理解为随时间变化。但与此同时，一个系统确实会随着时间而变化。符号系统、语言、文学史、诗学史——无论是什么，都会随着时间而变化，而要分析这种随时间的变化，就必须从历时性的角度来思考。

Now in Saussurian linguistics, the relationship between synchrony and diachrony is very much the same. To consider language in toto is to consider it at a given moment synchronically. That is to say, you don’t think of language as a system if at the same time you’re thinking of it unfolding historically. Jakobson, you will notice, introduces an element of time into the synchronic analysis of a semiotic system by saying that you’ve got to take account both of archaic and innovative features, but nevertheless they are simply flagged as archaic or innovative and not understood as changing in time as long as they are read or analyzed synchronically. But at the same token, a system does change through time. A semiotic system, language, the history of literature, the history of poetics–whatever it might be, changes through time, and to analyze that change through time you think of it diachronically.

索绪尔认为，从共时角度来看，某个事物（比如一个符号系统）各部分之间的关​​系并非必然存在，它们可能存在其他多种关系，但它们却是固定的。也就是说，它们就是它们现在的样子，不可能是别的样子。然而，随着时间的推移，如果你研究的是一个符号系统、语言或其他任何事物，变化就会发生，而且是必然的。当你回顾过去时，它确实发生了（笑），所以变化在某种意义上是决定性的。但与此同时，它又不是规律性的。顺便一提，这挑战了传统语言学中的某些观点，例如你们可能都知道的：元音大移位。结构主义的语言观认为，所谓的大元音移位——即在中世纪到近代早期某个神秘时期内，所有元音音位都上升了一个音级——表面上看似规律，实则是一种历时现象，无法用规律性来解释。因此，共时与历时之间的关系就是如此。

Now Saussure argues that the relationship among the parts of something viewed synchronically–a semiotic system, let’s say–are not necessary in the sense that they might be any number of other relationships, but they are nevertheless fixed. That is to say, they are what’s there and they can’t be other than what they are, whereas through time, if you’re studying a semiotic system or studying language or whatever it might be, change takes place and it’s necessary. You’re looking back on it and it simply did happen, [laughs] so change is determinant in some sense. But at the same time, it’s not regular. This, by the way, is a challenge to certain ideas in traditional linguistics like, for example, the one you probably all know: the great vowel shift. A structuralist’s view of language has to argue that the great vowel shift, in which every vowel sound goes up a notch in some mysterious period between the medieval and the early modern, that this only has the appearance of regularity but that it is actually a diachronic phenomenon that can’t be understood in terms of regularity. So the relationship between synchronic and diachronic is of that kind.

现在，当你在阅读中看到人们谈论如何从现有数据中推断出大量材料——比如说语言系统或其他符号系统——时，情况就变得稍微复杂一些了：换句话说，我如何从一个句子（parole）中推断出语言（langue）——实际上，我隐瞒了索绪尔使用了第三个术语“语言”（langage）来谈论所有句子的总和，但我们暂且不讨论这一点——语言是如何从“parole”中推断出来的。换句话说，语言被视为存在于空间中的某种东西，也就是说——或者如列维-斯特劳斯所说，是“可逆时间”，这意味着你可以在其中前后穿梭，但时间的展开并非其关键所在。所以，在空间层面，言语（parole）是在时间层面展开的，而言语，因为它具有时间性——因为我们每个人的任何言语在某种意义上都是历史性的（笑），因为句子的开头比结尾在历史上更早——正因如此，历时性与言语、句子或话语的展开之间存在着一种平行关系，尽管这种关系有时确实令人困惑。我们并不想把句子当作历时性的来谈论，但同时，它确实存在于那个事物以组合方式在时间中展开的水平轴上。

Now matters are complicated a little bit on those occasions in your reading when people are talking about the way in which a mass of material–a system of language or other semiotic system, let’s say–is inferred from existing data: in other words, the way in which I infer language, langue, from a sentence, parole–I’m actually concealing from you that in fact Saussure uses a third term, langage, to talk about the sum of all sentences, but we won’t get into that–the way in which language is inferred from parole. Now language, in other words, is viewed as something in space, that is to say–or as Levi-Strauss calls it, “revertible time,” meaning you can go backward and forward within it, but the temporal unfolding is not the important thing about it. So in space, whereas parole, speech, unfolds in time so that parole, because it is temporal–because any speech any of us makes is in a certain sense historical, [laughs> because the beginning of the sentence is earlier in history than the end of the sentence–for that reason, there’s a relationship between diachrony and the unfolding of parole, or of a sentence or of an utterance which is parallel, though at the same time admittedly confusing. One doesn’t really want to talk about a sentence as diachronic, but at the same time it does exist on that horizontal axis in which things in a combinatory way unfold in time.

第二章 结构主义的兴起

Chapter 2. The Emergence of Structuralism

好了。那么，关于共时性和历时性就说到这里吧，这是我们无法回避的。从某种意义上说，它是结构主义的核心，但我认为我在上一讲的结尾并没有充分阐述这一点。现在来说说结构主义。20世纪60年代，结构主义散发着一种令人难以置信的光环。它从法国席卷美国，以一种令人震惊、惊叹并改变人们生活的方式席卷而来。像康德这样的人在阅读休谟的著作时，仿佛从教条的沉睡中醒来，或者至少，他们在接触结构主义时感觉自己正在经历这样的觉醒。我认为，这发生在我读哈佛研究生的时候，当时完全没有人关注结构主义。在耶鲁、约翰·霍普金斯和康奈尔，人们都在关注它，但在哈佛，一位聪明的本科生引领我走进了结构主义的世界，他似乎是剑桥唯一一个（笑）了解结构主义的人。他对结构主义了如指掌，并尽其所能地让我迅速跟上进度；但对于全国学术界乃至学术界以外的人们来说，结构主义都是一种具有变革意义的思想现象。当然，它也以各种方式，引领了此后理论领域的大部分发展。

All right. So much then for synchrony and diachrony, something we can’t get away from. It’s in a way the central fact of structuralism but which I don’t think I did adequate justice to at the end of the last lecture. Now structuralism. There was an incredible aura about structuralism in the 1960s. It crashed on the shores of the United States coming in from France in a way that stunned, amazed, and transformed people’s lives. People like Kant reading Hume woke up from their dogmatic slumbers or, at least, that they felt that that’s what they were doing when encountering structuralism. I think to me it happened when I was a graduate student at Harvard and absolutely nobody else was paying any attention to it at all. At Yale, Johns Hopkins, and Cornell people were paying attention to it, but at Harvard I was initiated to structuralism by a bright undergraduate who seemed to be the only [laughs] person in Cambridge who knew anything about structuralism. Boy, did he know about structuralism, and he got me up to speed as quickly as he could; but it was a phenomenon that was transformative intellectually for people in the academic, and beyond the academic, world all over the country. Of course it led, in all sorts of ways, to most of what’s been going on in theory ever since.

令人惊叹的是，作为法国文学理论领域蓬勃发展且无可争议的贡献，结构主义仅仅持续了两年，因为在1966年的一次著名会议上，雅克·德里达（我们将在周四阅读他的著作）彻底颠覆了它。我稍后会再谈到这一点。但同时，说它仅仅持续了两年也并不公平。结构主义的持久贡献，既得益于符号学，也源于其自身独特的视角，至今仍能在整个文学理论领域感受到。具体的贡献并非全部集中在1964年第一批结构主义文本被翻译成英文到1966年巴尔的摩会议召开这段时期，但这些持久的具体贡献同样极其重要。罗兰·巴特有一本精彩的著作，名为《论拉辛》。如果你对法国新古典主义戏剧感兴趣，并且还没有读过这本书，那么你很难想象还有什么比它更令人振奋的著作。列维-斯特劳斯和雅各布森合著了一篇关于波德莱尔的文章，题为《猫》（Les Chats），这是一篇杰出的作品，也是当时学院派诸多研究的典范。人类学家埃德蒙·利奇曾对《圣经·创世记》进行结构主义分析。事实上，他选择研究《创世记》并非偶然，我稍后会解释这一点。

The amazing thing about it is that as a flourishing and undisputed French contribution to literary theory, it lasted two years because in 1966 at a famous conference, Jacques Derrida, whom we’ll be reading on Thursday, blew it out of the water. I’ll come back to that. At the same time, to say that it really only lasted two years simply isn’t fair. The lasting contribution of structuralism as it’s indebted to semiotics, but on its own terms as well, is something one still feels and senses throughout literary theory. The concrete contributions, not all between 1964 when the first structuralist texts were translated in this country and 1966 when the conference in Baltimore took place, but the lasting concrete contributions are also terribly important. There’s a wonderful book called On Racine by Roland Barthes. Those of you interested in French neoclassical theater cannot imagine, if you haven’t read it already, reading a more bracing book. There is an essay on Baudelaire, “Les Chats,” or “The Cats,” written conjointly by Levi-Strauss and Jakobson, an extraordinary performance which was the model of a good deal else that was done in the academy during that period. The anthropologist Edmund Leach wrote a structuralist analysis of Genesis in the Bible. Indeed, it’s no accident that he writes about Genesis, as I will indicate in a minute.

随后，除了上述所有贡献之外，结构主义者最持久、最丰富的贡献或许要数我们今天所知的叙事学领域了。几周后，我们将结合弗洛伊德的理论来探讨彼得·布鲁克斯的著作，届时会深入研究叙事学。但在此之前，叙事学的关键文本依然是罗兰·巴特的长篇论文《叙事的结构分析》。在这篇论文中，他将詹姆斯·邦德系列小说视为一个二元对立系统，并运用这种二元分析方法揭示了小说深层的结构；茨维坦·托多罗夫的重要著作，其中《十日谈的语法》尤为关键；此外，还有热拉尔·热奈特的大量著作，这些著作收录于他名为《形象》的系列丛书中。下周二，我们将阅读保罗·德曼的著作，其中也多次引用了热奈特的观点。所有这些工作以及叙事理论、叙事学中的许多其他工作，都直接得益于结构主义思想，或者实际上是结构主义思想的一个方面。

Then subsequently, and in addition to all of that, probably the most lasting and rich contributions of the structuralists were in the field that we know as narratology. We’ll be taking a look at that when we read Peter Brooks’ text in conjunction with Freud a couple of weeks from now, but in the meantime the key texts in narratology are, again, by Roland Barthes in a long, long essay called “The Structural Analysis of Narrative” in which he approaches a James Bond novel as a system of binary pairs and unpacks a deep structure in the novel as a result of this binary analysis; important books by Tzvetan Todorov, crucial among them The Grammar of The Decameron; and then a good deal of work published in a series of books called Figures by Gérard Genette, whom you will find quoted repeatedly in the work of Paul de Man that you’ll be reading for next Tuesday. All of this work and a great deal else in the theory of narrative, narratology, is directly indebted to, or is actually an aspect of, structuralist thought.

第三章 形式主义与符号学的关系

Chapter 3. The Relationship Between Formalism and Semiotics

我之前承诺过要谈谈形式主义和符号学之间的关系，尤其是在列维-斯特劳斯，特别是雅各布森等人的著作中，这种关系是如何被阐释的。正如你从雅各布森的分析中看到的，结构主义从形式主义中汲取了功能的概念。雅各布森本人最初当然是俄国形式主义学派的成员。他后来移民到布拉格，在那里他加入了一个自称为结构主义者的圈子，之后又从那里前往巴黎，最终定居美国。因此，雅各布森无疑是一位真正意义上融合了两种思想体系的人物，他既是形式主义者，又成为了结构主义者。我们可以在他的作品中看到这两种思想的融合。

Now I promised that I would talk a little bit about the relationship between formalism and semiotics as it clarifies itself in the work of writers like Levi-Strauss and, in particular, Jakobson. Structuralism takes from formalism, as you can see from Jakobson’s analysis, the idea of function. Jakobson is originally, of course, himself a member of the school of Russian formalists. He eventually immigrates to Prague, where he is in a circle of people who are already calling themselves structuralists, and moves from there to Paris and then to the United States. So Jakobson, of course, is the one figure who definitely harkens back to both worlds, having been a formalist and having become a structuralist. One can see the amalgam of these two sets of ideas in his work.

因此，从形式主义中，我们可以得到功能的概念，以及共时功能和自功能之间的关系，进而得到共时性和历时性之间的关系。从符号学中，我们可以得到否定性知识的概念——也就是说，例如在列维-斯特劳斯对俄狄浦斯神话的分析中，不存在所谓的“真实版本”，不存在所谓的“原始版本”，也不存在某种“正统版本”，其他一切都只是它的一个版本。你所知道的，仅仅是它与你所知道的其他事物之间的区别——这是符号学的基本前提之一，同时也是结构主义的基本前提，因为正是在这里，结构主义可以被理解为一个独立的实体。与形式主义不同，结构主义对对象，对对象的本质，有着一种全新的追求。

From formalism then, you get the idea of function and the relationship between syn-function and auto-function, which becomes the relationship between synchrony and diachrony. From semiotics you get the idea of negative knowledge–that is to say, in Levi-Strauss’ analysis of the Oedipus myth, for example, the notion that there is no true version, there’s no originary version, and there’s no sort of positive version of the myth of which everything else is a version. You simply know what you know as it is differentiated from the other things that you know–one of the essential premises of semiotics, which is essential, at the same time, in structuralism, because here’s where structuralism can be understood as an entity in itself. Unlike formalism, structuralism has an ambition with respect to the object, to the nature of the object, which is quite new.

我认为，要概括这一点，最好的方法是引用罗兰·巴特在《结构主义活动》一文中，第871页右栏下方的一句格言。巴特说：“结构主义者获取现实，将其分解，然后重新组合……” 正是在这里，我们可以看到结构主义和形式主义的根本区别。形式主义获取对象，但并不对其进行分解。它视对象如实存在；它只是将其分解为各自的功能，动态地展现这些功能之间的关系，以及它们作为支配与从属系统的运作方式，所有这些都被理解为事物被制造的方式，被组合的方式——但除此之外，它不考虑任何其他因素。果戈理的《外套》、塞万提斯的《堂吉诃德》、斯特恩的《项狄传》：这些都是实物，不存在通过对个别文本的评论而创造出虚拟对象（例如“小说”）的问题。然而，从某种意义上说，正如你从列维-斯特劳斯对俄狄浦斯神话的分析中再次看到的那样，结构主义正在做的正是如此。

I think that the best way to epitomize that is to turn to an aphorism of Roland Barthes’ in the essay “The Structuralist Activity,” on page 871 toward the bottom of the right-hand column, where Barthes says, “Structural man takes the real, decomposes it, then recomposes it…” This is the moment in which you can see the radical difference between what structuralism is doing and what formalism is doing. Formalism takes the object and it doesn’t decompose it. It sees the object as it is; it just breaks it down into its respective functions, showing them dynamically in relationship with each other and as a system of dominance and subordination, all of it understood as the way in which something is made, the way in which it is put together–but there’s no question of anything other than the object. Gogol’s “Overcoat,” Cervantes’Don Quixote, Sterne’s Tristam Shandy: these are objects, and there’s no question of somehow or another creating a virtual object, for example “the novel,” out of one’s remarks about individual texts. In a way, though, that’s what, as you can see again from Levi-Strauss’ analysis of the Oedipus myth, structuralism is doing.

正如巴特所说，“结构主义者获取现实，将其分解，然后重组……”他的意思是，你选取一堆变体或版本，选取一堆数据——不一定是所有数据，而是与任何给定想法或概念相关的具有代表性的数据——然后，你就会问，而这正是他引入粗略构成单元概念的地方：“所有这些数据的基本构成单元是什么？哦，对了。我明白了，我们可以把它们归纳成一个模式。”我们稍后会稍微探讨一下。“是的，我明白了。事实上，当我整理从所有属于这个范畴的个体实体或版本中收集到的数据时，我就可以开始观察到一种虚拟对象。”这并非是对任何特定对象的重组，而是对一种从分析中开始浮现的虚拟对象的重组：在列维-斯特劳斯的文本中，这种虚拟对象就是俄狄浦斯神话的意义。这就是结构主义分析通过整理、分析和分类从所有可用的俄狄浦斯神话版本中获取的数据而得到的虚拟对象。因此，结构主义的分解并非仅仅为了了解事物的运作方式（例如拆解发动机的零件），而是为了将这些零件用于分析一个整体材料，从而使所有这些零件能够重新组合成一个新的虚拟对象。这就是巴特所说的“结构主义活动”的本质。

As Barthes says, “Structural man takes the real, decomposes it, then recomposes it…” What he means by that is that you take a bunch of variants or versions, you take a bunch of data–not necessarily all the data, but a representative amount of the data relevant to any given idea or concept–and then you say, and this is where he gets into the idea of gross constituent units: “What are the basic constituent units of all of these items of data? Oh, yeah. I see we can put them into a pattern.” We’ll work on this a little bit in a minute. “Yeah, I see how this is working. As a matter of fact, there is a kind of virtual object that I can begin to observe as I organize the data that I garner from all the individual entities or versions that fall under this umbrella.” That’s the recomposition not of any particular object, but of a kind of virtual object which begins to emerge from one’s analysis: in the case of Levi-Strauss’ text, the meaning of the Oedipus myth. That’s the virtual object that structuralist analysis arrives at by arranging, analyzing and classifying the data that it can get from all of the available versions of the Oedipus myth. So structuralism decomposes but not just for the sake of seeing how something works, like taking apart the parts of an engine, but rather in order to lend the parts to an analysis of a body of materials that makes it possible to recompose all of those parts in a new virtual object. That’s what’s going on in what Barthes calls “the structuralist activity.”

第四章 列维-斯特劳斯与俄狄浦斯神话的意义

Chapter 4. Levi-Strauss and the Meaning of the Oedipus Myth

那么，我们快速看一下列维-斯特劳斯关于俄狄浦斯神话的图表（如果你愿意这么称呼它的话），它在你课本的第864页，然后简单介绍一下。他引用了很多版本。我们暂且不讨论具体有多少个版本。顺便说一句，如果他研究的是北美印第安神话，或者像他作为人类学家研究的那种神话的各种版本，他引用的版本数量肯定会更多，但他确实引用了一些版本——其中一个是弗洛伊德的版本，一个是索福克勒斯的版本，除此之外还有其他一些版本。他说：“嗯，当你观察这些不同的版本时（他指着黑板上的图表），你会发现一些事情基本上都在发生，而且它们可以归入某些特定的类别。我们可以把它们分成几列——也就是说，根据它们共同的主题来分类，但我们也可以把这些列排列成行，这样我们就可以分析它们之间的关联。”例如，有一组事件、偶然事件，或者说意外事故等等，它们属于“血缘关系的过度决定”这一列。也就是说，当安提戈涅试图埋葬她的兄弟，并为此走到墙边时，这种行为可能显得有些过激，这就是血缘关系的过度决定。
