So quickly let’s take a look at the Levi-Strauss chart, if you want to call it that, of the Oedipus myth which is on page 864 in your text and just say a word or two about it. He takes a lot of versions. Let’s not trouble ourselves with how many. He doesn’t have nearly as many versions by the way as he would have if he were studying a North American Indian myth or the sorts of myths that he did study in a variety of versions as an anthropologist, but he has some versions–one of them, by the way, Freud’s version, one of them Sophocles’ version, and a variety of versions besides those. He says, “Hmm, as you look at these various versions [gestures towards graph on chalkboard], you can see that certain things are basically happening, and they fall into certain discrete categories. We can put them in columns–that is to say, in terms of the way in which they share a common theme, but we can also put those columns in a row so that we can analyze the way in which the columns relate to each other.” For example, there’s a group of events, happenstances, sort of naming accidents and so on, that falls into a column called “over-determination of blood relations.” That is to say, when Antigone tries to bury her brother and goes to the wall for that, in ways that you might find excessive, that’s an over-determination of blood relations.

然后你会注意到，与此同时，神话中存在一系列事件——从俄狄浦斯的家族史一直追溯到他的后代，以此类推——这些事件都与血缘关系的轻视有关。人们似乎并不像他们应该的那样重视血缘关系，而这导致了诸多不幸的发生。此外，神话的各个版本中都反复出现一个问题，那就是对源于大地之物的某种奇特执念：怪物、卡德摩斯故事中散落的怪物牙齿化作字母表，以及英雄们与怪物对抗的各种方式，例如俄狄浦斯与斯芬克斯的搏斗。所有这些怪物都被理解为并非由父母所生，或并非由两者结合而成，而是从大地中涌现而出。它们是土生土长的，或者用列维-斯特劳斯的话来说，是“本土的”。

Then you notice that at the same time, there’s a series of actions in the myth–going all the way back to Oedipus’ family history and then down through the history of his offspring and so on–a series of actions which have to do with the undervaluation of blood relations. People, well, they don’t really seem to care as much about blood relations as they should, and as a result of that, bad things happen, too. Then there’s a column of issues which have to do with the way in which recurrently, in all of the versions of the myth, there seems to be a strange preoccupation with that which is born from the earth: monsters, the teeth of monsters that are scattered and become the alphabet in the story of Cadmos, and the variety of ways in which heroes have to confront monsters as Oedipus confronts the sphinx. All of these monsters are understood as not being born from parents, or as being born from two things, but instead as emerging from the earth. They are thonic, or “autochthonous” in Levi-Strauss’ word.

这个神话似乎对“自生性”有着一种奇怪的执着，但这种执着又被另一种方式所抵消——也就是说，这种抗拒“自生性”的方式，仿佛关键在于坚持二元亲子关系——这种关系孕育了我们，让我们从“我们之中有一个人由两个人所生”的观念中获得人性的慰藉。然而，另一方面，神话中也存在着许多与“自生性”截然相反的执着。例如，俄狄浦斯家谱中许多人物名字的首字母是λ（Lambda），比如拉布达库斯（Labdacus）、拉伊俄斯（Laius）等等。λ看起来像一个跛脚的人，对吧？俄狄浦斯（Oedipus）的意思是“肿胀的脚”、“跛脚的人”。第四栏所呈现的，正是我们自身构成中存在着“自生性”迹象的观点。我们跛行的原因在于我们脚底沾染了泥土，我们出生时所用的泥土的某些成分粘在我们身上。这在俄狄浦斯神话的展开中是一个反复出现的模式，一个反复出现的观念。这很奇特，但值得注意的是，这正是该神话传播到其他文化的契机之一。亚当的意思是“红土”。亚当诞生于泥土之中，因为红土取自大地，他由此被创造。俄狄浦斯神话中似乎也存在着对“本土性”（autochthony）的关注，这也是该神话与基督教人类起源神话之间一个有趣的联系。

There seems to be a strange preoccupation with autochthony in this myth, but this is offset by the way in which–that is to say, with fending off autochthony, as if the crucial thing were to insist on the binary parental relationship that produces us, to be reassured in our humanity by the idea that one of us is born from two. But then on the other hand, there are all kinds of things in the myth which are also preoccupied with autochthony in precisely the opposite way. Lambda, the letter that begins so many of the names of the figures in Oedipus’ genealogy–Labdacus, Laius and so on–lambda looks like a limping person, right? Oedipus means “swell foot,” “one who limps.” What emerges in the fourth column is the idea that there are signs of autochthony in our own makeup. The reason we limp is that we have a foot of clay, that something of the earth from which we were born sticks to us, and this is a recurrent pattern, a recurrent idea, in the unfolding of the Oedipus myth. It’s a peculiar thing, but notice that this is one of those occasions on which the myth explodes into other cultures. Adam means “red clay.” Adam is born from the earth in the sense that red clay is taken from the earth and he is created, and there seems to be this same preoccupation with autochthony in the Oedipus myth as well, one of the interesting links of that myth with the Christian myth of the origin of man.

所以这里有四列：过分重视血缘关系、低估血缘关系、否认本土性以及坚持本土性。我暂时就讲到这里，因为我们稍后会再回来探讨这四列——它们都围绕着“二”与“一”展开——究竟有何有趣之处：也就是说，我们究竟是源于两个还是源于一个。我想在某种意义上回到这个问题上，来说明事物（例如观念）究竟是源于两个不同的事物，还是源于同一个事物，这个问题本身其实是结构主义活动的寓言。这正是结构主义的核心所在。也正因如此，列维-斯特劳斯才能在神话中找到的不仅仅是任何思想，而是他自己对神话的思考，这才显得如此有趣，甚至有些奇特。当然，这或许与你认为分解是为了重组，创造一个虚拟的系统对象——注意我用虚线标出了这一点[指向黑板]——其中存在某种循环性有关。我希望我已经把列维-斯特劳斯的四柱理论解释清楚了，但如果你仔细看看这四柱理论[笑]，你会问自己：“他到底是怎么想出这个理论的？”他自己说：“哦，嗯，也许我可以用别的方法。”然后你就会问自己：“这怎么能成为决定性的？怎么能成为权威的？”对吧？

So you’ve got four columns: over-evaluation of blood relations, under-evaluation of blood relations, denial of autochthony, and persistence of autochthony. I’m going to leave it at that for now because we’ll come back later to see what interesting thing is going on in the way in which these four columns, all about two versus one: that is to say, whether or not we are born from two or born from one. I want to come back to that in the context of showing that in a certain way, the question of whether things–ideas, for example–come from two, two different things, or whether ideas come from one object, is after all this question is itself an allegory of the structuralist activity. That’s what structuralism itself is about. That’s what makes it so interesting and even perhaps peculiar that Levi-Strauss is able to find not just any thought in a myth but the very thinking that he himself is doing about the myth. That, of course, may have something to do with your sense that surely decomposing in order to recompose, creating a virtual systemic object–notice that I have made this a dotted line [gestures towards chalkboard]–that there is a kind of a circularity in that. I hope I have explained Levi-Strauss’ four columns intelligibly, but if you look at those [laughs] four columns you say to yourself, “How on earth did he come up with that?” He himself says, “Oh, well, maybe I could have done it some other way,” and you say to yourself, “How can this become decisive? How can it become authoritative?” Right?

你可以看出他在做什么——顺便说一句，你可以通过思考他遗漏的事情来证实这一点。伊俄卡斯忒上吊自杀了，但他没有提及此事。这在四列中都没有提到，但显然这与血缘关系的过度决定或决定不足有关——你可以自行选择。她感到内疚是因为她犯了乱伦罪，对吗？俄狄浦斯出生时腿筋受伤，被暴露在西塞隆山上。列维-斯特劳斯也没有提及此事，但显然这就是俄狄浦斯跛脚的原因。俄狄浦斯就像字母λ一样跛脚，对吗？所以很明显，这一定与本土性的持续存在有关。最后，如果你读《俄狄浦斯在科罗诺斯》，在结尾，俄狄浦斯死后被大地吞噬；“你本是尘土，仍要归于尘土。”这与俄狄浦斯神话中的“我来自哪里（大地），我又将去往何处”有异曲同工之妙。他在科罗诺斯成为了当地的守护神。由于被那里吞噬，他成为了当地的主宰或守护神。因此，所有我们自己想到的——他没有想到，也没有把它们画进图里——都可以被画进他的图里。如果是这样，我们就不得不对自己说：“这或许有道理。也许这是一种合理且有趣的整理素材的方式。”所以，我确实认为应该这样说，来为这种看似有些随意的做法辩护。

You can see what he’s doing–and by the way you can confirm it by thinking of things that he leaves out. Jocasta hangs herself, but he doesn’t mention that. It’s not in any of the four columns, but obviously that has something to do–you can take your choice–either between the over-determination or under-determination of blood relations. She feels guilty because she committed incest, right? Oedipus at his birth is hamstrung and exposed on Mount Cithaeron. Levi-Strauss doesn’t mention that either, but obviously that’s why Oedipus limps. Oedipus is a limping person like the letter lambda, right? So plainly that must have something to do with the persistence of autochthony. Finally, if you read Oedipus at Colonus, at the end of it Oedipus, when he dies, is swallowed up by the earth; “dust thou art, to dust thou shalt return.” The equivalent of this in the Oedipus myth is that “where I came from [the earth] is where I will go.” He becomes a kind of genius of the place at Colonus. As a result of having been swallowed up there, he becomes a kind of presiding spirit or genius of the place. So all of those things which we ourselves thought of–he didn’t think of them and he didn’t put them in his diagram–can, however, be put in his diagram. If that’s the case, we have to say to ourselves, “There might be something in this. Maybe this is a plausible and interesting way of arranging these materials.” So I really do think that ought to be said in defense of what may seem, however, to be a somewhat arbitrary exercise.

第五章 诗歌功能

Chapter 5. The Poetic Function

现在谈到雅各布森，你可能会说，我一直强调“分解以便重组”，但你并没有在雅各布森的论述中看到这一点。你可能会想：“嗯，他似乎只是在搞形式主义。他把任何言语行为分解成六种功能。他谈论这六种功能之间的相互决定关系以及最终结果。这听起来不就是形式主义吗？”你可能会这样说。那么，要证明雅各布森的论述是结构主义的，一个方法是指出，在这篇文章中——顺便说一句，这篇文章还有很多内容，你的编辑没有给你——它主要讨论的是韵律，这是雅各布森长期以来的研究专长：俄罗斯韵律、捷克韵律等等，虽然有点技术性，但一切都与诗歌功能有关。毕竟，这篇文章讨论的是诗歌功能，也就是形式主义者所说的文学性。

Now turning to Jakobson, you may say with all this emphasis I’ve been throwing on “decomposing in order to recompose” that you don’t see that going on in what Jakobson is saying. You may say to yourself, “Well, he seems to be just doing formalism. He breaks any speech act into six functions. He talks about the inter-determinacy of those six functions with a certain result. That sounds just like formalism,” you say. Well, one way to show the way in which what Jakobson is doing is structuralist is to say that after all in this essay–there’s a lot more of the essay, by the way, which your editor doesn’t give you. It’s mostly about versification, which is the long-standing specialty of Jakobson’s work: Russian versification, Czech versification and so on, a little technical, but it is all about the poetic function. After all, this essay is about the poetic function, what the formalists would call literariness.

但雅各布森对诗歌功能这一概念确实做出了重要的贡献，其本质在于：诗歌功能——这是我第一次引用这句话。它在第858页左栏，有点拗口。“诗歌功能将等价原则从选择轴投射到组合轴。”现在你明白了。“诗歌功能将等价原则从选择轴投射到组合轴。”什么是等价原则？如果你理解了这一点，你就掌握了很大一部分。等价原则可以理解为雅各布森在“失语症”一文中所说的“隐喻”，也就是说——你还记得我上次讲过符号如何在垂直轴上聚集吗[指向黑板]？如果我们把语言理解为一个系统，那么有些符号与其他符号的关系方式，可能与其他一些符号的关系方式截然不同。然后我突然记忆力大减，想不起“船”的同义词。但我希望我已经把我的意思表达清楚了，并指出任何给定的符号都可以以多种方式与其他符号组合。这些组合方式就是雅各布森所说的“等价原则”。

But Jakobson has a real contribution to make to this notion of the poetic function, and what it is is basically this: the poetic function–and I’m going to quote this for the first time. It’s on page 858 in the left-hand column and it’s a mouthful. “The poetic function projects the principle of equivalence from the axis of selection into the axis of combination.” Now you understand. “The poetic function projects the principle of equivalence from the axis of selection into the axis of combination.” What is the principle of equivalence? If you’ve got that, you’ve got a good deal of it. The principle of equivalence can be understood as what Jakobson in the “aphasia” essay calls “metaphor,” that is to say the way in which–you remember last time I talked about how signs cluster in the vertical axis [gestures towards chalkboard], and if we understand language as a system, there are some signs that relate to other signs in ways that they probably don’t relate to yet other signs. Then I had an incredible lapse of memory. I couldn’t remember a synonym for “ship,” but I hope that I got my point across to you and indicated that there are varieties of ways in which any given sign clusters with other signs. Those ways of clustering are what Jakobson calls “the principle of equivalence.”

它是什么呢？嗯，它指的是符号之间相似或不相似的方式。如果这听起来太模糊，或许最好不要用“差异”或“相似”这样的语言，而要用“对立”这样的语言：换句话说，就是符号之间几乎同义的方式，或者符号之间真正对立的方式。显然，它像韵律一样可以延伸。你不仅有完全押韵，还有半押韵。这些关系以各种方式延伸，但等价原则指的是符号（无论你如何理解它们，它们都被理解为音素、词素、语素）之间相似或不相似的方式。我们组合这类符号的便捷程度，正是关注诗歌功能的人所追求的。如果话语似乎包含各种等价关系的主导地位，那么这个在组合轴上展开的话语，正如[指向黑板]，是将等价原则——称之为隐喻，称之为相似或相异原则——从选择轴投射出来的结果；也就是说，将语言作为一个系统的轴（也许是一个虚拟的轴）投射到组合轴，也就是那个真实的轴——因为没有人怀疑言语的存在——那个真实的轴，在这个轴上，语言不是一个系统，而是变成了在时间中展开的言语。

What is it? Well, it’s the way in which signs either are similar to each other or are dissimilar to each other. If that sounds too vague, maybe it’s better not to use language of difference or similarity but actually to use language of opposition: in other words, the way in which signs are virtually synonymous, or the way in which signs are really and truly opposed to each other. Obviously, it stretches just as in versification. You don’t just have full rhyme; you have slant rhyme. These relationships stretch in varieties of ways of this kind, but the principle of equivalence is the way in which signs understood as phonemes, lexemes, tagmemes–how ever you want to understand them–the way in which signs are similar or dissimilar. The readiness with which we combine signs of that kind is what a person attending to the poetic function looks for. If the utterance seems to involve a predominance of equivalences of various kinds, then this utterance, which is unfolding on the axis of combination, right [gestures towards chalkboard], is the result of having projected that principle of equivalence–call it metaphor, call it a principle of similarity or dissimilarity–from the axis of selection; that is to say, that axis, perhaps a virtual one, in which language is a system to the axis of combination, that real axis–because nobody doubts the existence of speech–that real axis in which language is not a system but has become speech unfolding in time.

然而，诗歌功能的原则可以理解为对原本是转喻的事物进行隐喻化。换句话说，如果我写一个句子，我所做的就是把词语并列在一起，这就是转喻。转喻是对符号的选择，如果你愿意这么理解的话，这些符号根据语法和句法规则以及逻辑规则恰当地并列在一起；当然，也可能通过转喻这种修辞手法的理解方式来理解。如果我用“小屋”（hut）代替“房子”（house）——我举的例子实际上来自雅各布森的《失语症》一文——如果我说“小屋很小”（The hut is small），那么这里就隐含着与房屋、棚屋、豪宅和其他建筑物之间的转喻关系，但这种关系或许只有通过展开句子的逻辑才能真正得到解决，就像我说“小屋很小”一样。因此，组合过程——借用修辞术语“转喻”（metonymy，意为“相邻的事物”）——本质上是转喻的。另一方面，在选择轴上可供选择的符号，如果具有隐喻性，则会出于特定目的而被选中。显然，如果我只是造句，我选择符号并非因为它们具有隐喻性，而是因为它们彼此之间易于并列，这可能是出于语法、句法或逻辑方面的原因。

The principle of the poetic function, however, can be understood then as the metaphorization of what is otherwise metonymic. In other words, if I put together a sentence, what I’m doing is I’m putting words next to each other, and that’s what metonymy is. Metonymy is a selection of signs, if you will, that go appropriately next to each other according to the rules of grammar and syntax and according to the rules of logic, right; but also perhaps in the ways in which the rhetorical device of metonymy can be understood. If I say “hut” instead of “house”–I’m using an example actually taken from Jakobson’s “aphasia” essay–and if I say, “The hut is small,” there is a metonymic relationship implied with houses, shacks, mansions, and other sorts of edifice, but which can only really be resolved, perhaps, by the unfolding of the logic of the sentence as in when I say, “The hut is small.” So combinatory processes–borrowing the rhetorical term “metonymy” as “that which is next to each other”–are basically metonymic. The available signs to be selected, on the other hand, on the axis of selection are selected for certain purposes if they are metaphoric. Obviously, if I’m just making a sentence, I’m not selecting signs because they’re metaphoric. I select them because they go easily next to each other, either for reasons of grammar or syntax or logic.

第六章 雅各布森的六个函数

Chapter 6. Jacobson’s Six Functions

现在我们来整体看一下雅各布森的六种功能[指向黑板]。我认为这一点也不难，而且我认为雅各布森对这六种功能的分析简直精彩绝伦。事实上，我对雅各布森关于这六种功能的论述深信不疑，以至于我觉得关于话语本身已经没什么可说的了[笑]。当然，在不同的语域中有很多东西可以讨论，但就雅各布森的分析精神而言，除了一个可能存在的瑕疵之外，你几乎找不到任何可以挑剔的地方，而这个瑕疵我可能要到下次才会提到。总之，它的效果令人惊叹。

Now let’s look at Jakobson’s six functions [gestures towards board] taken all together. I think this is by no means difficult, and I think that Jakobson’s analysis of the six functions is just absolutely, totally brilliant. In fact, I’m so profoundly convinced by what Jakobson says about these six functions that I really think there isn’t much [laughs] else to say about an utterance. Obviously in different registers there’s lots to say, but in the spirit of Jakobsonian analysis there’s no possible complaint you can make about this except possibly one, which I probably won’t get to until next time. In the meantime, it’s just staggeringly effective.

让我举个例子，一个肯定很无聊的表达——我绞尽脑汁也想不出比这更无聊的表达来说明任何话语都包含这六种功能的例子：“下雨了。” 哦，天哪，正如人们常说的，“兴奋会带来雨水”。总之，假设我是说话者——也就是说，我是一位浪漫主义诗人。我说——如果我是一位诗人，这么说可能不太明智，但我的确是一位浪漫主义诗人——我说，这话听起来像是要把大家都吵醒，“下雨了。” 好吧。如果我是一位浪漫主义诗人，我到底想表达什么呢？（笑）我想表达的是“我在雨中歌唱”或者“我的心中在下雨”。换句话说，我说“下雨了”时表达了一种情感，所以“下雨了”这个表达的这种情感功能，正是雅各布森所说的情感功能。

Let me use the example of an expression which is surely as uninteresting–I’ve groped as much as I could to find the most uninteresting possible expression to show the way in which any utterance whatsoever entails these six functions: “It is raining.” Oh, boy, “Excitement rains,” as they say. In any case, let’s say that I am an addresser–that is to say, I’m a Romantic poet. I say–probably ill advisedly if I’m a poet, but I’m a Romantic poet–I say, sort of waking everybody up when I say it, “It is raining.” All right. What do I mean [laughs] if I’m a Romantic poet? What I mean to say is “I’m singing in the rain” or “It’s raining in my heart.” In other words, I’m expressing something emotional in saying “It is raining,” so that sense of the expression “It is raining” is what Jakobson calls the emotive function.

现在有人在对我说话。信息的重点在于接收者。说话者是发话人，但信息是针对接收者的。这个接收者是一个没穿外套就出门的小孩，他的父母说：“下雨了。”对吧？这句话——当然，作为一种意动功能，作为一种命令，作为一种针对接收者的信息——它的意思是“穿上外套”。但你不一定会说“穿上外套”，你会说“下雨了”，这就是意动功能。这就是雅各布森所说的“指向接收者的集合”：也就是说，信息的基本主导意义，即“集合”，是指向接收者的集合。

Now I’m being addressed. The thrust of the message is toward the addressee. It’s being spoken by an addresser, but it’s aimed at an addressee. That addressee is a small child going out the door without his coat on, and his mother or father says, “It is raining,” right, which means–of course as a conative function, as a command, as something which has a design on the addressee–what it means is “Put your coat on.” But you don’t necessarily say, “Put your coat on.” You say, “It is raining,” and that’s the conative function. That’s what Jakobson calls “the set to the addressee”: that is to say, the basic dominant bearing that the message has, the “set,” is a set to the addressee.

现在，任何话语都有了语境。我想我们都不会否认这一点：我是个气象员，我是个气象学家，对吧？我甚至不用往窗外看。我看看图表，然后自信地对着麦克风宣布：“下雨了。”对吧？大家都认真对待我的话。“下雨了”这个说法的指称功能是传递信息。我是个气象员，我应该知道自己在说什么。所以，如果气象员告诉我“下雨了”，我就相信真的在下雨。我把手伸出门外，果然，真的在下雨，而“下雨了”这个表达的主要指称功能——指称功能——得到了证实。我不会指望气象员在说“下雨了”的时候，暗地里告诉我他正在哭泣，对吧？[笑声] 对吧？我希望他能告诉我真实的天气情况，对吧？我听他说话就是为了这个。

Now there’s a context for any utterance. This much I suppose none of us would think to disagree with: I’m a weatherman, I’m a meteorologist, right? I don’t even have to look out the window. I look at my charts and I announce confidently through the microphone, “It is raining.” Right? Everybody takes me seriously. The referential function of “It is raining” is supposed to convey information. I’m a weatherman, and I’m supposed to know what I’m talking about. So if a weatherman tells me “It is raining,” I believe that it is raining. I put my hand out the door and, sure enough, it is raining, and the referential function–the dominant in the expression “It is raining” as referential function–has been confirmed. I don’t expect the weatherman to be telling me somehow secretly that he’s crying when he says “It is raining,” right? [laughter] Right? I expect him to tell me the truth about the weather, right, and that’s what I’m listening to him for.

好了。现在来说说“如何与人沟通”。雅各布森举了多萝西·帕克笔下约会的精彩例子：“哦，天哪。好吧，我们到了，是啊，我们到了，[笑]是啊，我们确实到了，”等等，对吧——换句话说，处于一种极度紧张的状态，语无伦次，对吧，所以你在约会，对吧，却什么也说不出来。[笑]我真为你感到难过。[笑][笑声]你在约会，却什么也说不出来，于是你说：“下雨了，”当然，你的对方说：“是啊，下雨了，”你说：“雨下得很大，”她说：“嗯，是啊。也许很快就会停。”所以对话继续进行，这就是寒暄的功能——确认联系是否畅通：“测试一下，一、二、三；你能听到我说话吗？” 这就是建立联系的目的：任何确认你确实在和某人沟通的内容，我们说的任何话都包含这个成分。我的意思是，如果我是一个物理学家，我和另一个物理学家约会，我会说：“E 等于 MC²。” 但我说的不是“E 等于 MC²”；我是在用一些话来填补空隙。所以再一次，这是建立联系的目的，任何在合适的语境下的信息都具有这个功能。而建立代码的目的则是，当我们不确定在特定场合是否能充分地向对方传达代码时，我们会退一步，确保我们说的话清晰明了，换句话说，就是对代码进行定义。我说：“田野里有一匹母马。” 有人问：“什么是母马？” “嗯，这是一匹母马。” “嗯，这是一匹母马”是元语言功能。

All right. Now “the set to the contact.” Jakobson gives you those wonderful examples from Dorothy Parker’s representation of a date: “Oh, boy. Well, here we are, yeah, here we are, [laughs] yeah, we sure are here,” and so on, right–in other words, in a state of abject and acute nervousness filling the air with words, right, so that you’re on a date, right, and you can’t think of anything to say. [laughs] I really feel sorry for you. [laughs] [laughter] You’re on a date and you can’t think of anything to say so you say, “It is raining,” and of course your interlocutor says, “Yeah, it’s raining,” and you say, “It’s raining hard,” and she says, “Well, yeah. Maybe it’ll stop soon.” So the conversation continues, and that’s phatic function–checking to make sure the contact is working: “testing one, two, three; can you hear me?” That’s what the set to the contact is: anything that confirms that you’re actually sort of in communication with somebody, and anything we can say has that component. I mean, if I’m a physicist and I’m going out on a date with another physicist, I say, “E equals MC squared.” Only I’m not saying “E equals MC squared”; I’m filling the air with words. So once again, it’s the set to the contact, and any message in the right context has that function. The set to the code is when we’re not sure that we adequately share the code with another person on a given occasion so that we back away from simply saying things to make sure that what we’re saying is clear, in other words to define them. I say, “There’s a mare in the field.” Somebody says, “What is a mare?” “Well, it’s a female horse.” “Well, it’s a female horse” is the metalingual function.

但我们说的是“下雨了”。这才是真正有趣的地方。[笑] 就这六种功能而言，“下雨了”最有趣的地方在于它的元语言特性，因为“它”到底是什么？对吧？有人跟我说“下雨了”，我会说：“什么？你在说什么？‘它’是什么？我完全不知道你在说什么。” 我注意到其他语言也有这种奇怪的现象，比如“Il pleut”、“Es regnet”。这些东西到底是什么意思？“il”是什么？“es”是什么？“it”又是什么？是上帝吗？是木星普鲁维乌斯吗？是云层吗？嗯，它某种程度上确实是指云层，但这显然不是“it”的意思，对吧？“it”是一种语法和句法上的异常现象，即使是语言学家也很难分析和解释；所以，当我试图说“It is raining”（下雨了）时，如果我和一个字面主义者交谈，我当然可以预料到，元语言功能会启动，实际上，它会让我吃苦头。带着元语言功能说“It is raining”可不是一件轻松的事。“It is raining”到底是对“it”的一种定义吗？[笑]

But we’re talking about “It is raining.” This is where it really gets interesting. [laughs] The most interesting thing about “It is raining” in terms of these six functions is metalingual, because what on earth is “it”? Right? Somebody tells me “It is raining.” I say, “What? What are you talking about? What is ‘it’? I have absolutely no idea what you’re saying.” I’ve noticed that other languages have this same weird phenomenon” “Il pleut,” “Es regnet.” What on earth does any of that mean? What is “il”? What is “es”? What is “it”? Is it God? Is it Jupiter Pluvius? Is it the cloud canopy? Well, it sort of is the cloud canopy, but that’s sort of clearly not what’s meant by “it,” right? “It” is a kind of grammatical and syntactical anomaly which is extremely difficult even for linguists to analyze and to explain; so that when I try to say, “It is raining,” I can expect, if I am talking to a literalist, of course, the metalingual function to kick in and, in fact, bite me in the shin. It’s no picnic with the metalingual function in mind saying, “It is raining.” What kind of a definition of “it” is “It’s raining?” [laughs]

所以问题出现了，但这些问题很有意思，它们构成了“下雨了”这一表达的六大功能之一。可惜的是，诗歌功能本身并不怎么有趣。这是这个例子唯一的不足之处，但仍然有很多值得探讨的地方：“ih-ih”和“raining”中的“ih”，我们可以听到——“raining”中的双“ih”，这些单音节词暗示着一种快速的宣告，随后又带有一种持续感，这种感觉在我们意识到即将下雨时总是会体会到：“下雨了nnnnnnning”，因此，这个词的延展具有某种语义价值，它告诉我们这是一场持续不断的雨——换句话说，我们可以从多种角度来思考“下雨了”的诗歌功能。如果诗歌功能占据主导地位——就像我之前说的，如果一位浪漫主义诗人说“下雨了”，那就太不聪明了——那么对于任何想要做到这一点的人来说，都将是一项艰巨的任务。但是，在任何给定的话语的特定情况下，任何功能都可能占据主导地位。

So problems arise but they’re interesting problems, and they are a function, one of the six functions, of the expression “It is raining.” Poetic function is unfortunately not very interesting. That’s the one drawback of this example, but there’s still plenty to say: “ih-ih” and the “ih” in raining, which one can hear–the double “ih” in raining, the monosyllables suggesting a kind of a quick declaration of something followed by a sense of duration that one always feels when one is aware of rain coming: that “It is rainnnnnnning,” so that the duration of prolongation of the word has a kind of semantic value indicating to us that this is something ongoing–in other words, a variety of ways in which the poetic function of “It is raining” can be considered. For the poetic function to be dominant–as I suggested when I said a Romantic poet wouldn’t be very smart if he or she said “It was raining”–would really be taxing for anyone who wanted to make it so. But any function could be the dominant in a certain situation of any given utterance.

所以，这或许足以作为对雅各布森理解话语结构的分析。它之所以具有结构，是因为我们观察到某种来自选择轴、等价原则以及选择轴的压力，这种压力影响着组合的方式——也就是说，它具有隐喻结构而非转喻结构。你说“下雨了”，这简直不可思议。还有什么比“下雨了”更平淡无奇的呢？突然间，你注意到那一串“i”。你注意到它的其他种种细节。最平凡的话语的组合方式，很可能以某种形式几乎是不可避免的。我想我应该使用更强有力的论证，用“不可避免地”来表达：它很可能不可避免地蕴含着诗歌功能的某些方面。诗歌功能占主导地位的地方就有了文学性，这当然是俄国形式主义者长期以来关注的科学对象；但雅各布森以一种我认为是结构主义的方式对其进行了完善，因为他坚持认为，如果元素是等价的，那么从选择轴上组合元素的过程就具有二元性——二元性指的是“相同”、“相反”、“相似”、“不同”，以及这些关系“相同”、“相反”、“相似”和“不同”可以投入使用的各种模式。

So that then, sort of, perhaps serves to suffice as an analysis of Jakobson’s understanding of the structure of an utterance. It has a structure insofar–that is to say a metaphoric as opposed to a metonymic structure insofar as we observe the presence of some kind of pressure from the axis of selection, the principle of equivalence and the axis of selection, bringing itself to bear on the way in which the combination takes place. It’s just incredible that you say, “It is raining.” What could be more prosaic than “It is raining?” All of a sudden you notice that string of “i’s.” You notice all kinds of other things about it. The way in which the most banal utterance is combined is likely in one form or another almost unavoidable. I suppose I should use the strong argument and say “unavoidably”: is likely unavoidably to entail aspects of the poetic function. Where the poetic function is dominant you have literariness, and that of course, is the old object of scientific attention of the Russian formalists; but it is refined in a way that, I think, is structuralist by Jakobson because he insists on the binary nature of the process of combining elements from the axis of selection if they are equivalent–binary being “same,” “opposite,” “similar,” “dissimilar,” and the variety of patterns in which those relations, “same,” “opposite,” “similar,” and “dissimilar,” can be launched into use.

第七章 元语言与诗歌功能

Chapter 7. Metalanguage and Poetic Function

现在我终于可以开始进行一些评论了，我想我会先从这里开始。我可能不会说完，但我们总可以把话题延续到下一节课。既然我们一直在讨论雅各布森，那么我想提请大家注意一下他那篇在我看来堪称卓越的文章中的一个问题。这个问题出现在第858页。他自己也意识到这是一个问题。他承认这是一个问题，但他想说的是，他已经通过他所说的解决了这个问题。这个问题出现在页面大约三分之二的位置，它探讨的是诗歌功能和元语言功能之间的关系，也就是他所说的，信息集合和代码集合之间的关系。他是这么说的：

Now I’ve actually reached the point at which possibly I could get involved in some elements of critique, and I suppose I’ll begin. I may not finish but we can always carry over into the next lecture. So since we’ve been talking about Jakobson, let me call your attention to one problem in what seems to me otherwise to be a truly remarkable exercise of thought. That problem arises on page 858. He himself recognizes that it’s a problem. He acknowledges it’s a problem, but he wants to say that he’s solved it in saying what he says. It’s about two thirds of the way down the page and it’s about the relationship between the poetic function and the metalingual function, between the set to the message and the set to the code, as he puts it. This is what he says:

有人可能会反对说[没错，我们确实在反对，对吧？]，元语言在将同义词组合成等式句时，也同样会按顺序使用等价单位：A = A（“母马是马的雌性”）。然而，诗歌和元语言截然相反[它们不一样，对吧？它们截然相反]：在元语言中，顺序被用来构建等式[换句话说，证明一个项可以用其他项来理解]，而在诗歌中，等式被用来构建顺序。好的。从某种意义上说，这显然是正确的。是的，也就是说，我知道什么时候我在说元语言，什么时候我在说诗。或许你也知道，雅各布森实际上触及了结构主义的一个痛点，因为他诉诸于意图：也就是说，他认为元语言表达具有一种意图，而诗歌表达具有另一种意图。这意味着什么？它有其起源；它源于一种意图意识，正如在非结构主义的传统中，事物起源于先前的原因，而非它们之间结构性的关系。换句话说，如果结构主义是对起源的批判，正如埃德蒙·利奇对圣经文本《创世记》的分析，正如列维-斯特劳斯对俄狄浦斯神话的理解——从二元而非一元出发——那么，当你必须根据其起源，即它们背后的意图，来区分你体系中的两个实体：诗歌功能和元语言功能时，会发生什么呢？

It may be objected [Yes, and here we are objecting, right?] that metalanguage also makes a sequential use of equivalent units when combining synonymic expressions into an equational sentence: A = A (“Mare is the female of the horse”). Poetry and metalanguage, however, are in diametrical opposition to each other [They’re not the same, right? They’re in diametrical opposition to each other]: in metalanguage the sequence is used to build an equation [in other words, to prove that one term can be understood in terms of other terms], whereas in poetry the equation is used to build a sequence. Okay. Now in one sense this is true, obviously. Yes, that is, I know when I’m speaking metalanguage and I know when I’m speaking poetry. Maybe you know it too, but what Jakobson has actually done is he’s sort of exposed a structuralist nerve, because he has appealed to intention: that is to say, he’s said the metalingual expression has one intention and the poetic expression has another intention. What does that mean? It has a genesis; it has an origin in an intending consciousness just as in traditions that are not structuralist, things have origins in prior causes and not in their structural relationship between two things. In other words, if structuralism is a critique of genesis, as is the case with Edmund Leach’s analysis of the biblical text Genesis, as is the case certainly with Levi-Strauss’ understanding of the Oedipus myth, from two and not from one–if structuralism is a critique of genesis, what happens when you have to make a distinction between two entities in your system, the poetic function and the metalingual function, in terms of their genesis: that is to say, in terms of the intention that stands behind them?

正如我所说，这个例子看似微不足道，因为我们都非常乐意同意雅各布森的观点，即我们一眼就能看出元语言功能和诗性功能的区别，但他实际上并没有说我们一眼就能看出区别。也许如果他当时说“任何人都能看出什么是元语言功能，什么是诗性功能”，那就更好了。他实际上说的是，元语言功能的目的是一种用途；诗性功能的目的是另一种用途。

As I said, the example seems trivial because we’re all more than prepared to agree with Jakobson that we know the difference when we see it between the metalingual and the poetic functions, but he’s not actually saying we know the difference when we see it. Maybe it would have been better if he had said, “Well, anybody can see what’s metalingual and what’s poetic.” Maybe it would have been better if he had. What he says instead is that metalingual is intended to do one thing; poetic is intended to do another thing.

实际上，这引出了一个关于所有六种功能的棘手问题。我站在你面前说“下雨了”，你怎么知道我的意图呢？我是紧张地客套话，还是真的不高兴？我是真的觉得你疯了——外面确实在下雨，但我没看到任何人穿外套？还是我其实只是在假装自己是英语教授——我其实是气象学家？你根本不知道这些。你必须推断我的意图，对吧？如果为了做出这些区分而推断意图，那么结构主义强调结构而非起源的原则又该如何完整地保留下来呢？如果我们必须推断一个直接原因，一个积极的原因，才能理解甚至六种功能之间的区别，我们又该如何坚持我们是以否定而非肯定的方式去认识事物呢？这是一个反问句，我未必同意，但这确实是一个值得您自行探讨的潜在反对意见。

That opens, actually, a can of worms about all six functions. I stand here in front of you and I say “It is raining.” How do you know what I am intending, right: whether I’m nervous and sort of just being phatic; whether I am really unhappy or happy; whether I think you’re crazy–it is in fact raining outside and I don’t see any coats; or whether I am actually sort of just masquerading as an English professor–I am really a meteorologist? You don’t know any of these things. You have to infer an intention, right? If you infer an intention in order to make these distinctions, how can the structuralist imperative of structure rather than genesis be preserved intact? How can we insist that we know things negatively and not positively if we have to infer a direct cause, a positive cause, in order to grasp distinctions even between the six functions? That’s a rhetorical question with which I don’t necessarily agree but it is a potential objection that you may wish to explore on your own.

关于对列维-斯特劳斯的批判，我之前已经略有提及，但还有另一个方面。这一点我留到下次再谈，因为你们会发现，你们正在阅读的德里达的文章很大程度上是关于列维-斯特劳斯的，所以它能自然地衔接我们今天讨论的内容和周四要讨论的内容：先回顾一下列维-斯特劳斯论证的某些方面，然后再深入探讨德里达的观点。谢谢。下次见。

Now the critique of Levi-Strauss I have already hinted at, but there’s another aspect of it too. That I will defer until next time because you’ll find that the essay of Derrida’s that you’re reading is largely about Levi-Strauss, so it will make a natural segue between what we’re talking about today and what we’ll be talking about Thursday, to return first to certain aspects of Levi-Strauss’ argument and then get going with what Derrida is saying. Thank you. See you then.

第十讲 - 解构（一）

Lecture 10 - Deconstruction I

第一章 雅克·德里达的起源与影响

Chapter 1. Origins and Influence of Jacques Derrida

保罗·弗莱教授：那么，为了引出今天的主题，我们首先要谈到课程大纲中一位颇具影响力的人物，他最近去世了。在他晚年乃至今天，他的思想焕发了新的活力。他后期的作品并没有完全否定他早期的思想或风格，而是开始将他思想的核心应用于伦理和政治问题。他和一些其他作家，例如意大利哲学家乔治·阿甘本，被认为是当今时代关于文本、文学和其他领域的“伦理转向”的代表人物。因此，德里达的声誉以及对理论感兴趣的人们阅读他的作品的趋势至今依然存在，但我们这一系列讲座所阅读的材料可以追溯到更早的时期。

Professor Paul Fry: So anyway, to get launched on today’s topic, obviously we confront one of the more formidable figures on our syllabus, a person who recently passed away and who in his last years and into the present has had a kind of second life as a person who in his later work didn’t at all repudiate his earlier thoughts or indeed his earlier style, but nevertheless did begin to apply central aspects of his thinking to ethical and political issues. He and a number of other writers like, for example, the Italian philosopher Giorgio Agamben, are the figures whom we identify with what’s called “the ethical turn” in thinking about texts, literature and other matters that is very much of the current moment. Hence Derrida’s reputation and the tendency of people interested in theory to read him is alive and well today, but the materials that we are reading for this sequence of lectures date back much earlier.

今天您全文阅读的这篇文章——《人文科学语言中的结构、符号与游戏》——发表于1966年约翰·霍普金斯大学举办的“人类科学”研讨会上。这场研讨会原本意在为克劳德·列维-斯特劳斯加冕，他的著作在几年前才在美国学术界崭露头角。列维-斯特劳斯本人也出席了研讨会，他发表了演讲，也坐在听众席中。然而，德里达的这篇文章却被广泛解读为——远非对列维-斯特劳斯的加冕——某种程度上是对列维-斯特劳斯的否定。我必须告诉您，列维-斯特劳斯如今依然健在，已是耄耋之年，他对后来发生的事情让他自己的著作的重要性被取代，深感愤慨。我认为，后来的这一切可以追溯到德里达的演讲。

The essay that you read in its entirety for today, “Structure, Sign and Play in the Language of the Human Sciences,” was delivered on the occasion of a conference about “the sciences of man” at Johns Hopkins University in 1966. It was an event that was really meant to be a kind of coronation of Claude Levi-Strauss, whose work had burst upon the American scene only a few years earlier. Levi-Strauss was there. He gave a talk, he was in the audience, and Derrida’s essay was widely taken–far from being a coronation of Levi-Strauss–as a kind of dethroning of Levi-Strauss. I have to tell you that Levi-Strauss, who is still alive, a very old man, expresses great bitterness in his old age about what he takes to be the displacement of the importance of his own work by what happened subsequently. What happened subsequently can, I think, be traced to Derrida’s lecture.

思考这篇演讲以及德里达的整体作品——乃至解构主义本身——所面临的诸多难题之一，正是它究竟在多大程度上真正偏离了结构主义的范畴。在结构思考中，我们能在许多列维-斯特劳斯的著作中发现一种自觉意识，而德里达在他的文章中也坦然承认了这一点。他反复引用列维-斯特劳斯的论述来佐证自己的观点，但随后又以一种反驳列维-斯特劳斯的方式指出，即便在他自己的论述中，也存在一些他尚未完全思考透彻的地方。因此，即便事后看来，这并非是对列维-斯特劳斯的彻底否定，甚至算不上是一次毁灭性的批判。我认为，德里达在这篇文章中坦诚地承认，他在多大程度上是站在列维-斯特劳斯的肩膀上。

One of the million complications of thinking about this lecture and about Derrida’s work in general–and, for that matter, about deconstruction–is indeed to what extent it really is a significant departure from the work of structuralism. There is a self-consciousness in the thinking about structure that we find in many places in Levi-Strauss that Derrida freely acknowledges in his essay. Again and again and again he quotes Levi-Strauss in confirmation of his own arguments, only then in a way to turn on him by pointing out that there is something even in what he’s saying there that he hasn’t quite thought through. So it is not anything like, even as one reads it in retrospect, a wholesale repudiation or even really a very devastating critique of Levi-Strauss. Derrida, I think, freely acknowledges in this essay the degree to which he is standing on Levi-Strauss’s shoulders.

总之，这一非凡事件在西方理论家的想象中，确实带来了一种近乎一夜之间的变革感，使我们从六十年代中期对结构主义的痴迷，转向了七十年代乃至八十年代初对解构主义的关注。德里达无疑是这一变革的核心人物。多年来，他每年春天都会以访问学者的身份来到耶鲁大学。他影响了众多学者，他们的研究成果至今仍在美国乃至世界各地发挥着重要作用。此后，他又与加州大学欧文分校建立了类似的合作关系，并在那里继续发挥着影响力。许多人至今仍记得他在耶鲁时期所展现出的鼓舞人心的力量。一位批评家称耶鲁大学存在“诠释学黑手党”，这种说法很大程度上源于德里达的存在，以及我们自己的保罗·德曼，还有与他们联系较为松散的杰弗里·哈特曼和哈罗德·布鲁姆——以及一位名叫J·希利斯·米勒的学者，他离开耶鲁前往加州大学欧文分校，也导致德里达决定去那里与米勒在一起，而不是继续留在这里。

In any case, this extraordinary event in the imaginations of people thinking about theory in the West did, however, tend to bring about a sense of almost overnight revolution from the preoccupation we had in the mid-sixties with structuralism to the subsequent preoccupation we had throughout the seventies and into the early eighties with deconstruction. Derrida was, of course, a central figure in this. He was here at Yale as a visitor in the spring for many years. He influenced a great many people whose work is still current throughout the United States and elsewhere. He–after that–had a comparable arrangement with the University of California at Irvine and his influence there continued, a key figure whom many of us remember from his period at Yale as a galvanizing presence. The idea that there was what was called by one critic a “hermeneutical mafia” at Yale arose largely from the presence of Derrida together with our own Paul de Man and, more loosely connected with them, Geoffrey Hartman and Harold Bloom–and also a scholar named J. Hillis Miller, whose departure for the University of California, Irvine resulted also in Derrida’s decision to go there and be with Miller rather than to continue to stay here.

这就是所谓的耶鲁学派。它在某些圈子里产生了非凡的影响，但在其影响范围之外，却弥漫着一种敌对的氛围。我认为，这种氛围在很多方面都与所谓的“人文危机”有关——州议员和大学理事会普遍认为，在学术界人文发展过程中，某种程度上需要被克服、被摒弃、甚至被遗忘的东西（笑）。至于个中缘由，我想，或许只能在这样的课程背景下略作探讨，但这些缘由却引人入胜，而且在我们思考解构主义本身及其所影响的各种思维方式时，还会反复出现。

That was the so-called Yale school. It generated extraordinary influence in some circles but, well beyond its influence, an atmosphere of hostility which had in many ways to do, I think, with what might still be called “the crisis in the humanities” as it is widely understood by state legislators and boards of trustees as somehow or another something needing to be overcome, backed away from, and forgotten [laughs] in the development of the humanities in academia. The reasons for this we can only imply, I think, probably, in the context of a course of this nature, but are nevertheless fascinating and will recur as we think not just about deconstruction itself but about the sorts of thinking that it has influenced.

第二章 德里达的风格

Chapter 2. Derrida’s Style

现在你已经读过一些德里达的作品了。你读完了他的一篇散文，也读了另一篇《差异》的一部分，你觉得他的作品很难懂。事实上，除了觉得他的作品很难懂之外，你可能还会想：“他为什么非要这样写？”换句话说，你会对自己说：“好吧，他的作品确实很难懂，但他是不是故意把事情搞得更复杂了？”你会说：“我从没见过这样的散文。”你可能还会想说：“这太荒谬了。他为什么不一次只说一件事呢？”当然，这一切都是他有意为之。他的想法是，解构作为一种思维过程，恰恰是一种回避式的舞蹈，在这种舞蹈中，人们不满足于泾渭分明的立场，不满足于任何可以被理解为受制于某个笼统术语——德里达经常称之为“先验所指”——的观念。这正是《结构、符号与游戏》的核心所在。关于这一点，我们还有很多话要说。

Now you have now read some Derrida. You’ve read all of one essay and you’ve read part of another, “Différance,” and you’ve found him very difficult. Indeed, in addition to finding him very difficult you’ve probably said, “Why does he have to write like that?” In other words, “Yeah, okay. He’s difficult, but isn’t he making it more difficult than it needs to be?” you say to yourself. “I’ve never seen prose like this,” you say. “This is ridiculous. Why doesn’t he just say one thing at a time?” you might also want to say. Well, of course it’s all deliberate on his part, and the idea is that deconstruction is, as a thought process, precisely a kind of evasive dance whereby one doesn’t settle for distinct positions, for any sort of idea that can be understood as governed–this is what “Structure, Sign and Play” is all about–as governed by a blanket term, what Derrida often calls a “transcendental signified.” We’ll have much more to say about this.

德里达的散文风格——一种像螃蟹一样横着绕着论点走的迂回方式——力求尽可能避免给人以源于某个确定概念的印象，因为，解构恰恰是对我们假定自身思维可以源于某个确定概念的根基的解构。此外——这一点需要牢记，这当然也是德里达和德曼之间的关键区别之一——我们将在周二详细讨论他们之间的区别：德里达并非文学理论家。尽管他有时确实会谈到我们称之为“文学”的文本，事实上他经常这样做，但德里达的立场及其逻辑表明，我们实际上无法可靠地区分各种文体。换句话说，我们也不能将文体作为一个笼统的术语；因此，他是说服我们根本不存在文学、法律文本、神学文本、哲学文本或科学文本这种东西的最具影响力的人物之一。存在的只有话语，而思考文本领域就意味着思考充满差异的事物。[笑] 不言而喻，这是德里达的核心概念，然而它却无法被分类或归类，因此我们不能说德里达是一位文学理论家。

Derrida’s prose style–its kind of a crab-like, sideways movement around an argument–is meant as rigorously as it can to avoid seeming to derive itself from some definite concept, because, of course, deconstruction is precisely the deconstruction of the grounds whereby we suppose our thinking can be derived from one or another definite concept. Also–this is to be kept in mind, and this is of course one of the key distinctions between Derrida and de Man–we’ll have more to say about distinctions between them on Tuesday: Derrida is not a literary theorist. Though he sometimes does talk about texts that we call “literary,” indeed he very often does, nevertheless Derrida’s position and the logic of that position suggest that we can’t really reliably discriminate among genres. In other words, we can’t use genre either as a blanket term; and therefore he is one of the people–one of the most influential people in persuading us that there’s no such thing as literature, legal texts, theological texts, philosophical texts, or scientific texts. There is discourse, and to think about the field of texts is to think about something which is full of difference. [laughs] Needless to say, it’s the central word in Derrida, which is nevertheless not classifiable or categorizable, and so for that reason we can’t really say Derrida is specifically a literary theorist.

第三章 埃菲尔铁塔与华莱士·史蒂文斯的《罐子轶事》

Chapter 3. The Eiffel Tower and Wallace Stevens’ “Anecdote of the Jar”

到目前为止，我一直在谈论困难和困惑，但鉴于我们都对此感到紧张——我也一样——我想提醒大家，我们已经在进行解构，而且解读德里达时遇到的许多问题实际上都已经解释过了。让我们先从一张热身练习纸开始，这张练习纸可以作为我画的这些小图的参考[指向黑板]。显然，你们看着这些图会说：“啊哈，这就是纵轴”，对吧？当然，一旦我们讨论到女性主义，女性主义对纵轴也会有一些自己的看法。到时候我们会深入探讨这个问题。

Now I’ve been talking so far about difficulty and confusion, but in view of the fact that we’re all in a state of tension about this–I’m in a state of tension about it too–let me remind us that we’ve already been doing deconstruction and that much of what’s problematic in reading Derrida really has already been explained. Let’s begin with a kind of warm-up sheet which we can anchor in these little drawings I’ve made [gestures towards chalkboard]. Obviously, you look at these drawings and you say, “Ah ha. That’s the vertical axis,” right? Of course, once we get to feminism, feminism will have certain ideas of its own about the vertical axis. We will be getting into that when the time comes.

与此同时，埃菲尔铁塔（指向黑板）完美地展现了垂直轴的虚拟性。也就是说，如果你见过一条竖立的虚线，那就是埃菲尔铁塔。它空无一物，透明无比。然而，不知何故，如果你站在塔顶——如果你身处埃菲尔铁塔顶端的观景台——整个巴黎仿佛都呈现在你的脚下。也就是说，你眼前的这条轴线是一个绝妙的组合。它和周围的地标建筑并无二致，与你脚下所站之处的地位截然不同，而更像是巴黎天际线上的关键标志：巴黎圣母院、凯旋门等等，都排列成行，构成了一幅绝妙的画面。据罗兰·巴特在题为《埃菲尔铁塔》的文章中记载，居伊·德·莫泊桑曾在一个著名的轶事中对此颇为愤慨：

In the meantime the Eiffel Tower [gestures towards chalkboard] is a wonderful way of showing the degree to which the vertical axis is virtual. That is to say, if you ever saw a dotted line standing upright, it’s the Eiffel Tower. There’s nothing in it. It’s empty. It’s transparent. Yet somehow or another, if you’re at the top of it–if you’re in the viewing station at the top of the Eiffel Tower–suddenly all of Paris is organized at your feet. That is to say, it’s a wonderful axis of combination that you’re looking at. It is just there with its landmarks, not having the same kind of status as that which you are standing on, but rather just in a kind of row as the key signs, as it were, of the skyline of Paris: so you get the Notre Dame, the Arc de Triomphe and so on, all sort of lined up in a row, and there it is. Guy de Maupassant in a famous anecdote complained rather bitterly about this, according to Roland Barthes in an essay called “The Eiffel Tower”:

莫泊桑经常去塔楼里的餐厅吃饭（他指着黑板），尽管他并不特别喜欢那里的食物。“这是唯一一个，”他说，“我不用看到它的地方。”换句话说，如果——正如索绪尔再次指出的那样——我们“双脚稳稳地踏在”埃菲尔铁塔的“地面”上，我们就能摆脱它以某种方式主宰一切的观念。如果我们真的身处其中，我们就不必再担心它如何将周围的一切组织成某种严谨的展开模式。毕竟，我们确实会从周围环境中推断出埃菲尔铁塔的存在。它建于十九世纪。它绝非巴黎天际线的成因。它就像语言（langue）与言语（speech）的关系一样，是后天形成的。埃菲尔铁塔是一种虚拟事物，它以一种可以说是任意的方式组织事物。

Maupassant often ate at the restaurant in the tower [up here someplace] [gestures towards the chalkboard] even though he didn’t particularly like the food. “It’s the only place,” he said, “where I don’t have to see it.” In other words, if–as Saussure says, once again–we “put both feet squarely on the ground” of the Eiffel Tower, we’re liberated from the idea that somehow or another it’s a governing presence. If we’re actually there, we no longer have to worry about the way it organizes everything around it into a kind of rigorous unfolding pattern. After all, there’s a very real sense in which we infer the Eiffel Tower from its surroundings. It’s built in the nineteenth century. It’s by no means causative of the skyline of Paris. It’s something that comes in belatedly just as langue comes in belatedly with relation to speech. The Eiffel Tower is a virtuality that organizes things, as one might say, arbitrarily.

某种程度上，华莱士·史蒂文斯的著名诗歌正是对这些理念的一种反思。我相信你一定认得这首诗，它就是史蒂文斯的《罐子轶事》，但我还是简单地引用一下这首诗的内容。

Sort of as a reflection on these same ideas, you get the famous poem of Wallace Stevens. I am sure you recognize this as Stevens’ “Anecdote of the Jar,” but I will quickly quote to you the poem.

我在田纳西州放了一个罐子，它圆圆的，放在一座小山上。它使荒芜的旷野环绕着那座小山。

I placed a jar in Tennessee, And round it was, upon a hill. It made the slovenly wilderness Surround that hill.

荒野向它袭来，蔓延开来，不再荒芜。[正如德里达所说，中心限制了自由发挥，对吗？]罐子在地上是圆的，高耸入云，像个港口。

The wilderness rose up to it, And sprawled around, no longer wild. [As Derrida would say, the center limits free play, right?] The jar was round upon the ground And tall and of a port in air.

它占据了所有地方。罐子是灰色的，空空如也。里面既没有鸟也没有灌木，这在田纳西州是绝无仅有的。

It took dominion everywhere. The jar was gray and bare. It did not give of bird or bush, Like nothing else in Tennessee.

换句话说，它被随意地置于自然界自由玩耍的中心，这种自由玩耍充满了繁衍的活力，充满了一种令人愉悦的过剩，这正是德里达在谈到“剩余物”时所指的一部分：符号的剩余性，符号的补充性。德里达的意图中包含着一种高潮般的元素，因此，当他在文章结尾谈到“痕迹的种子性冒险”时，你应该着重强调“种子性”这个词。总之，这个罐子只是随意地置于这一切的中心，组织着一切，却不参与任何事物的本质。换句话说，它是一个结构之外的中心：“一个非中心的中心”，我们稍后会再谈到这一点。

In other words, it is arbitrarily placed in the middle of the free play of the natural world, a free play which is full of reproductive exuberance, full of a kind of joyous excess which is part of what Derrida’s talking about when he talks about what’s “left over”: the surplusage of the sign, the supplementarity of the sign. There’s an orgasmic element in what Derrida has in mind, so that when he speaks of “the seminal adventure of the trace,” toward the end of your essay, you want to put some pressure on that word “seminal.” Well, in any case the jar is just arbitrarily in the middle of that, organizing everything without participating in the nature of anything. It is, in other words, a center which is outside the structure: “a center which is not a center,” and we’ll come back to that in a minute.

如今的双子塔——我早在2001年之前几十年就开始用这个例子了——如今却多了一份当时所没有的悲怆和哀伤；它们所暗示的，某种程度上——这种暗示令我们悲痛欲绝——是垂直轴线的短暂易逝。双子塔在纽约的作用，正如埃菲尔铁塔在巴黎的作用。它是一个俯瞰全城的绝佳地点，一个让人感受到一切都围绕着它运转的绝佳地点。米歇尔·德·塞托曾写过一篇关于双子塔的精彩文章——同样，也是在2001年之前——他对此论点进行了深入的阐述。我推荐您阅读。

Now the Twin Towers–and I first started using this example decades before 2001–the Twin Towers have a kind of poignancy and pathos today that they would not have had then; but what they suggest is in a way today–which overwhelms us with grief–the ephemerality of the vertical axis. The Twin Towers had the same function in New York that the Eiffel Tower has in Paris. It was a wonderful place from which to see the city, a wonderful place from which to feel that everything was organized at its feet. There’s a very fine essay about the Twin Towers–again, long before 2001–by Michel de Certeau, which makes this argument in sustained form. I recommend it to you.

总之，这又是一个我们可以从自身经验中汲取的例子，它揭示了我们内心深处那种不安的感觉：从经验不可还原的时间性本质中推断出一个空间瞬间——从经验本身推断出一个瞬间作为其必然原因——总是充满问题。正如德里达所说，它必然会将这种万物同时存在于空间中的完整存在感置于系统秩序之中——正如德里达所说，它必然会将其“抹去”。换句话说，在某种意义上，你离不开它。德里达从未真正声称你可以舍弃它。如果你想获得一种结构感，你就必须进行某种此类推断，但同时，这种推断最好加上引号，因为它总是脆弱的、短暂的，甚至其存在本身都值得怀疑，因此必然需要以这种方式来理解。

In any case, it’s another example that we can take from our experience of the uneasy sense we may have that to infer a spatial moment from which the irreducibly temporal nature of experience is derived–to infer a moment from the fact of this experience as a necessary cause of it–is always problematic. It always necessarily must, as Derrida would say, put this sense of a spatial full presence of everything there at once in systematic order–as Derrida would say, must put that “under erasure.” In other words, in a certain sense you can’t do without it. Derrida never really claims that you can do without it. If you want to get a sense of structure, you’ve got to have some sort of inference of this nature, but at the same time it had better be in quotes because it is always tenuous, ephemeral, dubious even as to its existence, and necessarily needs to be understood in that way.

第四章 列维-斯特劳斯与俄狄浦斯神话

Chapter 4. Levi-Strauss and the Oedipus Myth

好的。现在，我们再来看看我们今天阅读的内容中已经涉及的其他方面：请看第921页，那里有几段德里达引用列维-斯特劳斯关于神话本质的论述。在引用完列维-斯特劳斯的这两段话之后，我将简要回顾一下列维-斯特劳斯对俄狄浦斯神话的分析，并向你们展示德里达是如何既从列维-斯特劳斯的论述中获益，又最终能够批判列维-斯特劳斯的观点。第921页左侧栏底部：

All right. Now other ways in which we’ve already been involved in the subject matter of what you’ve been reading today: take a look at page 921, a couple of passages in which Derrida is quoting Levi-Strauss on the nature of myth. Once having quoted you these two passages from Levi-Strauss, here’s where I’ll return just for a moment to Levi-Strauss’s analysis of the Oedipus myth and show you how it is that Derrida is both benefiting from what Levi-Strauss has said and ultimately able to criticize Levi-Strauss’s position. Bottom of the left-hand column, page 921:

“与认知话语（即以某种原则、先验所指或统摄性术语为基础的话语——换言之，在特定时刻，某种使一切知识得以流淌之物）相对立，关于神话的结构性话语——神话话语——本身必须是神话形态的。它必须具有它所谈论之物的形式。”[德里达接着说] 这正是列维-斯特劳斯[本人]在[以下摘自列维-斯特劳斯最著名的著作之一]《生与熟》中所说的。我只想引用结尾部分，右侧栏中间，仍然在第921页。列维-斯特劳斯说：

“In opposition to epistemic discourse [that is to say, the kind of discourse which has some principle or transcendental signified or blanket term as its basis–in other words, something which in a given moment makes it possible for all knowledge to flow from it], structural discourse on myths–mythological discourse–must itself be mythomorphic. It must have the form of that of which it speaks.” [And Derrida then says] This is what Lévi-Strauss [himself] says in [the following passage taken from one of Levi-Strauss’ most famous books] The Raw and the Cooked. I just want to quote the end of it, the middle of the right-hand column, still on page 921. Levi-Strauss says:

“我试图模仿神话思维的自发运动，但我的事业——既短暂又漫长——却始终未能满足它的需求，也未能尊重它的节奏。因此，这本关于神话的书本身就是一个神话。”换句话说，在这里，列维-斯特劳斯承认了一些关于他自己作品的观点，而这些观点在他上次你读过的《结构人类学》中对俄狄浦斯神话的分析文章中却没有承认。

“In wanting to imitate the spontaneous movement of mythical thought, my enterprise, itself too brief and too long, has yet to yield to its demands and respect its rhythm. Thus is this book on myths itself and in its own way a myth.” In other words, here is a moment when Levi-Strauss is admitting something about his own work which he is not admitting in his analysis of the Oedipus myth in the essay from Structural Anthropology that you read last time.

列维-斯特劳斯在这里的意思是，他对神话的研究方法本身也只是神话的一种形式。也就是说，它参与了神话式的思维方式。它运用了列维-斯特劳斯在《结构人类学》一文中称之为“神话主题”或“思维的粗略构成单元”的概念。它以我们所见的方式运用和操纵这些思维的粗略构成单元，但请注意列维-斯特劳斯在那篇文章中的观点，这与德里达刚才引用的段落有所不同。他实际上是说：“这种形式的神话是科学的。例如，我用来得出这一科学结论的版本之一，就是弗洛伊德对俄狄浦斯神话的解读。换句话说，弗洛伊德、索福克勒斯，以及我所能利用的所有其他版本，作为版本本身都具有同等的价值，但它们都不是先验的指称，都不是一个包罗万象的术语，也都不是神话的因果解释或意义。神话的意义只能在我的科学体系中发现。”

What Levi-Strauss is saying here is that his approach to myth is itself only a version of the myth. That is to say, it participates in the mythic way of thinking about things. It uses what in the Structural Anthropology essay he calls “mythemes” or “gross constituent units” of thought. It deploys and manipulates those gross constituent units of thought in the ways that we saw, but notice what Levi-Strauss is saying in that essay as opposed to the passage Derrida has just quoted. He says in effect, “This form of the myth is scientific. One of the versions that I have made use of to arrive at this scientific conclusion is, for example, Freud’s version of the Oedipus myth. In other words, Freud, Sophocles, all of the other versions I have at my disposal, have equal merit as versions, but none of them is a transcendental signified, none of them is a blanket term, and none of them is the causal explanation or meaning of the myth. The meaning of the myth is discoverable only in my science.”

当然，弗洛伊德本人自认为是一位科学家，他对神话的解读也被认为是科学的。那么，弗洛伊德对神话的解读究竟是关于什么的呢？二选一！[笑] 换句话说，是关于乱伦问题，关于血缘关系过度决定和血缘关系决定不足的问题。他对这个问题进行了彻底的考察，最终得出结论：这就是神话的本质。换句话说，列维-斯特劳斯的结论在弗洛伊德那里就已经出现了。此外，列维-斯特劳斯在做什么呢？他是在否认弗洛伊德的影响，对吧？这是我的神话，不是他的神话——对吧？——这当然正是原始部落中发生的事情。这是俄狄浦斯情结的完美例证。列维-斯特劳斯否定了父亲，而否定父亲的行为，恰恰暴露了他自己也落入了弗洛伊德率先分析的神话模式之中。明白了吗？所以，在这种语境下，当你声称自己所做的是科学的，你就把自己置于危险境地。德里达在这篇文章中批评列维-斯特劳斯的地方，正是列维-斯特劳斯不加防备地说出类似“我的工作是科学的”这样的话的时候；但也有很多时候，德里达总是引用列维-斯特劳斯的话来佐证这一点，列维-斯特劳斯并没有这样说——列维-斯特劳斯承认他的作品，也就是他的观点，会不稳定地融入到被观察的对象之中。

Now, of course, Freud himself thought he was a scientist, and his reading of the myth was also supposed to be scientific. What was Freud’s reading of the myth about? Two or one! [laughs] It was, in other words, about the problem of incest, the problem of the over-determination of blood relations and the under-determination of blood relations. It was a thorough examination of that problematic leading to the conclusion that that’s what the myth was about. In other words, Levi-Strauss’s conclusions are already anticipated in Freud. Furthermore, what is Levi-Strauss doing? He’s denying the influence of Freud, right? It’s my myth, not his myth–right?–which of course is precisely what happens in the primal horde. It is a perfect instance of the Oedipus complex. Levi-Strauss is repudiating the father and, in repudiating the father, showing himself to fall into the very mythic pattern that Freud had been the first to analyze. Okay? So when you say that what you’re doing is scientific in a context of this sort, you are making yourself vulnerable. The moments in this essay in which Derrida is criticizing Levi-Strauss are those moments in which Levi-Strauss has unguardedly said something on the order of “My work is scientific”; but there are lots of occasions, and he always quotes Levi-Strauss tothis effect, when Levi-Strauss is not saying that–when Levi-Strauss is conceding that his work, that is to say his viewpoint, disappears unstably into the thing viewed.

第五章 德里达与符号学

Chapter 5. Derrida and Semiotic Science

好的。现在也请看一下——因为我们一直在这样做——请看一下第917页，左侧栏，德里达在那里谈论的不是列维-斯特劳斯，而是索绪尔。他在这里谈论符号的本质，他非常关注概念与声音意象之间的关系——也就是说，所指与能指之间的关系——这正是索绪尔科学的基础：也就是说，所指与能指的配对关系是索绪尔科学的基础，是其基石。所以，在左侧栏，第917页，大约在中间偏下的位置，德里达是这么说的。他说：

All right. Now also take a look at–because we’ve been doing this too–take a look at page 917, the left-hand column, where Derrida is talking not about Levi-Strauss but about Saussure. Here he’s talking about the nature of the sign, and he is concerned, very much concerned, about this relationship between the concept and the sound image–which is to say, the signified and the signifier–that is the basis of the science of Saussure: that is to say, the relationship that’s involved in the pairing of signified and signifier is the basis, the cornerstone, of the science of Saussure. So here’s what, a little more than halfway down, the left-hand column, page 917, Derrida has to say about that. He says:

……“符号”这一意义一直以来都被理解和界定为“所指的符号”，即指称所指的能指，能指本身又不同于其所指。如果抹杀能指与所指之间的根本区别，那么作为形而上学概念的“能指”一词本身就应该被抛弃[也就是说，一个先验的所指：换句话说，概念在某种意义上生成能指——对吧？——这正是索绪尔相关思考的基础]。这就引出了我之前在谈到索绪尔时举的那个带问号的例子。假设我把“所指”和“能指”之间的关系看作是两个项之间的关系——毕竟，表示“树”这个概念的一种方式[指向黑板]就是写下“树”这个词，并加上引号。所以，如果我去掉引号，剩下的就只是一个词，没有任何迹象表明它是一个概念。请注意，这现在是一种雅各布森所谓的“元语言”关系。它暗示“树”是“凉亭”的另一个词。换句话说，这不是指称与所指之间的关系，而是指称与指称之间的关系，因此这种关系的二元性被打破了，我们开始理解言语或文字的组合结构，即一个指称引出另一个——我认为——指称：德里达实际上是说，“让我们摒弃‘指称’这个词”，但他也可以说，“让我们摒弃‘所指’这个词”。我认为一个指称，它通过联想——正如索绪尔所说——通过联想引发一个后续的指称，这个指称又引发另一个指称，如此往复。用解构主义的语言来说，这就是我们所说的“链”，即意义链：它不是一种组织模式，而是一种不断自我复制和自我扩展的模式，它不可简化地呈线性发展，并通过一系列时间关联向前推进。

… [T]he signification “sign” has always been comprehended and determined, in its sense, as sign-of, signifier referring to a signified, signifier different from its signified. If one erases the radical difference between signifier and signified, it is the word signifier itself which ought to be abandoned as a metaphysical concept [which is to say, a transcendental signified: in other words, the idea that the concept in some sense generates the signifier–right?–which is the basis of Saussure’s thinking about this]. Here’s where I come back to that example that I already gave you with a question mark next to it when I was talking about Saussure. Suppose I think of the relationship between “signified” and “signifier” as the relationship between twoterms–because after all, one way of signifying the concept “tree” [gestures towards the board] is to write the word “tree” and put quotation marks about it. So if I take away the quotation marks, all I have is the word with no indication that it’s a concept. Notice that this is now a relationship which Jakobson would call “metalingual.” What it suggests is that “tree” is another word for “arbor.” In other words, it’s a relationship not between a signified and a signifier but between a signifier and a signifier, so that the binarism of the relationship is broken down, and we begin to understand the combinatory structure of speech or writing as one signifier leading to another–I think– signifier: Derrida says in effect, “Let’s banish the word ‘signifier,’” but he might as well say, “Let’s banish the word ‘signified.’” I think a signifier, and it triggers by association–as Saussure would say–it triggers by association a subsequent successive signifier, which triggers another, which triggers another. That’s what gives us, in the language of deconstruction, what we call “the chain,” the signifying chain: not an organizational pattern but an ever self-replicating and self-extending pattern, irreducibly linear and forward-progressing through a sequence of temporal associations.

当你揭开概念与能指或声音意象之间关系的神秘面纱时，随之而来的一件事就是，你也揭开了存在于某种空间中的一系列联想与联想实际发生的方式（必然存在于时间之中）之间的关系的神秘面纱：换句话说，如果一个能指导致另一个能指——如果像历史那样，一件事接着一件事，言语就是一个又一个能指——那么这实际上就是索绪尔最初所谈论的联想的本质。但它并非存在于一个系统性的空间中；它存在于一个不断展开的时间中，对吗？这些就是不再满足于将符号理解为一个概念，然后我们事后赋予其意义或能指的这种理解方式所带来的一些含义。我们现在面临的情况是，我们发现自己被卷入了一场意义的洪流之中，所有这些意义在某种意义上都存在于我们出现之前，并像顺流而下一样，被一个能指依次取代另一个能指的方式所推动。而当我们后来采用“补充性”和“差异性”等概念时，我们可以更精确地思考这种推动方式。

One of the things that happens when you demystify the relationship between a concept and a signifier or a sound image is that you also demystify the relationship between a set of associations, which exist somehow in space, and the way in which association actually takes place, which is necessarily in time: in other words, if one signifier leads to another–if like history, where there’s one damn thing after another, speech is one damn signifier after another–then that is actually the nature of the associations that Saussure has been talking about in the first place. But it doesn’t exist in a systemic space; it exists in an unfolding time, right? These are some of the implications of no longer being satisfied with the way in which a sign can be understood as a concept to which we attach belatedly a signification, a signifier. What we have is a situation in which we find ourselves caught up in a stream of signification, all of which is, in a certain sense, there before we came along and are moved, as down a stream, by the way in which one signifier succeeds another in ways that later on, as we take up concepts like “supplementarity” and différance, we can think of a little bit more precisely.

第六章 “事件”与历史

Chapter 6. “Event” and History

好的。那么，最后，德里达的文章从一开始就以另一种方式印证了我们之前所说的，结构主义危机在于需要否定对起源或原因的通常理解。在结构主义中，如果某物出现，它就出现在两个事物之间。也就是说，它既不是这个也不是那个，或者说，它“出现”为既非此也非彼的存在。换句话说，它并非源于某个先行的单一原因而产生。相反，它是在某个场域内作为差异而出现的。

Okay. So now finally then, there’s one other way in which Derrida’s essay from the very outset confirms what we’ve been saying about the crisis of structuralism being the need to deny ordinary understandings of genesis or cause. In structuralism, if something emerges, it emerges from between two things. That is to say, it’s not this and it’s not this, or it “emerges” as that which is not this, not this. It doesn’t, in other words, derive from an antecedent single cause as an effect. It emerges, on the other hand, as difference within a field.

这正是德里达在你文章第915页左栏第一段中以极其复杂的方式阐述的内容：这是他在1966年约翰·霍普金斯大学那次著名会议上发表的第一句话。他说：

Now that’s what Derrida is talking about with extraordinary intensity of complication in the first paragraph of your essay, page 915, left column, first paragraph: his first words uttered at the famous conference in- at Johns Hopkins in 1966. He says:

或许在结构概念的历史中，发生过一些可以称之为“事件”的事情……这正是结构主义面临的最大难题。当结构主义思考昨天与今天有何不同时，它不得不说：昨天存在着某种共时性的数据横截面，而今天则存在着略有不同的共时性数据横截面。但结构主义既无法，也更不愿——更重要的是——去解释昨天的数据是如何演变成今天的——换句话说，它不愿解释变化本身。它看到的只是连续的横截面，并将其称为“历史”。我在这里先抛砖引玉，我们之后还会再谈到这一点：它不会说“一件事导致了另一件事”，而是说“一件事接一件事”——这是我之前对历史的一种戏谑说法。

Perhaps something has occurred in the history of the concept of structure that could be called an “event” [évênement, something which emerges, something which is there now and wasn’t there before]… That’s the most problematic issue for structuralism. When structuralism thinks about how yesterday things were different from the way they are today, it has to say: yesterday there was a certain synchronic cross-section of data, and today there’s a slightly different synchronic cross-section of data. But structuralism is unable and furthermore–much more importantly–unwilling to say anything about how yesterday’s data turned into today’s data–in other words, to say anything about change. It sees successive cross-sections, and it calls that “history.” I am anticipating here, and we’ll come back to this in other contexts: but it doesn’t say “one thing led to another”; it says “one thing after another”–in my facetious reference to history as I have already given it to you.

这就是德里达在第一段中刻意想要探讨的问题：

Now this is what Derrida is deliberately struggling with in this first paragraph:

……一个“事件”（引号），如果这个带有强烈感情色彩的词不包含某种含义的话——而结构主义思想的功能恰恰在于削弱或质疑这种含义。但无论如何，我还是要谨慎地使用“事件”（引号）这个词，就像给它加上引号一样。在这个意义上，这个事件将具有断裂（也就是说，事物之间的涌现，对吧——断裂：火山裂开，熔岩喷涌而出，对吧——一个事件）和加倍（加倍指的是“发生了某些事情”）的外在形式。正如鲍勃·迪伦会说的那样，“发生了一些事，但这不是什么新鲜事。事实上，这是对你一无所知之物的复制，因为，琼斯先生，你对那些你一无所知却一直存在的东西知之甚少——正如德里达所说——它们早已存在：某种东西浮现出来，但同时又向我们强调它早已存在，一直都存在。”

… an “event” [quote, unquote], if this loaded word did not entail a meaning which it is precisely the function of structural–or structuralist–thought to reduce or to suspect. But let me use the term “event” [quote, unquote] anyway, employing it with caution and as if in quotation marks. In this sense, this event will have the exterior form of a rupture [that is to say, an emergence among things, right–a rupture: the volcano parts and there you have lava, right–an event] and a redoubling [a redoubling in the sense that “something has happened”]. As Bob Dylan would say in effect, “Something has happened, but it’s not something new. It is, in fact, a replication of what was unbeknownst to you because, Mr. Jones, you don’t know very much of what was, unbeknownst to you, there always–as Derrida says–already: something that emerges but at the same time presses on us its status as having already been there, always already been there.”

好的。所以，从所有这些方面来看，理解结构主义是对起源论的一种有问题的批判——因为“事物并非由原因造成”的概念仍然很难理解和接受——例如，为什么我们不能说事物是由原因造成的呢？——符号的概念是思想基质与一系列衍生能指或能指系统之间任意的关系；超越神话、走向科学的概念，以及我们可以将现实归于垂直轴的概念——所有这些都是在质疑我们实际上已经着手构建的结构主义的完整性和内在安全性。我只想通过这冗长的引言向你们表明，摆在我们面前的许多工作实际上已经发生在过去，而且我们已经完成了。

All right. So in all these sorts of ways, understanding structuralism as a problematic critique of genesis–because it’s still very hard to grasp, to accept the notion of things not having been caused–why can’t we say things were caused, just for example?–the notion of the sign as an arbitrary relationship between a substratum of thought which is then somehow or another hooked onto a derivative series or a system of signifiers; the notion of getting outside of myth and being scientific, and the notion that we can ascribe reality to the vertical axis–all of these are ways of questioning the integrity, the security within its skin, of structuralism we have actually already undertaken. I only want to suggest to you with this long preamble that much of the work that lies before us is actually in the past and we have already accomplished it.

第七章 语言与写作

Chapter 7. Language and Writing

《结构、符号与游戏》是对“结构性”的批判。它不仅仅是对结构主义的批判，更是对任何具有中心的概念的批判，这种中心既是中心，又是促成性的因果原则。换句话说，我审视一个结构，然后说它有一个中心。我所说的中心是什么意思呢？我指的是一个统称，一个指导性概念，一个先验的所指，它解释了结构的本质，并且正如德里达所说，它允许在结构内部进行有限的自由游戏；但与此同时，结构本身也具有这种边界性。它可能像变形虫一样，但它仍然有边界——对吧？——因此，它同时限制了结构内部的自由游戏。这就像新批评家说文本具有结构一样。它具有某种在现象学传统中被称为“意向性结构”的东西。康德称之为“目的性”——也就是说，事物是按照某种指导模式组织起来的。

Now “Structure, Sign and Play” is a critique of “structurality.” It’s not just a critique of structuralism. It’s a critique of the idea of anything that has a center, one which is at the same time an enabling causal principle. In other words, I look at a structure and I say it has a center. What do I mean by a center? I mean a blanket term, a guiding concept, a transcendental signified, something that explains the nature of the structure and something also, as Derrida says, which allows for limited free play within the structure; but at the same time the structure has this kind of boundary nature. It may be amoeboid but it still has boundaries–right?–and so at the same time limits the free play within the structure. That’s like the New Critics saying that a text has structure. It has something that actually in the phenomenological tradition is called an “intentional structure.” Kant calls it “purposiveness”–that is to say, the way in which the thing is organized according to some sort of guiding pattern.

但把意向性结构称为中心，与谈论赋予它存在的意图主体、作者、存在者或理念完全不同，因为后者是外在的。那是先于结构的东西。那是起源。那是原因，对吧？换句话说，意图主体在外部，而我们可以说意向性结构在内部。但这本身就是一个问题。如何从意图主体推导出意向性结构，反之亦然？正如德里达令人费解地告诉我们的，中心既是中心，又不是中心。它既是组织结构的东西，又是实际上没有资格组织任何东西的东西，因为它不在结构之内；它在结构之外，像饼干模具一样从外部强加于结构之上，对吧？这便是德里达关于中心思考的一个引子。

But to speak of an intentional structure as a center is not at all the same thing as to speak of an intending person, author, being, or idea that brought it into existence, because that’s extraneous. That’s something prior. That’s genesis. That’s a cause, right? The intending author, in other words, is outside, whereas we can argue that the intentional structure is inside. But that’s a problem. How do you get from an intending author to an intentional structure and back? A center is both a center and not a center, as Derrida maddeningly tells us. It is both that which organizes a structure and that which isn’t really qualified to organize anything, because it’s not in the structure; it’s outside the structure, something that imposes itself from without like a cookie cutter on the structure, right? This then is an introductory moment in Derrida’s thinking about centers.

在第916页左下角的栏目中，他将形而上学的历史描述为对中心不断诉诸的历史：也就是说，诉诸于某种万物起源的理念，某种可以被理解为万物存在之根源的起源。这份清单编排得非常巧妙。这是左下角栏目的底部。它并非严格按照时间顺序排列，但同时又能让你感受到历代形而上学哲学家对第一因、起源以及决定一切事物的因素的思考。我仅从清单的末尾部分开始讨论：“先验性、意识或良知、上帝、人等等”。请注意，尽管这份清单并非严格按照时间顺序排列，但人确实取代了上帝。换句话说，他是在思考西方文化的发展。在中世纪以及某种程度上在近代早期，我们生活在一个以神为中心的世界里。就人而言，只要他能理解自身作为人的本质，他就会将自身理解为神圣创造的产物，理解为源自上帝的某种存在，理解为参与并受益于神圣临在的所有其他存在之一。然而，启蒙运动的兴起也伴随着人类中心主义的兴起，当启蒙运动达到顶峰时，从布莱克到马克思再到尼采，所有人都开始宣称，不是上帝创造了人，而是人创造了上帝。人已成为超越性的所指。在当下的历史时刻，一切都源于人类意识，所有概念，无论何种概念，都可以从这个角度来理解。

On page 916 in the lower left-hand column, he talks about the history of metaphysics as a history of successive appeals to a center: that is to say, to some idea from which everything derives, some genesis or other that can be understood as responsible for everything that there is. The list is very cunningly put together. This is bottom of the left-hand column. It’s not necessarily chronological, but at the same time it gives you a sense of successive metaphysical philosophers thinking about first causes, origins, and about whatever it is that determines everything else. I’ll just take up the list toward the end: “transcendentality, consciousness, or conscience, God, man, and so forth.” Notice that though the list isn’t strictly chronological, man nevertheless does succeed God. In other words, he’s thinking about the development of Western culture. In the Middle Ages and to some extent in the Early Modern period, we live in a theocentric world. Insofar as he understands himself as man at all, man understands himself as a product of divine creativity, as something derived from God, as one entity among all other entities who participate and benefit from the divine presence. But then of course, the rise of the Enlightenment is also the rise of anthropocentrism, and by the time the Enlightenment is in full cry you get everybody from Blake to Marx to Nietzsche saying not that God invented man, but that man invented God. Man has become the transcendental signified. Everything derives now in this historical moment from human consciousness, and all concepts of whatever kind can be understood in that light.

当然，他说了“人”之后，[笑]又说了“等等”。换句话说，人之后还有别的东西。换句话说，人是一个历史时刻。很多人都指出，在某个时期之前，根本不存在“人”这个概念；而在文化史上的某个特定时刻之后，从各种真实的意义上讲，“人”这个概念也随之消失了。德里达关于他所提出的“事件”的论点是，一个新的先验所指实际上已经取代了“人”。换句话说，世界不再以人类为中心；它是语言中心的。显然，德里达所说的事件——出现、断裂、一个产生影响的事件——就是语言的出现。

But then of course he says, having said “man,” [laughs] he says “and so forth.” In other words, something comes after man. Man is, in other words, an historical moment. There are lots of people who have pointed out to us that before a certain period, there was no such thing as man, and in a variety of quite real senses, after a certain moment in the history of culture, there is also no such thing as man. The argument Derrida is making about the emergence of his “event” is that a new transcendental signified has actually substituted itself for man. In other words, the world is no longer anthropocentric; it’s linguistic. Obviously, the event that Derrida is talking about–the emergence, the rupture, an event which makes a difference–is the emergence of language.

我真正想谈的是第916页右侧栏的内容：

What I really want to talk about here is something that is on page 916, the right-hand column:

出现的时刻（换句话说，大约在中间位置的事件）是语言入侵普遍问题的时刻（换句话说，是语言取代先前的先验所指——即人——的时刻）；是在没有中心或起源的情况下，一切都成为话语的时刻——前提是我们能对这个词达成共识——也就是说，一切都成为一个系统，在这个系统中，中心所指、原始的或先验的所指，永远无法绝对地存在于差异系统之外。他一方面声称语言存在，一方面又抹杀了语言。换句话说，他痛苦地意识到，语言只不过是新的上帝，新的人。许多对解构主义的批判都认为，解构主义只是将语言工具化，赋予它能动性和意识，仿佛它是上帝或人，然后又假装它不是。这是对解构主义的一种常见回应。

The moment [of emergence–the event, in other words, about halfway down] was that in which language invaded the universal problematic [in other words, that moment in which language displaced the previous transcendental signified, which was man]; that in which, in the absence of a center or origin, everything became discourse–provided we can agree on this word–that is to say, when everything became a system where the central signified, the original or transcendental signified, is never absolutely present outside a system of differences. He’s making a claim for language while erasing it. In other words, he’s painfully aware that language is just the new God, the new Man. Many critiques of deconstruction take the form of saying that deconstruction simply instrumentalizes language, gives it agency, and gives it consciousness as though it were God or man and then pretends that it isn’t. This is a common response to deconstruction.

德里达事先就意识到了这一点。他实际上是在说：“你看，我知道我们说一切皆语言是有风险的”，或者，如果你愿意的话，一切皆话语。与此同时，我们表达的又是另一种意思，因为此前我们面临的问题是：换句话说，我们面临的问题是，某种事物是结构的一部分——也就是说，上帝内在于万物之中，人类意识渗透到它所遇到的一切——换句话说，某种事物既是结构的一部分，同时又存在于结构之外。上帝创造了世界，然后，正如弥尔顿自己所说，祂“不受约束地退隐”，对吧？上帝并不在那里。上帝是隐藏的上帝：上帝是缺席于世的上帝，实际上，祂也是世界的结构。同样的话也适用于人。人将对世界的感知带入存在，然后置身事外，以某种方式通过审美或其他遥远的方式将其吸收。

Derrida is aware of it in advance. He says in effect, “Look, I know we’re running this risk in saying everything is language,” or, if you will here, everything is discourse. At the same time, we are saying something different, because hitherto we had this problem: in other words, we had the problem of something being part of a structure–that is to say God is immanent in all things, human consciousness pervades everything that it encounters–in other words, something which is part of a structure but which is at the same time outside of it. God creates the world and then sort of, as Milton says himself, “uncircumscrib’d withdraws,” right? God is not there. God is the Dieu caché: God is the hidden God who is absent from the world and is, in effect, also the structure of the world. The same thing can be said of man. Man brings the sense of what the world is into being and then stands aside and somehow sort of takes it in through an aesthetic register or in some other remote way.

语言并非如此。语言始终沉浸于自身之中。德里达认为，语言的特殊之处在于，将其视为置身事外的存在是毫无意义的。这是对结构主义批判的核心所在。语言并非与言语相悖；它始终显现于言语之中，对吗？这仅仅是一个无法维持的区分，因此他称之为“事件”。换句话说，琼斯先生，某种意义重大的事情已经发生，那就是语言，对吗？

Language doesn’t do that. Language is perpetually immersed in itself. Derrida is claiming that language is different in the sense that it makes no sense to talk about it as standing outside of what’s going on. This is an essential part of the critique of structuralism. Language is not other than speech; it is perpetually manifest in speech, right? It’s simply a distinction that can’t be maintained, which is why he calls it an “event.” In other words, something of significance has happened, Mr. Jones, and that is language, right?

第八章 语言、补充性和差异

Chapter 8. Language, Supplementarity, and DiffÃ©rance

好吧。所以我想，在剩下的时间里——唉，时间不多了——我们最好先问问“语言”到底是什么。我们讨论过它，也和它有过很多接触，但我们当然仍然对它一无所知。很快我们就会知道了。首先，我们最好先说明一点，正如我们引用的内容已经表明的那样，语言并不完全是索绪尔式的。也就是说，它并非一个符号系统，被理解为概念世界和能指世界之间稳定的关系。它并非一个语言可以被理解为某种表达思想手段的世界。解构主义质疑语言与思想之间的区别，因为它质疑能指与所指之间的区别，所以它并不完全是索绪尔式的——尽管正如德里达所说，它离不开索绪尔式的词汇。

All right. So I suppose in the time remaining and, alas, there isn’t a lot of it, we’d better ask what “language” is. We’ve talked about it. We’ve had a great deal to do with it, but of course we still haven’t the slightest idea what it is. Soon we’ll know. First of all, we’d better say, as is already clear from what we’ve been quoting, language is not quite Saussurian. That is to say, it is not a system of signs understood as stable relationships between a concept world and a world of signifying. It is not a world in which language can be understood as somehow or another a means of expressing thought. Deconstruction calls into question the distinction between language and thought in calling into question the distinction between signifier and signified, so it’s not quite Saussuria–even though, as Derrida says, it can’t do without a Saussurian vocabulary.

另一个问题——也与对索绪尔的批判相关——是，这种认为内在的、本质的东西是可以表达出来并且应该表达出来的观点；所以，如果我认为符号是表达思想的一种方式，请注意，如果我是索绪尔，我会把这种表达称为“声音意象”。换句话说，根据德里达的说法，在索绪尔的传统中，语言似乎更重视声音而非文字，而非图像。他声称这是形而上学历史中一种隐藏的偏见。换句话说，为什么我们要把语言视为言语，视为声音？为什么我们要把声音——以神圣逻各斯（logos，即“道”）的意义来理解：“太初有道”——为什么我们要把声音视为一种完全临在的同步性，它绝对存在于意识之中，或者存在于我们理解语言来源的任何地方？声音有什么特别之处？为什么人们对写作有这么多负面的评价？写作与声音并无不同。声音也是在时间中以组合的方式表达出来的。声音也可以被理解为铭刻在耳朵上。这是德里达经常使用的比喻，一种刻在耳朵上的文字。索绪尔试图区分某种原始的、直接的、非驱动性的事物——声音——和某种仅仅是重复的、仅仅是再现的、仅仅是声音的婢女的事物——即文字——德里达认为这种区分是形而上学的，但它需要受到质疑。

Another problem is–and also related to the critique of Saussure–is that this idea that what’s inward, what is essential, is something that can be voiced and should be voiced; so that if I think a sign is a way of talking about the expression of a thought, notice that I call–if I am Saussure–that expression a “sound image.” In other words, language, according to Derrida, in the Saussurian tradition seems to privilege sound over script, over what is graphic. He claims that this is a hidden bias in the whole history of metaphysics. Why, in other words, should we think of language as speech, as voice? Why do we think of voice–in the sense of the divine logos, the word: “in the beginning was the word”–why do we think of voice as a kind of fully present simultaneity that is absolutely present precisely in consciousness or wherever it is that we understand language to derive from? What’s so special about voice? Why do they say all of these terrible things about writing? Writing is no different from voice. Voice, too, is articulated combinatorially in time. Voice, too, can be understood as inscribed on the ear. This is a metaphor that Derrida frequently uses, as a kind of writing on the ear. The distinction, which Derrida takes to be metaphysical, that Saussure wants to make between something primary, something immediate and underivative–voice–and something merely repetitious, merely reproductive, merely a handmaiden to voice–namely writing–needs to be called into question.

现在，我们需要谈谈德里达用来支撑他对传统语言观念批判的几个关键术语。第一个术语与补充性概念有关。他指出，补充物要么是对不完整事物的补充，要么是对已完整事物的补充。例如，我服用维生素C。我也喝很多橙汁，所以我的维生素C摄入量很充足。如果我服用维生素C片，我就补充了已经完整的维生素C；但如果我不喝橙汁，那么我服用维生素C片当然是在补充不完整的维生素C，但无论哪种情况，我们都称之为补充。要记住这两种补充物之间的概念差异非常困难。

Now this is the point at which we need to say something about a number of key terms that Derrida uses to sustain this sort of criticism of traditional ideas of language. The first has to do with the notion of supplementarity. A supplement, he points out, is something that either completes something that isn’t complete or adds to something that already iscomplete. For example, I take vitamin C. I also drink a lot of orange juice, so I’ve got plenty of vitamin C, and if I take a vitamin C pill I am supplementing something that’s already complete; but if I don’t drink any orange juice, then of course if I take a vitamin C pill I am supplementing something that’s not complete, but either way we always call it a supplement. It’s very difficult even to keep in mind the conceptual difference between these two sorts of supplement.

传统意义上的符号是自足的、独立的。索绪尔将其视为科学对象，认为符号既是任意的又是差异性的。然而，在解构主义的批判下，符号的意义却在不断增殖，它不会停滞不前，其本质既是任意的又是差异性的，因此无法被理解为自足或独立的。符号会不断地渗入或溢出到后续的符号中，从而持续留下德里达所谓的“痕迹”。也就是说，当我们考察一个言语行为的展开过程时，我们会看到后续符号是如何被“污染”的。这并非贬义词，而是指受到先前符号的影响，就像“打开窗户，流感病毒”一样。补充性是理解语言表达同时具有线性和不断增殖、不断自我复杂化的本质的一种方式。

Now a sign traditionally understood is self-sufficient, self-contained. Saussure has made it a scientific object by saying that it’s both arbitrary and differential, but a sign understood under the critique of deconstruction is something that is perpetually proliferating signification, something that doesn’t stand still, and something that can’t be understood as self-sufficient or independent in its nature as being both arbitrary and differential. It is a bleeding or spilling into successive signs in such a way that it perpetually leaves what Derrida calls “traces.” That is to say, as we examine the unfolding of a speech act, we see the way in which successive signs are contaminated. That’s not meant to be a bad word but suggests being influenced, one might say, in the sense of “open the window and influenza,” by those signs that precede it. Supplementarity is a way of understanding the simultaneously linear and ever proliferating, ever self-complicating nature of verbal expression.

“差异”（différance）一词，除其他含义外，也是一种讨论声音与书写之间差异的方式。声音与书写虽有诸多共通之处，二者之间仍存在差异。顺便一提，声音与书写并非稳定的二元对立。在德里达的理论体系中，不存在稳定的二元对立。声音与书写的区别在于，书写能够提供声音无法提供的各种差异指示。德里达坚持将“差异”（différance）拼写错误，其趣味之一在于，就声音作为声音而言，我们无法区分“差异”（différance）和“差异”（différence）。实际上，或许可以略微区分，但这并非值得深究的差异。换句话说，“差异”（différance）一词，用字母“a”代替了“b”，而我们不妨回想一下《差异》（Différance）一文中关于“a”的论述，它象征着金字塔、阿尔法、起源，以及弑君，因为请记住，“a”代表着超越性的所指：上帝、人等等。只有当我们把语言理解为书面语时，才能领会 différance 中 a 的变奏，因为在口语中，这些差异模式并不会被注意到。

Now différance is a way, among other things, of talking about the difference between voice and writing. There is a difference between voice and writing even though they have so much in common. Voice and writing, by the way, are not a stable binary. There are no stable binaries in Derrida. The difference between voice and writing is that writing can give us all kinds of indication of difference that voice can’t give us. Part of the interest of misspelling différance, as Derrida insists on doing, is that we can’t, in terms of voice as sound, tell the difference between différance and différence. Actually, one can, slightly, but it’s not a difference worth lingering over. Différance, in other words, with its substitution of the a–and remember the riff in the essay “Différance” on a as a pyramid, as alpha, as origin, and as killing the king because the king, remember, is the transcendental signified: God, man and so forth.
