He’s talking about the way in which people in the culture industry who appreciate music are completely victimized by the coloratura local effect, what you might call–this is a conductor whom Adorno hated–the Toscanini effect: that flourishing of a particular moment in a concerto, the riding it into the ground at the expense of the whole, and everything that has what Adorno elsewhere calls “lip-smacking euphony”; in other words, a kind of cultivation of perfection of local sound, as opposed to an awareness of the total composition. So he says in the first passage:

当下的愉悦和表面上的欢愉成为一种借口，使听者得以逃避对整体的思考，而整体的内涵恰恰在于正确的聆听。听者沿着阻力最小的路径（毕竟，聆听如此美妙）被转化为默许的购买者。局部片段不再像现代主义中那样，对整体起到批判的作用。（换句话说，不和谐本身就是对我们通常认为的那种整体和谐的批判，对吗？因此，从某种意义上说，部分可以被理解为对整体的批判，而无需挑战或破坏整体。）局部片段不再对整体起到批判的作用。相反，它们阻碍了成功的审美整体对社会缺陷整体的批判。换句话说，除了艺术作品中真正实现的完整性之外，没有任何东西可以批判社会糟糕整体的虚假性。这些整体意义之间的差异，恰恰是批判的领域，在阿多诺看来，它或许——仅仅是或许——能够唤醒文化工业的受害者，使他们从幸福的顺从和默许的沉睡中醒来。

The delight in the moment and the gay façade become an excuse for absolving the listener from the thought of the whole, whose claim is comprised in proper listening. The listener is converted along his line of least resistance [because after all, it’s so beautiful to listen to] into the acquiescent purchaser. No longer do the partial moments serve as a critique of the whole as they sometimes do in Modernism. [Dissonance, in other words, is in and of itself a critique of that overarching harmony with which we associate wholeness, right? So there’s a real sense in which the parts can be understood as a critique of the whole without challenging or breaking down the whole.] No longer do the partial moments serve as a critique of the whole. Instead they suspend the critique which the successful aesthetic totality exerts against the flawed one of society. In other words, nothing can criticize the inauthenticity of the bad totalities of society except the authenticity of a genuine achieved wholeness in a work of art. The difference between these senses of the whole is precisely the zone of critique which in Adorno’s view might–just might–awaken the victim of the culture industry from the slumbers of happy conformism and acquiescence.

现在，在第二段中，为了进一步强调这一点：

Now in the second passage, just to reinforce this:

像贝尔格、勋伯格和韦伯恩这样的伟大现代主义作曲家被其他马克思主义批评家称为个人主义者（换句话说，像卢卡奇这样的人不喜欢卢卡奇所谓的“形式的拜物教”，即以牺牲社会指涉和表达为代价来物化形式），然而他们的作品只不过是与那些摧毁个性的力量进行的一次对话，这些力量无形的阴影巨大地投射在他们的音乐之上。在音乐中，集体力量也在消灭一种无法挽救的个性，但只有个体才能自觉地代表集体的目标来对抗这种力量。## 第四章 布洛赫的希望原则 ​​换句话说，艺术作品的整体性——已实现的、成功的、真实的整体性——以一种当前霸权的任何虚假整体性都无法做到甚至无法近似的方式，模拟了一个集体国家的整体性。换句话说，在纯粹的形式中——用阿多诺的话说——蕴含着一种政治。纯粹形式的实现，归根结底是由各个部分组成的，其中蕴含着一种政治意味，即模拟集体社会的实现。

Great Modernist composers like Berg, Schoenberg and Webern are called individualists by other Marxist critics [in other words, by people like Lukacs who don’t like what Lukacs would call “fetishization of form,” reification of form at the expense of social reference and expression], and yet their work is nothing but a single dialogue with the powers that destroy individuality, powers whose formless shadows fall gigantically on their music. In music, too, collective powers are liquidating an individuality past saving, but against them only individuals are capable of consciously representing the aims of collectivity. ## Chapter 4. Bloch’s Principle of Hope In other words, the totality–the achieved, successful, authentic totality–of the work of art models the totality of a collective state in ways that none of the false totalities of current hegemonies can possibly do or even approximate. In other words, there is an implicit politics–in Adorno’s argument–in pure form. The achievement of pure form, which is after all a collection of parts, is an implicit politics modeling the achievement of a collective society.

这就是阿多诺的论点。这确实引人入胜。正如我所说，这或许有些异想天开，因为很难想象有人会听勋伯格的音乐后说：“哎呀，也许我应该当个共产主义者。”[笑声][笑声] 换句话说，真正付诸实践需要一定的难度，但同时，从理智上讲，这在我看来是一种引人入胜的思维方式，而且确实值得深思，哪怕仅仅是因为马克思主义批评常常致力于批判西方文明主流美学的构成要素，而这种主流美学实际上是一种对整体性的迷恋。想想新批评，诗歌的统一性，将离散的本体论对象视为一个统一的整体。当然，这是马克思主义批评中常见的攻击，而像阿多诺这样的人物，作为这种整体性的倡导者，却将其视为集体性的模式而非自恋的个人主义模式，这非常有趣。

So that is the argument of Adorno. It’s a fascinating one. As I say, it’s perhaps somewhat quixotic because it’s kind of hard to imagine anyone actually listening to Schoenberg and saying, “Gee. Maybe I should be a communist.” [laughter] [laughs] Actually putting this to work, in other words, entails a certain amount of difficulty, but at the same time, intellectually, it seems to me to be a fascinating turn of thought and one that certainly does give one pause, if only because Marxist criticism is so often engaged in a critique of what it takes to be the mainstream aesthetic of Western civilization, which is a kind of fetishization of wholeness. Think of the New Criticism, the unity of the poem, the discrete ontological object as a unified whole. This is, of course, commonplace in being attacked by Marxist criticism, and it’s very interesting to see a figure like Adorno, a champion of this very wholeness, who sees it as a model not of narcissistic individuality, but rather of collectivity.

好了。最后——我不会在此过多赘述，因为这将是周四讲座的主题——马克思主义的最后一个美学选择令人惊讶。它实际上可以追溯到恩斯特·布洛赫的著作《希望的原则》。布洛赫在书中论证，在我们所处的这个世界——换句话说，在晚期资本主义下，希望被扼杀，所有人的可能性都被扼杀——已经没有任何希望可言。这是一种悲观的预言，布洛赫用它反驳了这样一种观点：尤其是在民间艺术、民俗、口头文化和大众文化中——换句话说，在被剥夺者和被压迫者的作品中，存在着一种乌托邦主义、一种浪漫情怀，以及一种并非是对过去事物的怀念（尽管它似乎表现为怀旧），而是对现实世界中根本不可能实现的未来的一种投射。

All right. Finally–and I won’t pause much over this because it’s going to be the subject of Thursday’s lecture–the last aesthetic option for Marxism is a surprising one. It actually goes back to a book by Ernst Bloch called The Principle of Hope, in which Bloch essentially argues that in the world as we have it–in other words, the grinding down of hope, the grinding down of possibility for all in late capitalism–there is no longer any hope available. This is a kind of gloomy prognosis with which Bloch counters the idea that especially in folk art, folkways, oral culture and in popular culture–in other words, in the expressions of longing one finds in the work of the dispossessed and the oppressed–there is a kind of utopianism, a romance, and a sense not so much of wishing for something past, even though it seems to take the form of nostalgia, but rather a projection of a possibility on the future which is simply unavailable in the real world.

当然，我能想到的最佳例子就是《大岩糖山》。这是一首由劳改营的囚犯演唱的歌曲，歌颂着酒水顺着山坡流淌成溪，一切都那么美好。换句话说，《大岩糖山》完美地诠释了恩斯特·布洛赫所理解的“希望原则”。弗雷德里克·詹姆逊也认真对待了这一点，这并非体现在你即将阅读的《政治无意识》节选中，而是体现在该书导论章节的前面部分。在那部分中，他谈到了浪漫主义取代破产的现实主义美学——被资产阶级挪用的现实主义美学——的重要性，以及浪漫主义如何在看似绝望的世界中表达被压迫者和被剥夺者的希望。所以，浪漫的理念，乌托邦式的憧憬，也是二十世纪马克思主义思想某种转向的最后一种可行的美学，这种转向既有趣又富有成效。

Of course, the best example I can think of is “The Big Rock Candy Mountain.” This is a song sung by people on chain gangs about liquor running down the sides of mountains in rivulets and everything just as it should be. “The Big Rock Candy Mountain,” in other words, is a perfect example of the “principle of hope” as Ernst Bloch understands it. This is something that’s picked up and taken very seriously by Fredric Jameson, not so much in the excerpt from The Political Unconscious that you’ll be reading for the lecture but in an earlier part of that introductory chapter in which he talks about the importance of romance replacing the bankrupt aesthetic of realism–the aesthetic of realism that has been appropriated by the bourgeoisie–and as expressing in a seemingly hopeless world the hopes of the oppressed and the dispossessed. So this too, the idea of romance, the idea of utopian evocation, is a last, viable aesthetic for a certain turn of Marxist thought which has been interesting and productive in the twentieth century.

好的。今天我们来看第二点和第三点，本雅明的参与式美学和阿多诺的现代主义整体论。我们来看看它们之间是如何相互冲突的。

All right. So today we take our numbers two and three, the participatory aesthetic of Benjamin and the Modernist totality of Adorno. We see the way in which they conflict with each other.

第五章 本杰明与机械复制

Chapter 5. Benjamin and Mechanical Reproduction

在某种程度上，我希望我们仍在阅读《恋物癖性格》这篇文章，因为它比你书中阿多诺和霍克海默合著的《文化工业》节选更贴近美学；但《文化工业》本身也是对本雅明《机械复制时代的艺术作品》的回应，正如1938年发表的《音乐中的恋物癖性格》一样。阿多诺是本雅明的挚友，两人曾就本雅明的《艺术作品》一文通信——顺便一提，这些信件后来在1973年的《新左派评论》上再版，有兴趣的朋友可以查阅，因为这为我们了解本雅明和阿多诺在这个问题上的分歧提供了另一种视角。

Now in some ways I wish we were still reading the “Fetish Character” essay because it has more to do with aesthetics than the excerpt you have in your book by Adorno and Horkheimer called “The Culture Industry”; but “The Culture Industry,” too, is a response, as was the “Fetish Character in Music” which was published 1938, to Benjamin’s “Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction.” Adorno was a close friend of Benjamin’s and exchanged letters about Benjamin’s “Work of Art” essay with him–letters, by the way, which were republished in The New Left Review of 1973, for those of you who are interested in looking at them, because this is another source of ways of seeing how Benjamin and Adorno were in conflict over this matter.

正如我所说，阿多诺和本雅明是非常亲密的朋友。本雅明在20世纪30年代只短暂地做过一段时间的马克思主义批评家。此前，他更感兴趣的是神秘主义文学和黑格尔哲学传统，即使在20世纪30年代，他也常常在两种可能性之间摇摆不定。他曾在1926年和1927年访问过莫斯科。他对当时苏联世界仍然充满活力的文化产生了浓厚的兴趣，正如我之前所说。与此同时，他与马克思主义剧作家贝托尔特·布莱希特结下了深厚的友谊，并深受其影响。但另一位非常亲密的朋友，一位同样有影响力的朋友，是移居耶路撒冷的犹太神学家格尔绍姆·肖勒姆。他是一位犹太复国主义者，希望本雅明能和他一起在耶路撒冷学习《托拉》，并投身于那个社群，而不是本雅明可能更倾向于的那种国际马克思主义社群，这尤其要归功于他与布莱希特的友谊。

Adorno and Benjamin, as I say, were very close friends. Benjamin was only for a relatively brief period in the 1930s a Marxist critic. He had hitherto been much more interested in cabalistic literature and in the Hegelian tradition of philosophy, and even in the 1930s he was famously torn between two possibilities. He had visited Moscow in 1926, ’27. He had become interested in what was still, after all, as I’ve said, a vibrant culture in the Soviet world. At the same time, he had become very close friends with the Marxist playwright Bertolt Brecht and had fallen also very much under his influence. But another very close friend, a friend equally influential, was the Jewish theologian Gershom Scholem, who had emigrated to Jerusalem, who was a Zionist, and who wanted Benjamin to join him studying the Torah in Jerusalem and to engage himself in that community, as opposed to the sort of international Marxist community toward which Benjamin was perhaps more leaning, especially owing to his friendship with Brecht.

因此，即使在20世纪30年代，即使在本雅明撰写《艺术作品》以及一篇篇幅更短、更具倾向性的文章《作为生产者的作者》（1936年）的时期——在《作为生产者的作者》中，他实际上详细探讨了他在《艺术作品》中只是顺带提及的内容——也就是说，在俄国，人们评判一个人不仅看他能否胜任工作，还看他能否谈论工作，能否把工作写下来，能否描述工作，能否写宣传册，能否给报社写信，换句话说，是否能够参与其中，是否不仅参与劳动，而且还参与对劳动的反思，这实际上意味着每个人都可以成为作者，而且每个作者都是生产者——也就是说，从事写作，而写作是劳动生产不可分割的一部分，所有这些都是本雅明关注的焦点——与此同时，即使在这一焦点之内，他的一部分内心也正被另一种矛盾所撕裂。方向。任何人在阅读《艺术作品》一文时，都无法忽视本雅明对“光环”的强烈怀旧之情。对本雅明而言，要说我们必须打破光环，代之以一种参与式模式，这种模式与机械复制互动并融入其中，这并非易事。

So even in the 1930s, even in the period when Benjamin wrote his “Work of Art” essay and also a shorter, even more tendentious essay called “The Author as Producer,” 1936, an essay in which he actually takes up at length something he mentions in passing in “The Work of Art” essay–that is to say, the way in which in Russia everybody is judged not just for being able to do a job but for being able to talk about doing a job, to be able to write it up, to describe it, to write a brochure about it, to write a letter to the paper about it, and in other words to participate, to be engaged not just in the labor force but also in reflections on the labor force in a way that really does mean that everyone can be an author and also that every author is a producer–that is to say, engaged in writing, which is part and parcel of the productions of labor, all of this was a focus of Benjamin’s–at the same time, even within this focus, part of him is being torn in another direction. No one can for a minute, in reading the “Work of Art” essay, fail to notice that Benjamin evinces tremendous nostalgia for the “aura.” It’s not an easy thing for Benjamin to say we have to tear down the aura and replace it with a kind of participatory mode that engages with and is involved in mechanical reproduction.

我不知道：我读书的时候，断断续续地在伯克利校园里的一家美术用品和画框店打工——干了好几年——当然，每个学生都需要一幅画挂在房间里；所以我们店里堆满了梵高的《向日葵》、马蒂斯的《舞者》和其他一些画作，都是18乘24英寸的，我们管它们叫“笔触版画”。这些版画裱在硬纸板上，然后一个巨大的——嗖！——像饼干模具一样的东西会压在上面，把笔触的纹理压印到版画上。如果你在学期初眯着眼睛看，就能看到这些版画就这样被压下来。 [做手势] 然后，在你还没反应过来之前，那一摞摞的版画就不见了，所以你确信无疑，因为你知道那一摞里有多少幅版画，240个学生的房间里都挂满了梵高的《向日葵》和[笑声][笑声]马蒂斯的《舞者》。你会对自己说，这就是机械复制的成果吗？你会再次问自己，这作为一种美学价值究竟是什么？没错，它把艺术从博物馆里带了出来。没错，这意味着没人需要花五十美元去排长队才能一睹《蒙娜丽莎》的真容。没错，它确实把艺术带到了人们的身边，但是，这种对这些机械复制的、笔触版画的迷恋——毕竟，它就是迷恋[笑声]——究竟意味着什么？这种迷恋是以牺牲人们对艺术史，甚至是对梵高和马蒂斯的真正了解为代价的吗？

I don’t know: when I was a student I worked on and off–I did this for years–in an art supply and picture framing store on the Berkeley campus, and of course, every student needed a picture to put in his room; so we had huge stacks of Van Gogh’s Sunflowers and Matisse’s Dancers and certain other paintings, all of them eighteen-by-twenty-four, which we called “brushstroke prints.” They were mounted on cardboard, and a huge–whhhhoooom!–cookie-cutter of some kind would come down on top of them, actually laminating into the print the appearance of brushstrokes. These things, if you squinted at the beginning of a semester you saw the stack going down like this. [Gestures.] Then before you knew it, the stacks were gone, and so you knew for a fact, because you knew how many prints were in that stack, that 240 students’ rooms were festooned with Van Gogh’s Sunflowers and [laughter] [laughs] Matisse’s Dancers. You said to yourself, This is the fruit of mechanical reproduction? You asked yourself, again, Just what is the value of this as an aesthetic? Yeah, it takes it out of the museum. Yeah, it means that nobody has to pay fifty bucks in order to wait in a long line in order to get a peep at the Mona Lisa. Yeah, it really does bring it home to the people, but how and in what way and at the expense of what genuine knowledge of art history, and even of Van Gogh and Matisse, does the fetishization–because it is, after all, [laughs] fetishization–of these little mechanically reproduced brushstroke prints amount to?

显然，这会带来一些复杂情况，而且这些复杂情况——正是我讲这个故事的重点——本雅明对这些复杂情况并非一无所知。他非常清楚，归根结底，他所倡导的那种美学的最大威胁在于它可能被资本所掌控。当然，我有点跑题了，因为阿多诺正是这样反驳他的，但与此同时，这确实是本雅明在20世纪30年代所处的境地。

Obviously, this introduces complications, and they’re complications–the whole point of my anecdote–they’re complications of which Benjamin is far from being unaware. He knows extremely well that, after all, the greatest threat to an aesthetic of the kind he propounds is that it can be commandeered by capital. Of course, I’m getting ahead of myself, because that’s precisely what Adorno says in opposition to him, but in the meantime that was the situation of Benjamin in the 1930s.

第 6 章阿多诺与墨守成规

Chapter 6. Adorno and Conformism

与此同时，阿多诺去了美国。本雅明自1933年起就一直住在巴黎。阿多诺去了美国，但他憎恨那里。阿多诺的世界观中的阴郁，与其说是源于他在魏玛共和国时期所经历的脆弱的民主形式（尽管这些经历也带有某种不祥之兆），不如说是源于纳粹主义的兴起（因为和本雅明一样，他也得以逃离纳粹的魔爪）。他所感受到的阴郁，以及贯穿他作品的阴郁——毕竟，他的写作始于20世纪40年代中期——是他接触美国文化的结果。

Adorno, in the meantime, had gone to the United States. Benjamin was living in Paris ever since 1933. Adorno had gone to the United States, which he hated. The gloom of Adorno’s view of the world is not so much the result of his experience of the weak forms of democracy in the Weimar Republic, sort of ominous as those experiences were; not even perhaps so much the rise of Nazism, because like Benjamin he was able to flee that. The gloom that he felt and the gloom that pervades his writing, which after all starts in the mid 1940s, is the result of his exposure to American culture.

他简直无法忍受我们，也无法忍受我们的文化。他无法忍受“爵士乐”。要知道，那时还没有比波普爵士乐的时代，我一直觉得，如果阿多诺再多待一段时间，或许就能理解了。那时的爵士乐不再是保罗·怀特曼（Paul Whiteman）指挥的那种爵士乐了，而是更加严肃的爵士乐。他无法忍受电影。我最近看了一部叫《1940年的百老汇旋律》（Broadway Melody of 1940）的电影，至于原因我就不细说了，里面有弗雷德·阿斯泰尔（Fred Astaire）和埃莉诺·鲍威尔（Eleanor Powell）跳踢踏舞。弗雷德·阿斯泰尔和他的搭档乔治·墨菲（George Murphy）原本默默无闻，却被选中成为埃莉诺·鲍威尔的男主角。这简直就是塞缪尔·斯迈尔斯（Samuel Smiles）式的成功故事，两人都时不时需要做出自我牺牲。这部电影简直就是为了激怒阿多诺而拍的。 [笑声] [笑] 然而，从阿多诺永远不可能体会到的角度来看，这确实很迷人。

He simply could not stand us or our culture. He couldn’t stand “jazz.” Remember this was not yet the age of bebop, and I’ve always felt that maybe if Adorno had hung around a little longer he could have been reconciled. It was no longer the jazz of the aptly named conductor Paul Whiteman. It was jazz that was somewhat more serious. He couldn’t stand the movies. I have just been, for purposes I won’t go into, watching a film called “Broadway Melody of 1940” with Fred Astaire and Eleanor Powell tap dancing. Fred Astaire and his sidekick, George Murphy, are grabbed out of obscurity in order to be the leading gentlemen of Eleanor Powell. It’s a perfect sort of Samuel Smiles success story, replete with the necessity of occasional self-sacrifice on the part of both of them. It is made for the wrath of Adorno, this film. [laughter] [laughs] It’s nevertheless, in ways that Adorno could not possibly ever come to feel, quite charming.

但阿多诺对美国文化毫无兴趣。他预见到了美国社会学中那种痴迷于美国社会受顺从主义支配的趋势。他认为这是文化产业无处不在、压迫性极强的控制所致，以至于我们所有的怪癖、奇特之处和微小的原创性都会被文化产业仔细评估。文化产业会为它们找到合适的定位，然后，我们就会像其他人一样被收买。在阿多诺看来，我们根本无法摆脱文化产业这种铁板一块、无处不在的监视和支配。

But Adorno wanted no part of American culture. He was in anticipation of that whole trend of American sociology obsessed with the way in which American society is dominated by conformism. He takes this to be the effect, the result, of the pervasive, oppressive thumb of the culture industry, so that our very eccentricities, our very quirks and little originalities, all of them are assessed carefully by the culture industry. A niche is found for them, and the next thing you know, we’re suborned just like everybody else. There is for Adorno no sideways escape from the monolithic, ubiquitous surveillance and dominance of the culture industry.

第七章 本雅明、旁观者与分心

Chapter 7. Benjamin, the Spectator, and Distraction

好的。现在，《机械复制时代的艺术作品》显然受到了1934年以前俄罗斯艺术发展前景的影响：尤其是维尔托夫的电影，以及其他一些方式，在这些方式中，本雅明认为观众确实可以成为参与者。本雅明认为，在这样的语境下，艺术作品高高在上的光环被成功打破是一件好事，我们不再以狂热的专注和沉思的姿态站在艺术作品前，而是主动与它们接触，它们也主动与我们接触。我们彼此相遇，融入其中；我们成为它们的一部分。

All right. Now the “Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction” is influenced obviously by the promise of Russian art before 1934: the films of Vertov in particular, and other ways in which it’s possible for Benjamin to say that the spectator really can be a participant. It’s possible for Benjamin to say that in such contexts it’s a good thing that the pedastaled aura of the work of art has been successfully torn down, that we no longer stand in rapturous attention and in contemplative postures before works of art but that we reach out to them and they reach out to us. We meet halfway and we become engaged with them; we become part of them.

那么，这在本文中是如何运作的呢？主要是通过将设备的劳动功能插入到所呈现的领域中来实现的。这是一个复杂的概念，本雅明以多种方式加以阐述。他的意思是，观众是从生产方式的视角来观看对象，观看所讨论的领域——也就是说，观众通过参与生产过程而参与其中。最显而易见的是，当我观看一部电影时，我观看这部电影，当然，必然是从摄影机的视角；换句话说，我的眼睛与摄影机的眼睛融为一体。非常有趣的是，20世纪30年代的柏林，克里斯托弗·伊舍伍德在他的《柏林故事集》中写了一篇名为《我是一台摄影机》的故事，故事就发生在柏林。我常常觉得，克里斯托弗·伊舍伍德的《我是一台摄影机》的概念与本雅明作品中对这一概念的挪用方式之间存在某种共生关系——或者这仅仅是一种巧合。但对本雅明来说，从某种意义上说，观众为了成为参与者，就是摄像机，换句话说，就是摄像机的眼睛。

Now how does this work in this essay? Primarily through the insertion of the labor function of the apparatus in the represented field. Now this is a complicated idea that Benjamin develops in various ways. What he means by this is that the spectator sees the object, sees whatever the field in question is, from the perspective of the mode of production–that is to say, the spectator participates by joining the process of production. Most obviously this means that when I watch a film, I see the film, necessarily of course, from the standpoint of the camera eye; my eye, in other words, joins that of the camera. Very interesting that in Berlin in the 1930s, Christopher Isherwood in his Berlin Stories wrote one story called “I Am a Camera” that took place in Berlin. I have often thought there’s some sort of symbiosis between the notion of “I Am a Camera” in Christopher Isherwood and the way in which it may be appropriated–or it may simply be a happy coincidence–in the work of Benjamin. But in a certain sense for Benjamin, the spectator, in order to be a participant, isthe camera, is in other words the camera’s eye.

这会带来什么后果呢？嗯，从某种意义上说，观众也成了评论家。本雅明一直把摄像机的镜头比作“测试”。他甚至把它比作职业能力测试。这就好比在剧院里，演员的试镜——我出现在导演面前，背诵几句台词，然后要么被告知改天再来，要么就直接拿到角色——在电影里，演员对着镜头进行的永无止境的“试镜”就相当于把剧院里的试镜换成了电影演员的“试镜”。毕竟，有摄像机在记录演员的表演——顺便说一句，不是上面这台摄像机——但通常情况下，摄像机可以选择后期剪掉不好的镜头。[笑] 要是他们（指着摄制组）能这么做就好了，但电影摄像机可以剪辑。电影摄影机是剪辑“过程”的一部分，因此镜头前的演员会不断地接受测试和试镜，就像你参加职业能力倾向测试找工作时一样。

What is the consequence of this? Well, the spectator is, in a certain sense, then, a critic. Benjamin keeps comparing the eye of the camera with a “test.” He even compares it with the vocational aptitude test. It’s as though what in the theater would count as an audition–I appear before the director, I recite certain lines of the script, and I’m either told to come back another day or I’m given the part–it’s as though to substitute what counts as an audition with the perpetual audition of the film actor before the camera, because after all, there is the camera recording what the film actor is doing–not this camera up here, by the way–but ordinarily, the camera has the option of later on throwing out what isn’t any good. [laughs] Would that they [gestures to film crew] could, but the film camera can edit. The film camera is part of an editing “process, so that the actor in front of the camera is perpetually being tested and auditioned in just the way that you might be tested or auditioned if you took a vocational aptitude test for a job.

这就是本雅明的观点，他想表达的是，如果观众采取了摄像机的视角，那么观众本身就变成了评论家，就像体育迷一样。本雅明丝毫没有假装成为这种评论家就意味着成为一名优秀的评论家——完全不是。本雅明同意那些人的说法：“我们去看电影是因为累了。我们只是想娱乐消遣。” 事实上，我们心不在焉。正如本雅明所论证的，我们是处于心不在焉状态的评论家。德语中有一个词是“Zerstreutheit”。我们心不在焉。换句话说，即使我们同时以摄像机的视角观看事物，我们也始终无法真正集中注意力。从摄像机的视角——我稍后会再谈到分心——观察事物是一种特权，因为它能揭示出我们原本不会注意到的现实真相，正如本雅明反复告诉我们的那样。摄像机能够拍摄慢动作，能够拍摄我们原本无法看到的入射角。它能够实现各种各样的效果。

That’s Benjamin’s point, and what he means to say is that if the spectator then takes the camera’s eye position the spectator, him- or herself then becomes a critic, like a sports fan. Benjamin doesn’t pretend for a moment that to become a critic of this kind is to be a good critic–not at all. Benjamin agrees with people who say, “Well, we go to the movies when we’re tired. All we want is to be entertained.” In fact, we are distracted. We are critics, as Benjamin argues, in a state of distraction. The German word is Zerstreutheit. We are zerstreut. We are perpetually, in other words, not quite paying attention even while at the same time we are seeing things from the camera-eye point of view. To see things from the camera– I’ll come back to distraction in a minute–from the camera-eye point of view is a position of privilege because it exposes, as Benjamin tells us again and again, things about reality that we wouldn’t otherwise notice. The camera is capable of slow motion, and it’s capable of angles of incidence that we couldn’t otherwise see. It’s capable of all kinds of effects.

让我来列举一下。我认为在第1235页左侧栏的顶部有这样一段话：“……借助某些技术，例如放大或慢动作，摄影复制可以捕捉到自然视觉无法捕捉到的图像。”然后在第1245页，他给这个过程起了个名字。他说：“相机让我们接触到无意识的视觉，正如精神分析让我们接触到无意识的冲动一样。”换句话说，相机的视角是一种特权视角。它确实向我们展示了事物本来的样子，或者，即便不是本来的样子，至少也提醒我们，我们用肉眼看到的事物并不一定就是“它们本来的样子”。这或许并非是相机所看到的比我所看到的更真实，而是相机在提醒我们——简而言之，是在揭开我们固有观念的神秘面纱——提醒我们，我们看到的事物并不一定就是事物本来的样子。相机本身也可能带有偏见。慢动作是一种明显的偏见，加速也是一种明显的偏见；但是我们观察事物的速度也可能是一种偏见。

Let me enumerate them. I think it’s on page 1235 at the top of the left-hand column: “…photographic reproduction, with the aid of certain processes, such as enlargement or slow motion, can capture images which escape natural vision.” Then on page 1245, he gives this process a name. He says, “The camera introduces us to unconscious optics just as does psychoanalysis to unconscious impulses.” In other words, the camera’s-eye point of view is a privileged perspective. It does show us things as they are or, perhaps if not as they are, at least it reminds us that things as we see them with the naked eye aren’t necessarily “as they are.” It’s not, perhaps, so much a notion of privileging what the camera sees as real over against what I see. It’s a question of the camera reminding us–demystifying our ideology, in short–reminding us that things as we see them aren’t necessarily the way things are. The camera, too, may have its bias. Slow motion is an obvious bias, speed-up is an obvious bias; but the speed at which we see things may be a bias, too.

精神分析中的无意识并非在讲述真相。梦境本来就是疯狂的，对吧？[笑] 这正是梦的意义所在。它并非现实与意识中神秘世界的对立。它是无意识唤起的世界对意识的一种挑战，而非关乎何为真实、何为虚幻的问题。嗯，摄像机的视角也是如此，而这一切，在某种意义上，唤醒了观众，让他们不再自以为是地认为自己的视角就是真相。与此同时，不可否认的是，观众也会分心——记住“零散性”（Zerstreutheit）。

It’s not that the psychoanalytic unconscious is telling the truth. Dreams are crazy, right? [laughs] That’s the whole point of dreams. It’s not that it’s reality over against a mystified world seen in consciousness. It’s a challenge to consciousness by the world evoked in the unconscious, not a question of what’s real and what isn’t real. Well, it’s the same with the camera’s-eye point of view, and it’s all of this which, in a certain sense, awakens the spectator from the complacency of supposing his or her own perspective to be the truth. At the same time, admittedly the spectator is distracted–rememberZerstreutheit.

那么，接下来呢？关键在于：本雅明认为，分心与震惊之间存在一种辩证关系，而这种辩证关系对于真正的审美启示至关重要。或许最好的类比就是扫罗前往大马士革的路上。你肯定知道这个故事：扫罗骑着马，心不在焉地走着。他心不在焉，做着白日梦，等等，然后——砰！他突然从马上摔了下来，对吧？这让他大吃一惊，这种冲击如此之大，以至于他皈依了基督教。他站起来，拍拍身上的尘土，然后他的名字就变成了保罗，对吧？结果，他完全变了一个人。换句话说，如果他没有分心，这一切就不可能发生。对吧？这就是本雅明的观点。分心是启示的冲击得以发生的氛围或媒介，这就是分心的优势所在。

Well, what then? The point is this: there is a kind of dialectic between distraction and shock which is crucial, Benjamin thinks, to a genuine aesthetic revelation. Perhaps the best analogy is with Saul on the road to Damascus. You know how the story goes: Saul is trotting along on his horse and not paying a lot of attention. He’s distracted, daydreaming, whatever, and whhoooop! All of a sudden he falls off his horse, right? That’s a shock, and it’s such a shock that he’s converted to Christianity, and he stands up and he brushes himself off and his name is Paul, right? He’s a completely different person as a result. This couldn’t have happened, in other words, if he hadn’t been distracted. Right? That’s Benjamin’s point. Distraction is the atmosphere or medium in which the shock of revelation can take place, and that’s the advantage of distraction.

他举了一个绝妙的例子，说明即使我们是那种看电影时全神贯注的人，我们也会以心不在焉的状态去欣赏艺术作品。“哦，那不是我的风格，”我们会这样说。然而，有一种艺术作品，我们所有人都会在心不在焉的状态下欣赏，那就是我们对建筑的欣赏。我们只是匆匆穿过建筑。我每天都在英国艺术中心工作。我早已不再关注英国艺术中心这座建筑本身。换句话说，我是在心不在焉的状态下欣赏英国艺术中心的，但这并不意味着它不属于我的审美体验。然而，这确实表明，审美以及我们处理世界形态的方式可以在多种注意力状态下被吸收。从某种意义上说，欣赏建筑是与生俱来的；然而与此同时，除非我们像游客一样，拿着相机在泰姬陵前驻足凝望——本雅明也考虑到了这一点——除非我们处于那种特定的状态，否则我们对居住环境的感知，就只能处于一种你或许可以称之为“建设性分神”的状态。所有这些都构成了本雅明参与式美学的一部分。

He gives a wonderful example of the way in which we do receive works of art in distraction even if we’re the kind of person who does pay a lot of attention when they go to the movies. “Oh, that’s not me,” we say. Nevertheless, there is one way in which all of us receive works of art in a state of distraction, and that’s in our reception of architecture. We pass through architecture. I work in the British Art Center every day. I have long since ceased to pay any attention to the British Art Center as a building. I receive the British Art Center, in other words, in a state of distraction, but that doesn’t mean that it’s not part of my aesthetic experience. It does, however, show that the aesthetic and the ways in which we process the forms of the world can be assimilated in more than one kind of state of attention. It is in one’s bones, in a certain sense, to receive architecture; and yet at the same time, unless we are sort of tourists gaping in front of the Taj Mahal with a camera or something like that–and Benjamin does take that into account–unless we are in that particular mode, we receive the forms of our dwellings in a state of what you might call constructive distraction. All of that goes into Benjamin’s aesthetic of participation.

现在时间到了。关于阿多诺，我或许已经说得差不多了，虽然我承认我对他的《文化工业》一文着墨不多。也许我会在周四开始讨论詹姆逊之前，再简单提一下那篇文章。下周二，我们将探讨新历史主义。之后，我们会重新讨论托尼，并梳理我们之前练习过的各种视角，看看在解读托尼时，我们能如何运用这些视角。

Now I am out of time. Perhaps I have said just about as much about Adorno as I need to say, although admittedly I haven’t said much about the “Culture Industry” essay. Maybe I’ll come back to that briefly before launching into Jameson on Thursday. On Tuesday of next week, we’ll be talking about the New Historicism. Then we’ll bring Tony back and we’ll go through all of these various perspectives that we will have been rehearsing to see what we can do with them when we read Tony.

第十八讲——政治无意识

Lecture 18 - The Political Unconscious

第一章 马克思主义美学与弗雷德里克·詹姆逊

Chapter 1. Marxist Aesthetics and Frederic Jameson

保罗·弗莱教授：嗯，首先我想指出，弗雷德里克·詹姆逊（Fredric Jameson）的名字拼写是Fredric。我之所以要指出这一点，是因为大多数学者似乎都无法理解这个简单的事实，而且在大量的评论文献中，提到他时，大约有三分之一的地方都拼错了他的名字。所以我认为，让你们也成为少数精明之人​​，知道他的名字应该像我刚才提到的那样拼写，是很重要的。这很奇怪。我刚开始教书的时候，教过很多很多班英语129，当然，在第一学期，我们读的第一本书就是《伊利亚特》。而《伊利亚特》的拼写是Iliad。我真的说不清为什么在我教过的学生中，成百上千的学生，竟然有三分之一的人把《伊利亚特》拼写成“Illiad”，但有些词似乎就是很难拼写正确，[笑] 弗雷德里克·詹姆逊的名字就是其中之一，所以请注意。

Professor Paul Fry: Well, I’d like to begin by pointing out that the first name of Fredric Jameson is spelled F-r-e-d-r-i-c. The reason I point that out is that most scholars don’t seem to be able to grasp that simple fact and that references to him, which are rife in the critical literature, perhaps one-third of the time spell his first name wrong. So I thought it would be important for you to be among the cognoscenti and to know that it is spelled in the way that I just mentioned. It’s a strange thing. When I started teaching I taught many, many, many sections of English 129, and of course in the first semester, the first text that we read was The Iliad. Now “Iliad” is spelled I-l-i-a-d. Why it is that of the student population I taught over all those years, hundreds and hundreds of students, fully a third of them spelled it I-l-l-i-a-d I really couldn’t say, but there are words that simply seem to be insusceptible to being spelled correctly, [laughs] and one of those words is the first name of Fredric Jameson, so stand advised.

好的。上次我讨论了马克思主义文学研究方法中四种可能的美学选择，并进行了回顾。我提到了现实主义，包括恩格斯和卢卡奇所推崇的现实主义，以及1934年以后在苏联盛行的带有倾向性的现实主义；我还提到了瓦尔特·本雅明等人的参与式美学，以及阿多诺所推崇的“整体”的现代主义美学——后两种美学模式我们上次已经回顾过了——最后，作为第五种观点，我认为现实主义在某种程度上已经过时，它作为一种资产阶级视角，已经变得僵化，因此在马克思主义的视角下，需要用某种其他的美学方式来取代它。

Okay. Now last time I talked about four possible options of an aesthetic nature for a Marxist approach to literature, and passed them in review. I mentioned realism, both realism according to the tastes and theoretical preferences of Engels and Lukacs, and also tendentious realism as it pervaded the Soviet world, especially after 1934; then also the participatory aesthetic of figures like Walter Benjamin, and the high Modernist aesthetic of the “whole” embraced particularly by Adorno–those last are the two aesthetic modes that we passed in review last time–and finally, as a fifth notion, the idea that realism being somehow outworn, having developed hardening of the arteries as a kind of a bourgeois perspective on things, needs somehow or another to be replaced aesthetically in the Marxist view of things by something else.

或许最雄辩地倡导用某种东西取代现实主义美学的当属詹姆逊。他在《政治无意识》的导论章节（今天布置的作业也涵盖了这部分内容）中，专门写了一个名为“魔法叙事”的章节。该章节与诺思罗普·弗莱关于浪漫主义在社会中的作用（尤其是浪漫主义在社会中的宗教作用）的观点非常一致，他提出，以民间传说、民间故事、童话以及各种民间表达形式为核心的浪漫主义美学，才是更合适的审美选择。这种美学将民间传说、民间故事、童话以及各种民间表达形式视为解决其他方式无法解决的冲突的一种魔法手段。我昨晚发给你们的那段长文，我想快速地讲解一下，其目的是为了进一步推广这种美学，同时也旨在批判我们如果继续固守现实主义美学将会带来哪些后果。所以，詹姆逊在你们作业纸上的第二段文字中写道：

Perhaps the most eloquent proponent of replacing it with something is Jameson, who earlier in the introductory chapter of The Political Unconscious–much of which you’ve been assigned for today–writes a section which he calls “Magical Narratives” and which promotes, very much in keeping with the thinking of Northrop Frye about the role of romance in society–and particularly the religious role of romance in society–proposes that an aesthetic of the romance which entails folklore, the folk tale, the fairy tale, and various forms of folk expression as a magical resolution of conflicts that can’t otherwise be resolved, is the more appropriate aesthetic to take up. The long passage that I sent to you last night, which I’d like quickly to go over, is meant to further the promotion of this aesthetic and also to pose for us a critique of what the consequences would be of lingering with a realist aesthetic. So Jameson says, on the second passage on your sheet:

让斯科特、巴尔扎克和德莱塞作为现实主义现代形式兴起的非时间顺序的标志吧。[别忘了，巴尔扎克是恩格斯最喜欢的作家；斯科特至少在1927年是卢卡奇最喜欢的作家；德莱塞是所谓自然主义运动的代表人物，这位美国小说家非常恰当地被列入名单。詹姆逊正是在这种背景下提及了这些名字。]这些早期伟大的现实主义作品的特点在于其素材的根本性和令人振奋的多样性，以及与之相应的叙事技巧的多样性。在这样的时刻，对现实的普遍限定（换句话说，如果你是现实主义者，你唯一需要做的就是如实描述事物）对文本的语域产生了一种悖论式的解放作用，并释放出一系列异质的历史视角：斯科特的过去、巴尔扎克的未来以及德莱塞的商品化过程——这些视角通常被认为与关注历史当下相悖。换句话说，在斯科特对历史的辩证处理中，与当下形成对比的是，他设想了一种对封建过去的浪漫化描绘，而其他作家也是如此——我不想就此过多赘述。

Let Scott, Balzac and Dreiser serve as the [and remember that Balzac is the favorite author of Engels; Scott is the favorite author, at least in 1927, of Lukacs; and Dreiser is a figure from the so-called naturalist movement, the American novelist who is a very appropriate addition to the list. It’s in that context that Jameson is dropping these particular names] non-chronological markers of the emergence of realism in its modern form. These first great realisms are characterized by a fundamental and exhilarating heterogeneity in their raw materials, and by a corresponding versatility in their narrative apparatus. At such moments a generic confinement to the existent [in other words, the only thing you have to do if you’re a realist is talk about things the way they really are] has a paradoxically liberating effect on the registers of the text and releases a set of heterogeneous historical perspectives: the past for Scott, the future for Balzac, and the process of commodification for Dreiser–normally felt to be inconsistent with a focus on the historical present. In other words, in Scott’s treatment of history as dialectical, against the foil of the present there is envisioned a kind of romanticized evocation of a feudal past, and so it is in turn–I don’t want to linger long over this with the other writers.

的确，这种多元的时间性往往会被高度现实主义和自然主义所封闭和重新束缚[换句话说，它开始变得过于容易，表现和唤起现实的公式开始变得僵化，正如我所说，它们开始变得僵硬，开始以原本解放我们的方式束缚我们]。在这种模式下，一种完善的叙事机制，特别是作者去人格化的三重要求——即自由间接引语的叙述方式、作者去人格化、视角统一以及对场景再现的限制——开始使现实主义选项呈现出一种令人窒息的自我惩罚的假象。换句话说，“这就是我所能说的全部，也是我唯一能说的方式。没有其他文学表达的可能性，因为我现在感到被限制在对现实的物化之中，被坚持认为现实，对现实的唤起，是我唯一的文学选择，因此它不再具有解放意义。”

Indeed, this multiple temporality tends to be sealed off and re-contained again in high realism and naturalism [in other words, it starts getting too easy, and the formulas of representing and evoking the real begin to become, as I said, sclerotic. They begin to harden. They begin to confine us in ways that had hitherto been liberating] where a perfected narrative apparatus, in particular the threefold imperatives of authorial depersonalization–that is to say, the voice in style indirect libre, authorial depersonalization; unity of point of view, and restriction to scenic representation begin to confer on the realistic option the appearance of an asphyxiating self-imposed penance. In other words, “this is all I can say and this is the only way I can say it. There are no other possibilities of literary expression because I now feel confined to this reification of the real, this insistence that the real, the evocation of the real, is my only literary option, and so it’s no longer liberating.”

正是在晚期资本主义这种逐渐物化的背景下，浪漫主义再次被视为叙事异质性和摆脱现实原则束缚的场所。这在某种程度上是对弗洛伊德的讽刺，同时也承认弗洛伊德也参与了一种日益增长的绝望，即对必须将自身局限于现实的必要性感到绝望，从而唤起人们对摆脱现实原则的渴望——而如今，这种现实原则却成了令人压抑的现实表象的囚徒。

It is in the context of this gradual reification in late capitalism that the romance once again comes to be felt as the place of narrative heterogeneity and freedom from the reality principle. That is, in a way, a jab at Freud, but at the same time an acknowledgement that Freud participates in a sort of growing despair over the necessity of confining oneself to the real, evoking freedom from the reality principle to which a now oppressive realistic representation is the hostage.

第二章 三重地平线的浪漫

Chapter 2. Romance at the Three Horizons

好的。这就是弗雷德里克·詹姆逊的美学理论。在我们开始分析之前——也就是说，在我们开始从其他角度考察他的三个视域或同心圆式的阐释之前——我想先从这三个层面来探究这种浪漫主义美学，应该会很有意思。我们当然指的是“政治”、“社会”和“历史”三个层面：政治层面，正如他所说，是一种类似编年史的记录，记录了虚构语境中一系列事件的发生，这些事件由某个个体的声音构建成一个情节；社会层面，指的是詹姆逊所谓的“意识形态”（ideologemes）之间的冲突——或者说，是我们意识到这种冲突的方式——也就是说，不同阶级之间相互冲突的思维方式；最后是历史层面，詹姆逊称之为“必然性”。在文章结尾，他说这是“令人痛苦的事”，但就文学分析而言，正如我们将看到的，它与理解生产方式在历史长河中不断演进的交叠有关。关于生产方式，我们稍后会详细讨论，但我们基本的三个视域——我接下来要从中寻找浪漫主义美学——就是詹姆逊所说的政治、社会和历史。

Okay. So that’s the aesthetic of Fredric Jameson, and before we begin an analysis–that is to say, before we begin to consider his three horizons or concentric circles of interpretation–from other points of view, I thought it would be interesting to find this romance aesthetic in those three levels. We’re talking, of course, about the “political,” the “social,” and the “historical”: the political, the kind of chronicle-like–as he puts it–record of successive happenings in a fictive context, constructed as a plot by some individual voice; the social as the conflict–or emergence into our awareness of its being a conflict–of what Jameson calls “ideologemes”–that is to say, ways of thinking about the world as expressed by disparate and conflicting classes; and then finally the historical, which Jameson calls “necessity.” At the end of the essay, he says it’s “what hurts,” but in terms of literary analysis, as we’ll see, it has to do with understanding the overlap of the succession of modes of production as they unfold in historical time. We’ll have more to say about modes of production, but our basic three horizons, then–in which I am now going to look for the romance aesthetic–our basic three horizons, then, are what Jameson calls the political, the social and the historical.

詹姆逊有时称它们为同心圆，这一点很重要，因为你必须明白，当你经历这三个阶段时，你不会遗漏任何东西。政治包含在社会之中，社会又包含在历史之中。所有这些都不应被抛弃，而应被重新思考、重新审视。詹姆逊有时会用“重写”这个词，指的是随着研究的深入，研究对象文本也在经历这三个阶段。所以，他认为称它们为同心圆是恰当的。

It’s important that he does sometimes call them concentric circles, because you have to understand that as you advance through the three stages, you’re not leaving anything behind. The political is contained within the social and the social is contained within the historical. All of that is what is not to be left behind but is rather to be rethought, reconsidered. Jameson sometimes uses the word “rewritten,” thinking of the text that is the object of one’s study as one advances through these three stages. So that’s why he thinks it appropriate to call them concentric circles.

那么，创作行为的本质政治意义是什么呢？詹姆逊借用肯尼斯·伯克的说法，称之为“象征行为”。作为一名作家，我致力于以象征的方式解决矛盾——而马克思主义的核心始终是矛盾：也就是说，任何阶级的视角都与其自身的需求和欲望以及其他阶级之间存在着矛盾关系。无论如何，政治层面的象征行为旨在解决其他手段无法解决的矛盾。换句话说，它是一种幻想，是童话故事，是公主与乞丐的故事。它是强加于现实中根本不可能存在幸福结局的境况之上的任意幸福结局。换句话说，它是一种浪漫化的世界观，而现实主义的视角无论如何都会让我们感到更加局限。

So what is the essential political moment of the creative act? Well, it’s what Jameson, borrowing from Kenneth Burke, calls “the symbolic act.” As an individual writer, I undertake to resolve symbolically a contradiction–and Marxism is always about contradiction: that is to say, the way in which the perspective of any class exists in a contradictory relation both with its own needs and desires and with other classes. In any case, then, the symbolic act at the political level is designed to resolve a contradiction that can’t be resolved by other means. In other words, it’s a fantasy, it is the fairy tale, it is the princess and the pauper. It is the arbitrary happy ending tacked onto a situation for which in reality there would be no happy ending. In other words, it is a romance perspective about the world, the realistic approach to which would somehow or another leave us feeling much more confined.

《贫民窟的百万富翁》就是一个有趣的例子。这是丹尼·博伊尔执导的一部作者电影，它巧妙地运用整个宝莱坞体系，以个人行为化解了某种矛盾。当然，这些矛盾存在于印度教徒和穆斯林之间，存在于全球化带来的矛盾，存在于种姓制度的矛盾——所有这些矛盾，在现实层面都无法解决，却可以通过一个象征性的个人行为来解决：你中了彩票。你奇迹般地赢得了巨额奖金，成为了百万富翁。谁想成为百万富翁呢？嗯，我们都想成为百万富翁（笑），但只有我们中的一个，通过一系列完全不可思议的巧合，奇迹般地实现了这个梦想。

“Slumdog Millionaire” is an interesting example. It’s an auteur film made by Danny Boyle, an interesting example of an individual act which magically resolves a contradiction through the whole Bollywood apparatus that it brings to bear on it. The contradictions, of course, are rife between Hindu and Muslim, the contradictions entailed in globalization, the contradictions of caste–all of these contradictions, not to be resolved on a realistic plane, nevertheless can be resolved by an individual symbolic act: You hit the Lotto. You win against all odds a prize that makes you a millionaire. Who wants to be a millionaire? Well, we all [laughs] want to be millionaires, but only one of us miraculously, magically, through a series of completely implausible happenstances, is able to do so.

请注意：这并非不可能发生。确实有人中了彩票。确实有人赢得了价值 64,000 美元的谜题或其他类似的奖项。这并非完全不可能，但关键在于——我认为这才是影片结尾火车站那场盛大舞蹈的真正意义所在——即便现实中真的发生了，也无法解决矛盾。也就是说，你的生活不会像剧本里那样完美：你抱得美人归，一切都会完美无缺，全世界都会为你欢呼雀跃。这根本不可能发生。（笑）换句话说，中彩票也可能带来某种悲剧色彩，许多类似的故事都向我们揭示了这一点。在我看来，这最终体现了影片对自身象征意义的某种自觉意识。总之，这就是詹姆逊所理解的政治层面解读中的浪漫元素。

Now notice this: it’s not that it doesn’t happen. People do hit the Lotto. People do win the $64,000 question or whatever it is. It’s not that it’s absolute never-never land, but the point is–and I think this is really ultimately the point of that extravagant dance in the railroad station at the end of the film–the point is that even were it to happen in reality, it wouldn’t resolve contradictions. That is to say, your life would not have that kind of scripted perfection: You get the girl, everything is going to be perfect, and the whole world falls in line, dancing behind you. This just [laughter] doesn’t happen. In other words, it can be sort of tragic to hit the Lotto, as many stories of that kind have made clear to us. That, it seems to me, is finally how the film is somewhat self-conscious about its nature as a symbolic act. Anyway, that’s the romance element of the political level of interpretation as understood by Jameson.

现在，第二层揭示了这种童话式的冲突解决方式中必然包含的颠覆元素，这种冲突原本是无法用其他方式解决的。第二层还包含其他各种方面，但请记住，我是在探讨与此相关的其他问题之前，先从这三个层面来发现浪漫主义美学。在第二层，第1297页右侧栏，你会看到恩斯特·布洛赫对童话的理解。这部分内容位于第二层，大约在三分之二的位置。

Now the second level brings to the surface the element of subversion that has to be entailed in this same fairy tale resolution of a conflict that can’t otherwise be resolved. There are all sorts of other aspects at the second level, but remember I’m discovering the romance aesthetic here in all three levels before turning to other matters having to do with them. At the second level, on page 1297, the right-hand column, you have Ernst Bloch’s understanding of the fairy tale. This is at the second level, about two thirds of the way down.

例如，布洛赫对童话的解读，包括其中神奇的愿望实现、富足的乌托邦幻想以及科卡涅之乡的景象，通过将其展现为对史诗霸权式贵族形式的系统性解构和瓦解，从而恢复了这种“形式”的对话性（“大岩糖山”本质上就是科卡涅之乡）和对抗性内容……换句话说，童话不仅仅是一种象征行为，它更是对霸权的蔑视。换句话说，它是一种对抗行为，而这种对抗行为恰恰在其对抗层面承认了解决或和解的不可能性；因此，在第二个层面，即社会层面，不同阶级和视角的意识形态声音公开冲突之时，你不会得到解决，你得到的是颠覆和反抗。换句话说，你会看到各种声音交织在一起，这种紧张感并不是为了解决任何问题，而是为了揭示其中存在的冲突。

Thus, for instance, Bloch’s reading of the fairy tale, with its magical wish-fulfillments and its Utopian fantasies of plenty and the pays de Cocagne, restores the dialogical [“The Big Rock Candy Mountain” basically is the pays de Cocagne] and antagonistic content of this “form” by exhibiting it as a systematic deconstruction and undermining of the hegemonic aristocratic form of the epic… In other words, it’s not just a symbolic act, the fairy tale. It is a thumbing of the nose at hegemony. It is, in other words, an act of antagonism which, of course, recognizes the impossibility of resolution or reconciliation precisely in its register of antagonism; so that at the second level, the social level, in which the ideological voices of various classes and perspective are openly in conflict, you don’t get resolution. What you get is subversion and reaction. You get, in other words, a tension of voices that is not meant to resolve anything but is rather meant to lay bare the conflicts that are entailed.

然而，这样做却能带来詹姆逊所说的与浪漫主义相关的、自下而上的狂欢式起义：那种释放压力、那种对乌托邦可能性的憧憬，例如，在近代早期，当有人被冠以“混乱之王”的称号时，整个社会秩序会在一天之内颠倒过来，底层民众会被提升到权力地位，而你实际上也会在这一天拿到城堡的钥匙。在这一天，冲突得以表达，却无法得到解决，因为每个人都知道，明天一切又将恢复原状，一切照旧；但其中仍然蕴含着浪漫的元素，即民间表达同时也是一种愿望的表达，这种愿望类似于在第一政治层面上表达的愿望，但它表达的是一种集体的愿望——也就是说，代表一个阶级和一个视角，而且这种愿望也具有很强的自觉性，它并不指望以任何方式得到实现，而是以一种颠覆性的方式用来反抗它所抨击的主流意识形态。

Still, however, in doing this you get the kind of carnivalesque uprising from below which Jameson associates with romance: that letting off of steam, that entertaining of the possibility of utopia that you get, for example, in the early modern period on that day in which someone is called the Lord of Misrule, the entire social order for one day is inverted, the low are elevated to positions of authority, and for one day you get the keys to the castle, in effect. This is a day in which conflict is expressed and not resolved because everybody knows that tomorrow it’s going to be the same old-same old and back to business as usual; but there is still the romance element, the idea that folk expression is simultaneously the expression of a wish, a wish similar to the wish that’s expressed at the first political level but the expression of a wish which is collective–that is to say, in behalf of a class and a perspective, and which is also, with great self-consciousness, not a wish that can in any way expect to be fulfilled, but rather one that is used subversively with respect to the dominant ideology that it expresses its abrasiveness toward.

第三层面涉及在历史层面上任何特定时期都存在一种占主导地位的生产方式。生产方式是由一种总体性的社会或经济安排所产生的思想或生产体系。詹姆逊在他的著作中列举了这些生产方式，我们稍后会再回到这些内容，阅读他的列举并思考这些术语；但詹姆逊举了一个极好的例子，说明在十八世纪后期，启蒙运动如何开始成为新兴的商业资产阶级——一个成功的资本主义资产阶级——的主要表达形式。也就是说，推动工业化和资本发展的价值观源于封建和贵族理想，这些价值观不太现实，不太关注现实情况以及在现实世界中实际做事的方式。启蒙运动被理解为一种新兴生产方式，或者说是资本主义取代封建主义的一种表达形式。

The third level involves the way in which there is at any given time at the historical level a dominant mode of production. A mode of production is a system of thought or production generated by an overarching social or economic arrangement. Jameson lists them in his text, and we’ll come back to them and we’ll read that listing and we’ll think about those terms; but Jameson gives an excellent example of the way in which, in the latter part of the eighteenth century, the Enlightenment began to be the dominant form of expression of an emergent mercantile, successfully capitalist bourgeoisie. That is to say, the values that drove the development of industrialization and capital were those values emerging from feudal and aristocratic ideals that were less realistic, less engaged with actuality and the way in which you can actually get things done in the world. The Enlightenment is understood as an expression of an emerging new mode of production, or capitalism as it succeeds feudalism.

但詹姆逊指出——浪漫主义的元素就在这里，之后我们再讨论下一个要点——在启蒙运动兴起并似乎成为主流表达形式的同时，也出现了两种抵抗或抗争模式。一方面是浪漫主义，在这个语境下，它可以被理解为一种对贵族和封建理想主义的返祖式回归，浪漫主义内部的行为准则、信仰和乌托邦愿景，都试图在启蒙时代重新诠释那些看似过时的理想主义。因此，这是一种反动的生产模式，它与主流生产模式重叠或通过主流生产模式表达自身。与此同时，民众也对启蒙运动日益机械化的趋势产生了抵抗。随着政治经济学的兴起、社会工程的出现以及与功利主义相关的各种社会组织形式的出现，民众的抵抗也随之而来。你会看到民众以抗议、“打破框架”、扰乱劳动活动、反对工业化等形式进行抵抗，而所有这些——因为它坚持早期的农业和工业家庭手工业等形式——也具有返祖的意味，是对封建制度下劳动方式的回归。因此，这种抵抗也以民间表达的形式出现——在这种情况下，是对乌托邦式过去的渴望，更偏向农业，劳动方式更个人化，更以家庭手工业为导向——所有这些都体现了一种重叠的生产方式。因此，生产方式之间的张力，即历史层面（第三个历史层面）分析的重点，也可以从乌托邦式怀旧的浪漫主义角度来理解。

But Jameson points out–and here’s where romance comes in, and then after that we’ll move on to our next point–that at the same time you get Enlightenment, at the same time that that does seem to become the dominant form of expression, you also get two modes of resistance or contestation. On the one hand you have Romanticism, which can be understood in this context as a kind of atavistic throwback to aristocratic and feudal idealism, codes of conduct, beliefs, visions of utopia within Romanticism–all of them sort of trying to recode in an age of Enlightenment various sorts of idealism that had come to seem outmoded. So that’s a kind of, as it were, reactionary mode of production overlapping with or expressing itself through the dominant one. Then at the same time, you get folk resistance to the increasing mechanization of the Enlightenment. With Political Economy, with the rise of social engineering and with the various forms of social organization associated with Utilitarianism, you get folk resistance. You get popular resistance in the forms of protest, “frame-breaking,” disruption of labor activity, protest against industrialization, all of which also–because it insists on earlier forms of agricultural and industrial cottage industries and so on–is atavistic, also a throwback to the way in which labor is performed or conducted under feudalism. So that, too, in the form of folk expression–of longing for, in this case, a utopian past, more agrarian, more individualized as a mode of labor, and more cottage-oriented–in all of this you get an overlapping mode of production. So the tension among modes of production, which is the focus of analysis at the historical level, the third historical level, can also be understood in terms of the romance of utopian nostalgia.

第三章 三个视域的政治无意识

Chapter 3. The Political Unconscious at the Three Horizons

好的。那么，为了说明詹姆逊的美学理念，以及他对浪漫主义重要性的理解，是如何渗透到他对这三个层面分析的理解之中的，我们不妨这样说。这就是他的美学理念。那么问题来了：在这三个层面进行文学分析的阐释意义何在？也就是说，我们为什么要费这个劲去做？它究竟有何吸引人之处？从詹姆逊的角度来看——当然，这也是他著作的标题——这三种分析模式都旨在揭示、揭露、展现“政治无意识”的某个要素。至于解构主义，正如弗洛伊德所言，这种政治无意识揭示了与日常意识截然相反的东西——也就是说，它动摇了我们对事物的传统理解，向我们展示了在我们对事物的传统理解之下，存在着我们需要理解的规律、原因和动力。

All right. So that, then, just to show how Jameson’s aesthetic, his sense of the importance of romance, can be seen to pervade the way in which he understands analysis at all three of these levels. So that’s his aesthetic. The question then is: what is the interpretative payoff of undertaking literary analysis at these three levels? That is to say, why should we take the trouble to do it? What’s so interesting about it? Well, from Jameson’s point of view–this, of course, is the title of his book–each of these three modes of analysis is designed to disclose, to uncover, to lay bare an element of the “political unconscious.” As for deconstruction, as for Freud, this sense of a political unconscious exposes or reveals something that is antithetical to ordinary consciousness–that is to say, undermines our conventional understanding of things, shows us that beneath our conventional understanding of things there are laws and causes and dynamics at work that we need to understand.

然而，此处所指的无意识并非语言无意识，也非心理无意识，而是政治无意识。换言之，作为政治动物，我们的行为、参与的对话、以及生产方式都具有政治意义；也就是说，我们之所以从事某些活动（而非其他活动），是出于我们可能并未完全意识到的政治原因——因此，此类分析强调的是政治无意识。

In this case, however, the unconscious in question is not a linguistic unconscious; it is not a psychological unconscious. It is a political unconscious. Insofar, in other words, as we are political animals, the acts that we perform, the dialogues that we engage in, the modes of production that we participate in–all of them have political ramifications; that is to say, we do what we do, as opposed to doing other things, for political reasons of which we may not be fully aware–hence the emphasis in analysis of this kind on the political unconscious.

所以，我们再次回到这三个层次。回到“象征性”行为的概念：换句话说，象征性行为揭示了怎样的政治无意识？詹姆逊举了一个来自结构主义的精彩例子，我们可以看出，他非常依赖结构主义来理解某种事物以叙事形式呈现的方式，而这种方式并非显而易见。以卡杜维奥的脸部彩绘为例。列维-斯特劳斯在《野性的心灵》和《忧郁的热带》中都提出了这样的问题：为什么这些画作如此复杂？为什么脸部线条在垂直和水平方向上呈现出一种奇特的张力？换句话说，为什么在这种交叉阴影线、在这种垂直和水平关系中，你会感受到一种张力，一种审美上的美，同时也感受到一种紧张和复杂？

So again the three levels. Going back to the idea of the “symbolic” act: what political unconscious, in other words, is revealed by a symbolic act? Well, Jameson gives a wonderful example taken from structuralism, and you can see that he leans very heavily on structuralism for his understanding of the way in which something is going on in a narrative form of which it is not immediately apparent that anybody can be aware. Take for example Caduveo face painting. Levi-Strauss asks both in The Savage Mind and again in Tristes Tropiques: why the excessive complexity of these paintings? Why the curious tension in the marks on the faces between the vertical and the horizontal? Why, in other words, do you get a feeling of tension, of aesthetic beauty but also of tension and complication, in this cross-hatching, in this sense of the relation between the vertical and the horizontal?

詹姆逊的论点——他比列维-斯特劳斯阐述得更清晰——虽然列维-斯特劳斯也表达了类似的观点，并将卡杜维奥人在这方面与邻近的博罗罗人等部落进行了对比——他的解释是，卡杜维奥人是一个等级森严的社会，其中存在着公开且显而易见的不平等形式，作为部落成员，每个人都必须意识到这一点。而邻近的部落（这或许是部落自身也能观察到的）则通过交换部分财产的方式来解决等级制度中固有的矛盾，例如交换亲属礼物、结婚礼物等等——列维-斯特劳斯也谈到了这一点。这种部分财产的交换似乎在现实生活中，以实际的方式，为这些社会秩序提供了一种使社会比原本可能更加平等的途径。是的，它仍然是等级森严的，但与此同时，财富得到了分配，每个人都有自己维护尊严的方式，等等。

So Jameson’s argument, which he brings out more clearly than Levi-Strauss–but Levi-Strauss does say the same thing, contrasting the Caduveo in this respect with neighboring tribes like the Bororo–his explanation is that the Caduveo are a hierarchical society in which there are open and obvious forms of inequality that one must perforce be aware of as a member of the tribe, but that neighboring tribes, (and this is something that probably the tribe itself can observe) work out a way of seeming to resolve the contradictions inherent in hierarchy by the exchange of moieties, which is to say, of kinship gifts and wedding gifts and so on–that Levi-Strauss talks about. This exchange of moieties seems to impose on these social orders in real life, in real terms, a way of making society more equal than it might otherwise be. Yes, it’s still hierarchical, but at the same time, wealth is distributed, each person has his own form of asserting dignity, and so on.

卡杜维奥人没有这种组织形式。列维-斯特劳斯和詹姆逊的观点是，卡杜维奥人从未真正解决这个问题，因此他们只能维持一种简单的等级组织形式。根据列维-斯特劳斯和詹姆逊的说法，脸部彩绘是他们象征性地解决问题的一种方式，通过引入横向关系——换句话说，通过引入其他部落成功地用更平等的方式分配财富和声望来抵消等级制度的方法。其他部落能够在现实生活中以实际行动实现的象征性行为，卡杜维奥人则以个体的方式完成，每个女性都通过脸部彩绘来表达一种象征性的行为，一种表达政治无意识的象征性行为——因为我们推测，这种行为并非任何个体都能意识到的。

The Caduveo doesn’t have this. Levi-Strauss’s and Jameson’s point is that the Caduveo never really worked that out, so they’re stuck with a simple form of hierarchical organization. Face painting, then, according to Levi-Strauss followed by Jameson, is their way of symbolically resolving the problem by introducing the horizontal–by introducing, in other words, the ways in which other tribes have successfully offset hierarchy with ways of distributing wealth and prestige more equally. The symbolic act which other tribes were able to accomplish in real life, in real terms, the Caduveo accomplish individually, with each individual woman painting her face as a symbolic act, a symbolic act expressing the political unconscious– because this is not an act, we suppose, of which any individual is aware.

在俄狄浦斯神话中，我们更容易感受到故事中人物的无知，或者说缺乏意识，因为我们恰好读过列维-斯特劳斯《神话的结构研究》中关于这部分的内容。接下来的部分是（笑）卡杜维奥的脸部彩绘，但在《神话的结构研究》中，列维-斯特劳斯首先讨论的是俄狄浦斯神话。嗯，关键在于：“哎呀，这真是个可怕的矛盾，究竟是两个人所生，还是一个人所生？”显然，任何版本的俄狄浦斯神话，当然也包括索福克勒斯的版本，都不会自问：“哦，这真是个可怕的矛盾。我不知道我是两个人所生，还是一个人所生。”换句话说，这就是故事的无意识，而结构主义的分析方法将这种无意识揭示出来，使其浮出水面。詹姆逊没有直接讨论这个问题，因为它并非显而易见的政治问题，也不是一个可以用马克思主义分析的问题。或许最终它确实是——一切事物最终都是——但并非立竿见影。因此，他转而讨论卡杜维奥神话。这个神话的潜意识中显然包含一个政治问题，但对象征行为的结构分析旨在且必然会揭示出某种无意识的思维元素，无论其是否与政治相关。詹姆逊如此描述，政治无意识便由此在理解政治的第一层面——个体象征行为——得以显现。

The unawareness, the lack of consciousness of what’s going on in a story, is much more readily available to us in the Oedipus myth because that’s the part of Levi-Strauss’s “Structural Study of Myth” that we happen to have read. The nextpart is [laughs] Caduveo face painting, but in “The Structural Study of Myth,” Levi-Strauss begins by talking about the Oedipus myth. Well, the whole point of that is, “Gee, there’s a terrible contradiction, born from two or born from one.” Plainly, no individual version of the story, certainly not Sophocles’ version, is saying to itself, “Oh, this is a terrible contradiction. I don’t know whether I’m born from two people or born from one person.” That is the unconscious, in other words, of the story which is brought out, brought to the surface, by a structuralist analysis of the myth. Jameson doesn’t talk about it because it’s not in any obvious and immediate way a political problem or a problem susceptible of Marxist analysis. It is perhaps ultimately–everything is–but not immediately, and so he turns instead to a discussion of the Caduveo myth, which has as its unconscious an issue that’s obviously a political one, but it is nevertheless the case that a structural analysis of a symbolic act is designed to and will inevitably reveal an element of unconscious thought, political or otherwise. That then is the way in which the political unconscious, as Jameson describes it, is brought out at the first political level of understanding, the individual symbolic act.

现在进入第二个层面，即社会层面。正如詹姆逊所说，文本的自我重写并非个体行为，而是更符合巴赫金的精神，成为各种声音、观点的异质表达，仿佛它们通过文本本身书写自身。在此，所讨论的政治无意识必须从意识形态的角度来理解。换言之，人们会不自觉地表达一些观点和意见，这些观点和意见并非源于他们的个性，并非因为他们是谁（正如他们自己所说），而是源于他们的经济阶级和声望地位。换句话说，由于他们在世界上的位置，他们必然持有某些观点。他们将成为某些意识形态的代言人，而詹姆逊认为这些意识形态至少部分是无意识的。换句话说，人们并不知道，自己如此热切地表达和虔诚地相信的观点，其实是受到自己所处社会环境的影响的观点，因此，文学就变成了一种意识形态的戏剧，一种对未解决的冲突的再现，这种冲突体现在各种阶级或地位的声音中。

Now at the second level, the social, in which the text, as Jameson says, rewrites itself not as an individual act but as, very much in the spirit of Bakhtin, a heteroglossal expression of voices, of points of view, writing themselves as it were through the text–there the political unconscious in question is something that has to be understood in terms of ideologemes. In other words, people reflexively express, perhaps unbeknownst to themselves, views and opinions which are intelligible not arising out of their individuality, not because they are who they are, as they themselves might say–but rather because of their economic class and prestige status. In other words, because of their place in the world, it follows that they will hold certain views. They will be the mouthpieces, in other words, for certain ideologemes, and those ideologemes Jameson understands to be at least in part unconscious. One doesn’t know, in other words, that the opinions one so fervently expresses and so devoutly believes in are opinions conditioned by the social circumstances in which one finds oneself, so that literature then becomes a kind of drama of ideologemes, a representation of unresolved conflict that manifests in the variety of class or status voices brought to bear.

你可以看出，詹姆逊的著作在此处与巴赫金的著作最为接近，也最清晰地反映了我们之前已经接触过的巴赫金的一些关注点。詹姆逊举了一个很好的例子来说明这种冲突是如何运作的——因为这些冲突的奥秘之一在于，它们总是出现在一个共同的准则之中。这已经开始预示生产方式的概念。在第1296页的末尾，詹姆逊谈到了17世纪英国保皇党和议会党之间激烈的宗教争论，以及围绕克伦威尔统治时期、查理二世复辟和当时发生的巨大动荡（主要是宗教动荡）的所有争论；但对于任何马克思主义者而言——克里斯托弗·希尔是研究这一时期历史的领军人物，他以最清晰的方式阐释了这一时期——这种冲突都蕴含着一种潜在的政治无意识：也就是说，其最终动机是对权利的主张和阶级观点的表达。詹姆逊在第1296页底部这样写道：“……对话的通常形式本质上是一种对抗性的形式……”他在这里指的是巴赫金，巴赫金认为对话常常只是各种声音欢快的交响，是自下而上混乱的狂欢式表达，所有这些都像酵母一样发酵，最终以某种方式激发活力，并推动社会进步。

You can see this is the point at which Jameson’s work is closest to Bakhtin’s and most clearly reflects some of the preoccupations of Bakhtin as we have encountered them already. Jameson gives a very good example of the way in which this conflict works–because part of the mystery of these clashes is that they always present themselves within a shared code. This already begins to look forward to the idea of the mode of production. At the bottom of page 1296, Jameson is talking about the violent religious controversies of the seventeenth century in England between Cavalier and Roundhead, with all the controversies surrounding the interregnum of Cromwell, the restoration of Charles the Second, and the tremendous ferment, largely religious ferment, taking place during that period; but this ferment for any Marxist–and Christopher Hill is the leading historian writing about this period who has made it most clearly intelligible in these terms–for any Marxist this conflict has an underlying political unconscious: that is, its ultimate motives are an assertion of rights and an expression of class views. This is the way Jameson puts it, bottom of page 1296: “…the normal form of the dialogical is essentially an antagonistic one…” He’s alluding here to Bakhtin, for whom frequently the dialogical is simply a kind of happy cacophony of voices, a carnivalesque expression of chaos from below, all of which is a kind of yeast-like ferment, and somehow or another in the long run energizing and socially progressive.

但詹姆逊指出，意识形态也常常表达冲突，而且是对抗性的冲突。阶级斗争的对话正是两种对立的话语在共同准则的统一框架内展开较量的过程。例如，在17世纪40年代的英国，宗教这一共同的主导准则成为了霸权神学的主流表述被重新挪用和论战性修正的场所。换句话说，英国国教代表着——这也是当时使用的词语——“建制”。圆颅党的观点、各种形式的清教主义以及其他形式的宗教反叛都反对建制，然而它们都被纳入了基督教的话语体系之中。也就是说，它们必须在同一个战场上展开较量，而这正是此类冲突的本质。

But Jameson points out that the ideologeme is very often expressive of conflict as well, an antagonistic one, and that the dialogue of class struggle is one in which two opposing discourses fight it out within the general unity of a shared code. Thus, for instance, the shared master code of religion becomes in the 1640s in England the place in which the dominant formulations of a hegemonic theology are re-appropriated and polemically modified. In other words, the Church of England stands for–and this is the word that was used–“establishment.” Roundhead points of view, various forms of Puritanism and other forms of religious rebellion, are antiestablishment, and yet they are all coded within the discourse of the Christian religion. That is to say, they have to fight it out on a common battlefield, and that’s the way it is with conflict of this kind.

或许当代的例子并非主要集中在宗教领域。当然，今天我们也可以谈论宗教，但在六七十年代，这或许更多地是一个伦理问题。例如，想想性革命。这里同样存在一个共同点，即对性行为在人类生活中核心地位的认知；但你最终得到的——或许与其说是阶级冲突，不如说是代际冲突——代际冲突导致的是价值观的颠倒，并非一套全新的价值观，而只是对现有价值观的简单重新评价。一方认为不好的东西，另一方却重新评价并视为好。人们所警惕的，恰恰是人们争相拥抱的，如此循环往复。因此，你再次看到冲突，一场尚未解决的冲突，但这场冲突源于并参与到共同准则的符号结构之中，对吗？这就是社会对抗在第二层面上的表现方式，它通常涉及政治无意识的因素，因为其中存在潜在的利益，并将政治无意识的因素带到表面。

Maybe a contemporary example would be not so much in the sphere of religion. Well, today one could speak again of religion, but in the sixties and seventies it was maybe more a question of ethics. Think, for example, of the sexual revolution. Again there is a common ground, a sense of the centrality of sexual conduct to human life; but what you get in–not so much, perhaps, the conflict of classes as conflict of generations in this case–what you get in the conflict of generations is an inversion of values, not a new set of values exactly but a simple transvaluation of what exists. Everything that one faction considers bad, another faction transvalues and considers good. The very thing against which one is warned is the thing that one rushes to embrace and so on. So once again you get a clash, an unresolved clash, but a clash that arises from and participates in the semiotic structure of a common code, right? That’s the way in which social antagonism expresses itself at the second level, and it usually involves, because there are underlying interests, elements of the political unconscious and brings to the surface elements of the political unconscious.

最后，在第三层面，显现出来的，是生产方式在历史上相互碰撞和竞争所产生的张力或冲突。正如詹姆逊所说，以生产方式的先后顺序来思考问题的危险在于，每一种生产方式都可能被视为一个同步时刻。换句话说，如果你身处资本主义社会，你可能会被蒙蔽，认为没有其他生产方式可供选择。如果你身处父权制社会，你可能会被蒙蔽，认为没有其他生产方式可供选择。然而，正如詹姆逊所指出的，企业等级制度与父权等级制度之间的紧张关系——换句话说，这种紧张关系经常造成马克思主义和女权主义观点之间的分歧，并且已经造成了这种分歧——反映了完全不同时代的生产方式的共存：一种是当代的，另一种是完全的——至少就其曾经的主导地位而言——过去的，但它仍然存在，并且仍然与当代的生产方式重叠。

Finally, at the third level what comes out, what is made manifest, is the tension or clash among modes of production as they jostle each other historically. It’s understood that the danger, as Jameson puts it, of thinking in terms of a succession of modes of production is that each one of those modes of production might seem like a synchronic moment. In other words, if you’re in capitalism, you might get lulled into thinking that no other mode of production is available. If you’re in patriarchy, you might get lulled into thinking that no other mode of production is available; yet as Jameson points out, the tension between corporate hierarchy and patriarchal hierarchy–the tension, in other words, which very often drives a wedge and has driven a wedge in polemic between Marxist and feminist points of view–is a reflection of the coexistence of modes of production from completely different eras: one contemporary, one completely–at least insofar as it was the dominant–a thing of the past, and yet persisting and still overlapping with a mode of production that is contemporary.

第四章 文学分析：雪莱的《西风颂》

Chapter 4. Literary Analysis: Shelley’s “Ode to the West Wind”

这一切都只是历史事实，但在文学分析中，你会开始用更正式的术语来思考它。例如，你会发现诗歌形式的选择——我以雪莱的著名诗作《西风颂》为例——你会发现诗歌形式的选择本身就是詹姆逊所说的“形式意识形态”的一个例证，而这种意识形态可以从创作模式的冲突角度来理解。雪莱的《西风颂》的诗歌形式由五节组成，每一节的形式都完全相同。它既是十四行诗，又是三韵句——前十二行以对句结尾。这两种形式在雪莱的笔下融合为一个单一的诗节形式，但它们的编码方式却截然不同。它们各自的方面都蕴含着一种意识形态。三韵句被编码为“预言”，因为它源于但丁的传统。 《神曲》正是以这种诗体写成的，这种诗体表达了一种希望，这种希望化解了神圣、神圣启示以及天堂中的所有矛盾；因此，对于雪莱而言，三韵体表达了这首诗的希望，即西风将通过他成为政治预言的号角。如果冬天来了，春天还会远吗？革命即将到来，一切都将美好。

All of that is simply a matter of historical fact, but in literary analysis you begin to think of it in more formal terms, and you see, for example, the very choice of verse form–and I’m taking as an example Shelley’s famous poem “The Ode to the West Wind”–you see the very choice of verse form as an instance of what Jameson calls “the ideology of form” that can be understood in terms of the conflict of modes of production. The verse form of Shelley’s “Ode to the West Wind” has five strophes, and each strophe is exactly the same in form. It is simultaneously a sonnet and–the first twelve lines of which, concluding in a couplet–a succession of terza rima. Now these two forms brought together, synthesized as a single strophic form in Shelley, are coded in entirely different ways. Each aspect of them has an ideology. Terza rima is coded “prophecy” because it is in the tradition of Dante. It’s the verse form in which The Divine Comedy is written, and it is a mode that is expressive of hope that resolves all contradiction in the divine, in the revelation of the divine, in theParadiso; so that terza rima expresses for Shelley the hope of the poem, which is that the west wind will be through him the trumpet of a political prophecy. If winter’s here, can spring be far behind? Revolution is in the offing, everything’s going to be great.

但与此同时，这首诗也弥漫着一种悲观主义——或者说，一种现实主义；一种对预言这种概念相当牵强的认知。风为什么要听命于他？风只是风而已，它并非灵感。因此，这首采用三韵体写成的诗节，同时也是一首十四行的十四行诗。尤其是第一节，它不仅被编码为一首十四行诗，而且还特意引用了莎士比亚的第七十三首十四行诗，这首诗以“你或许能从我身上看到一年中的那个时节”开头——在那个时节里，我正在衰老。我的头发已经掉光了。我只是一个光秃秃的、破败的唱诗班，昔日甜美的鸟儿曾在此歌唱。换句话说，我处境艰难，我正在衰老，而且对此无能为力。诗的结尾，我心中的火焰即将熄灭。一切都毫无希望。人生就是如此：人终会老去。换句话说，寒冬已至，春日却迟迟不来。没有预言的可能，只有生命轨迹的真实写照。有起有落，有发展有衰败，而这些，正如十四行诗的形式所揭示的，是人生的简单事实，是诗歌理想主义、浪漫主义都无法凌驾的。

But at the same time, the poem is shot through with a kind of pessimism–a sort of, if you will, realism; an awareness that this notion of prophecy is rather farfetched. Why should the wind do his bidding? The wind is just wind. It’s not inspiration. Therefore, the very stanza which is written in terza rima is written at the same time as a sonnet, fourteen lines. The first stanza in particular is coded not just as a sonnet but also as an allusion specifically to one sonnet, Shakespeare’s seventy-third sonnet, which begins “That time of year in me thou mayest behold”–in which I’m getting old. I don’t have any hair left. I’m just a bare-ruined choir where late sweet birds sang. In other words, I am in a parlous state, I am getting old, and there’s nothing to be done about it. At the end of the poem, the embers of my fire are about to be snuffed out. There is just no hope for it. That’s the way it is: you get old. In other words, winter’s here and spring isn’t coming. There is no prophetic possibility. There is only the reality of the trajectory of a life spent. If there is rise, there is also fall. If there is development, there is also decline and decay, and these, as the sonnet form codes it, are simple facts of life that poetic idealism, that Romanticism, cannot override.

因此，雪莱的诗歌形式体现了一种思想张力：一方面是预言性的思想，这种思想可以与封建和神中心主义的世界联系起来，在这个世界里，现实的矛盾确实可以通过神学来解决；另一方面是一种原始现实主义传统，在这种传统中，我们只能接受事物的本来面目。这种张力通过十四行诗来表达——毕竟，这本身就是启蒙运动的雏形，而莎士比亚通常被认为是启蒙运动的先驱人物。因此，从形式上看，三韵体和十四行诗都参与了詹姆逊所说的“形式的意识形态”，它们分别反映了封建和启蒙时代的生产方式，也反映了与这些生产方式相关的态度。所以，这就是政治——或许最好称之为准意识，因为雪莱是一位极其具有自我意识的诗人——政治“准意识”在第三或历史分析层面上表达自身的方式的一个例子。

So what you get in Shelley’s verse form is a tension between ideas, the prophetic idea which you can associate with a feudal and theocentric world in which the contradictions of reality really can be resolved theologically, on the one hand, and a kind of proto-realist tradition in which we just have to come to terms with the way things are, coded through–which is, after all, proto-Enlightenment, and Shakespeare is often sort of thought of as a proto-Enlightenment figure–the sonnet. So formally, both the terza rima and the sonnet participate in what Jameson calls “the ideology of form,” and they reflect modes of production, feudal and Enlightenment respectively. They reflect attitudes that one can associate with those modes of production. So that’s an example of the way in which the political–perhaps one had better call it quasi-conscious because Shelley was an incredibly self-conscious poet–the way in which the political “quasi-conscious” expresses itself at the third or historical level of analysis.

第五章 三个层面的形式强调

Chapter 5. The Formal Emphasis at the Three Horizons

现在，从形式上讲——我已经略微谈到这一点，而且时间不多了，所以我会快速讲完——从形式上讲，我们可以把第一层面或政治层面的基本批判任务理解为主题化。也就是说，一个具体的象征性行为的情节结构试图表达什么主题？这个象征性行为中正在解决的矛盾是什么？在第二层面，我们运用的形式原则是巴赫金的“异质性”概念：声音的冲突，声音不再是个人的，而是社会的，是某种社会观点的代表，这种观点通过作者的写作表达出来。在第三层面，你会看到詹姆逊所说的“一系列技巧”，我已经对此略作思考。

Now in formal terms–and I have already sort of gotten into this, and I’ll go through it rather quickly because there isn’t much time left–in formal terms we can think of the essential critical task at the first or political level as one of thematization. That is to say, what theme is the plot structure of an individual symbolic act trying to express? What is the contradiction that’s being resolved in this symbolic act? At the second level, the formal principle that we do bring to bear is the idea, the Bakhtinian idea, of heteroglossia: the clash of voices, the way in which the voice is no longer individual but rather social, the representative of a social point of view that expresses itself through the individual author’s writing. At the third level, you get what Jameson calls “a repertoire of devices,” and I have already reflected a little bit on that.

让我再补充一个例子，同样来自浪漫主义时期，这与詹姆逊关于启蒙时代生产模式重叠现象尤为有趣的论述相呼应。浪漫主义时期有着悠久的品达式颂歌传统。华兹华斯在创作颂歌《不朽的预感》时仍然沿用了这一传统，但与此同时，他和柯勒律治也发展出了一种新的颂歌形式，我们称之为“对话诗”：柯勒律治的《午夜霜冻》和《这菩提树荫下是我的牢笼》，以及华兹华斯的《丁登寺》，都是对话诗的杰出代表。

Let me just add another example, also taken from Romanticism, in keeping with Jameson’s exemplification of the overlap of modes of production as being particularly interesting in the age of Enlightenment. In Romanticism there is a long tradition leading up to it of the formal Pindaric ode. Wordsworth is still making use of that tradition in writing his ode, “Intimations of Immortality,” but in the meantime he and Coleridge have developed a new kind of ode, if you will, which is called the “conversation poem”: Coleridge’s “Frost at Midnight” and “This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison,” Wordsworth’s “Tintern Abbey” are notable examples of the conversation poem.

现在，这种差异从生产方式的冲突角度来看，就非常清晰地展现出来了。正式颂歌，其源头可以追溯到品达为歌颂希腊贵​​族赞助人在奥林匹克运动会上的胜利而创作的诗歌——赛马、赛跑、摔跤：这才是正式颂歌最初的用途——它显然再次被赋予了封建贵族的色彩，而对话诗则正如其名，属于公共领域。它营造的是咖啡馆的氛围，人们坐在一起交谈，交换意见，彼此交流。这种诗歌总是面向某个特定的人，在某个时刻转向这个人，唤起这个人的特质，有时还会征求这个人的意见。换句话说，这是一种对话式的诗歌，它展现了公共领域中更加开放、民主的文化中那种互惠互利的交流。因此，从正式颂歌到对话诗的转变本身就可以理解为生产方式之间的转变，或者用詹姆逊的话来说，是由生产方式的巨大转变带来的“文化革命”。

Now the difference is very clearly intelligible in terms of a conflict of modes of production. The formal ode, derived ultimately from Pindar celebrating Olympic victories of aristocratic patrons in Greece–horse races, foot races, wrestling matches: that’s the original purpose to which the formal ode was put–plainly is coded once again as feudal-aristocratic, whereas the conversation poem belongs very much, as the word suggests, in the public sphere. It’s the atmosphere of the coffeehouse. It’s the atmosphere in which people sit down and talk together, exchange views, and address each other. It is a poem always of address to some individual person that turns to that person at a certain point, evokes the nature of that person, sometimes solicits that person’s opinions. In other words, it’s a poem that performs dialogism. It’s a poem that performs the sense of the give-and-take of a much more open, democratic culture in the public sphere. So you can see that the very transition from the formal ode to the conversation poem is itself intelligible as a transition between–or what Jameson calls “a cultural revolution” brought in by a seismic shift in–modes of production.

第六章 已知的诠释风险

Chapter 6. Acknowledged Interpretive Dangers

好的。这些例子以各种方式展现了这三个层次的运用方式。詹姆逊本人也提醒我们注意其中的危险。如果我们把叙事视为一种象征行为，我们就很容易要么因为强调事件的结构主义本质而忘记它基于现实，要么因为强调正在解决的社会矛盾而忘记形式的存在。正如詹姆逊所说，第一层次的两大危险分别是结构主义的危险和庸俗唯物主义的危险。分析象征行为的关键在于维持文本中形式要素和社会要素之间的平衡或综合。第二层次的问题在于，如果我们开始从不可调和的阶级冲突的角度思考，我们的分析就会变得僵化，仿佛阶级视角没有转变，仿佛一种视角不会取代另一种视角成为霸权：换句话说，仿佛变革没有发生，仿佛阶级冲突永远是老一套。老板总会贬低员工，员工总会在背后嘲笑老板。事情就是这样，而且永远都会如此。换句话说，阶级之间存在着历史无法改变的静态关系。

All right. So these exemplify, in various ways, what can be done with these three levels. Jameson himself reminds us of the dangers. If we think of a narrative as a symbolic act, we are much too prone either to forget that it’s based on reality by emphasizing the structuralist nature of what’s going on or to forget that form is involved at all by emphasizing the social contradiction that’s being resolved. As Jameson says, these two dangers at the first level are the danger of structuralism and the danger of vulgar materialism. The point in analyzing the symbolic act is to sustain a balance or a synthesis between formal and social elements within the text. At the second level, the problem is that if we start thinking in terms of un-reconcilable class conflict, our analysis can become static, as though class perspectives didn’t shift, as though one perspective might not succeed another as the hegemonic: in other words, as though change didn’t take place, as though there was always the same old-same old in class conflict. The boss is always going to speak demeaningly of the worker. The worker is always going to laugh at the boss behind his back. This is the way it is; this is the way it will always be. There are static relations in other words among the classes that history can’t resolve.

最后，在第三层面，存在着以僵局思维看待问题的危险——例如，将晚期资本主义视为一种根本无法逾越的僵局。想想阿多诺和他对文化产业的无比悲观吧。阿多诺身上似乎没什么希望，[笑]不是吗？同样地，你也可以说，可怜的詹姆逊把历史视为必然，历史视为痛苦，历史仅仅是已经发生的事情——同样地，你也可以说，詹姆逊或许也多少受到了这种僵局感的影响。这就是为什么我要引用马克思在《论费尔巴哈》第十一条论纲中的那句掷地有声的警告，就像这些人经常引用的那样：“哲学家们只是用不同的方式解释世界，而问题在于改变世界。”这才是马克思分析的最终重点。

Finally, at the third level, there is the danger of thinking in terms of impasse–late capitalism, for example, as an impasse that simply can’t be surmounted. Think of Adorno and his incredible gloom about the culture industry. There isn’t much hope in Adorno, [laughs] is there? And by the same token, you could argue that poor old Jameson talking about history as necessity, history as what hurts, history as just what has happened–by the same token, you could argue that Jameson, too, is perhaps a little bit subject to this sense of impasse, which is why I quote for you, as these people themselves often do, the ringing warning of Marx in the Eleventh Thesis on Feuerbach: “The philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways. The point, however, is to change it.” That is ultimately the focus of Marx’s analysis.

第七章 应用案例：拖车托尼

Chapter 7. Application: Tony the Tow Truck

让我们在剩下的时间里再来谈谈托尼。现在，如果采用詹姆森在纸上批评的那种现实主义视角来看待托尼，就会发现尼托和斯皮迪什么事都没发生。他们显然是反派，但同时，他们却安然无恙。他们在社会秩序中占据着自己的位置：一个是讲究的贵族，不愿弄脏自己；另一个则完全致力于生产力、打卡和职业道德，一个资产阶级的斯皮迪。他们就在那里；什么也做不了。他们对托尼不好，但什么事也没发生。没有人会责怪他们。

Let’s revisit Tony in the remaining minute. Now a reified realist approach to Tony, the kind that Jameson criticizes on the sheet, would point out that nothing happens to Neato and Speedy. They are manifest villains, and yet at the same time, nothing can happen to them. They simply have their place in the social order: one of them is a fastidious aristocrat who doesn’t want to get dirty, the other is completely committed to productivity and the time clock and the work ethic, a bourgeois Speedy. There they are; nothing to be done. They’re not nice to Tony but nothing happens to them. There is no recrimination.

但从第一层面来说，如果我们把这理解为一种象征性的行为，那么原本看似无解的冲突最终是通过友谊化解的——邦比和托尼之间的友谊；托尼认为，即便我只是个普通的上班族，也完全没问题。我有哥们儿，我们一起出去玩，喝啤酒，玩得很开心。生活很美好。换句话说，阶级结构和社会制度的存在都无关紧要。“我很快乐，”托尼实际上是在说，“我喜欢我的工作。”当然，这本身就是一种解决，[笑] 是一种象征性的行为，也是一种在故事可能出现的冲突发生之前就已解决的问题。

But then at the first level, if we understand this as a symbolic act, the resolution of what would otherwise be a hopeless conflict is through friendship–the friendship of Bumpy and Tony; the fact that it’s perfectly okay if I’m just a working guy. I’ve got my buddies. We go out. We drink beer. We have a good time. Life is great. It doesn’t matter, in other words, that there’s a class structure, that there’s a social system. “I’m happy,” Tony says in effect. “I like my job.” That in itself, of course, is a resolution, [laughs] is a symbolic act and a resolution in advance of the conflicts that the story might otherwise manifest.

在第二层，我们看到的是意识形态的话语。“我帮不了你，”尼托汽车说，“我不想弄脏自己。”“我帮不了你，”斯皮迪汽车说，“我太忙了。”“我可以帮你，”邦比说；但请注意，这一切都发生在同一个单一的语境中，这三句话的完整平行结构正是向我们展示这一点。在同一个语境中，这些无法真正解决的意识形态得以表达。

At the second level, you get the discourse of ideologemes. “I can’t help you,” says Neato the car. “I don’t want to get dirty.” “I can’t help you,” says Speedy the car. “I am too busy.” “I can help you,” says Bumpy; but notice that this is all within an individual, single code, and that’s what the complete parallelism of these three utterances shows us. Within a single code, these ideologemes, which can’t really be resolved, get themselves expressed.

好了。现在终于要谈到生产方式了：显然，尼托和斯皮迪同时出现在同一个故事里，就暗示着封建制度和资产阶级制度之间存在某种张力，但这种张力并非必然会自行消解。在我看来，这里需要注意的是拉力和推力之间的冲突。非常有趣的是——我之前也说过——拖车，也就是拉力物——托尼也是一种生产方式，对吧？他就是一辆拖车，对吧？而拉力物必须被推。邦比，就像那辆小火车一样，某种程度上是对早期一种动力较弱、效率较低的生产方式的回归。他必须推。想想砌墙的方式：在起重机和滑轮发明之前，预制墙必须由一群人推上去。在能够拉动物体的技术出现之前，推力是必不可少的劳动方式。之后，就有了起重机。你把钩子拉下来，然后把墙拉到位。在此之前，可能只有一个人站在椽子上用绳子拉，其他人都在地上推；因此，故事中推与拉的关系至关重要，它暗示了新旧生产方式的交融，所有这些都可以在詹姆逊的第三层分析——历史分析——中找到答案。

All right. Now finally modes of production: plainly, the very existence of Neato and Speedy in the same story suggests that there is a certain tension between the feudal and the bourgeois at work, but it’s not a tension that in any way necessarily works itself out. The important thing to notice here, it seems to me, is the conflict between pulling and pushing. It’s very interesting–and I’ve said this before–that a tow truck, something that pulls–and once again Tony is a mode of production, right? He’s a tow truck, right? And something that pulls has to be pushed. Bumpy, like the Little Engine that Could, is a sort of a throwback to an earlier, less energized, less powerful mode of production. He has to push. Think of the way walls get put up: a prefabricated wall before the invention of the crane and the pulley has to be pushed up by a bunch of people. Pushing is the essential labor mode before the kind of technology arises that makes it possible to pull something. After that, you have a crane. You run the hook down, and you just pull the wall up into place. Before then, you got maybe one person standing on a rafter with a rope kind of pulling but everybody else is down on the ground pushing; and so the relationship between pushing and pulling in the story is a crucially important one which suggests the overlap of older and newer modes of production, all of which can be resolved at Jameson’s third or historical level of analysis.

好的。关于詹姆逊和托尼就先说到这里。下次我们再来讨论托尼，届时我们会谈到新历史主义。

Okay. So much then for Jameson and for Tony. We’ll be coming back to Tony again next time in the context of talking about the New Historicism.

第十九讲——新历史主义

Lecture 19 - The New Historicism

第一章 新历史主义的起源

Chapter 1. Origins of New Historicism
