The thing about the way in which we approach any text, any utterance, any instance of language floating before us, is just to take for granted that it has an intention. As theorists and critics, we worry away at the question of how we can know intention, and all of this is a dangerous mistake because the fact is, in everyday practice any piece of language we encounter we just assume to have an intention.

好的。他们举了一个例子来检验这个假设，让我们意识到，如果我们自以为知道某件事的含义，那会面临怎样的风险。通常情况下，我们会脱口而出：“我知道那是什么意思”，或者如果我们不知道它的意思，我们会说：“即使我不知道它的意思，它肯定有某种含义。” 这就是我们理解语言的通常方式。然后他们说，假设你走在沙滩上，偶然发现四条线——“线”这个词本身就很危险——沙滩上的四道划痕，看起来很像华兹华斯的诗《沉睡封印了我的灵魂》的第一节：

All right. So they give us an example in which this assumption is tested and makes us realize what’s at stake in supposing that we know the meaning of something. Ordinarily, we just spontaneously say, “I know what that means,” or if we don’t know what it means, we say, “It must mean something even though I don’t know what it means.” That’s our normal approach to a piece of language. Then they say, Suppose you’re walking on the beach and you come across four lines–“lines” is already a dangerous thing to say–four scratches in the sand that look an awful lot like the first stanza of Wordsworth’s ‘A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal’:

沉睡封住了我的灵魂；我不再有任何人间的恐惧。她仿佛是一个感受不到岁月痕迹的存在。它就在那里，就在我们眼前的沙滩上；我们说，哦，有人来了，某个华兹华斯的爱好者来到这里，在沙滩上刻下了这些字，这样文本的意图就毋庸置疑了。这是华兹华斯写的。现在有人想提醒我们这节诗多么美妙，于是它就在那里。当然，我们很难知道它的含义，但至少我可以赋予它意义，因为毫无疑问，这是有意为之。

A slumber did my spirit seal; I had no human fears. She seem’d a thing that could not feel The touch of earthly years. There it is on the beach just right in front of us; and we say, Oh, well, somebody’s come along, some Wordsworth lover has come along here and scratched these lines in the sand, so that the intention of the text is unquestioned. Wordsworth wrote it. Somebody now wants to remind us of what a wonderful stanza it is, and there it is. Of course, it’s very difficult to know what it means, but at least I can ascribe meaning to it because, no doubt, it’s an intended thing.

但接下来会发生什么呢？一个巨浪袭来，把第二节诗句冲到了沙滩上，淹没在第一节诗句的下方，这当然会造成很大的问题。就是这样：

But then what happens? A huge wave comes along and leaves on the beach underneath the first stanza the other stanza, and this of course is highly problematic. There it is:

她如今不动，无力；她既听不见，也看不见；随着地球的昼夜循环，与岩石、石头和树木一同翻滚。现在我们真的困惑了。也许，正如克纳普和迈克尔斯所说，大海是一种泛神论的存在，喜欢写诗——所以这首诗是大海写的。也许，他们后来又说，潜艇里有一些小人，看着自己的作品说：“哇，太棒了。我们再试一次。”换句话说，我们可以推断出这节诗的作者有很多种，但更有可能的是，我们不会说大海写诗，也不会说潜艇里有一些小人写诗——我们更有可能说：“这真是个惊人的巧合，真的太惊人了，但这仅仅是个巧合。还能是什么呢？”

No motion has she now, no force; She neither hears nor sees; Roll’d round in earth’s diurnal course, With rocks, and stones, and trees. Now we are really puzzled. Maybe, as Knapp and Michaels say, the sea is a kind of a pantheistic being that likes to write poetry–so the sea wrote it. Maybe, they say later on, there are little men in a submarine who look at their handiwork and say, “Gee, that was great. Let’s try that again.” In other words, we can infer all sorts of authors for the stanza, but it’s much more likely that instead of saying that the sea writes poetry, or instead of saying there are little sort of homunculi in submarines writing poetry–instead of saying that, it’s much more likely that we’ll say, “This is an amazing coincidence, truly amazing, but it’s just a coincidence. What else could it be?”

克纳普和迈克尔斯的观点，就像你可能会对鹦鹉说“我的老板是个混蛋”这样的例子提出的观点一样——你知道鹦鹉并不是那个意思。鹦鹉只是在发出声音。也许是别人想表达这个意思，但对鹦鹉来说，那只是声音而已，好吗？或者像猴子在打字机上写莎士比亚的作品一样。我们被告知，如果时间足够，这是一项可以完成的任务，前提是有人在他们写完一个字后把纸片拿走（笑），然后再把它们重新组合起来。所有这些都是可能性，但我们突然意识到，那些文字，比如“我的老板是个混蛋”和“沉睡封印了我的灵魂”，是某种东西偶然写成的——而“由”某种东西“写”这件事本身就蕴含着某种意图——但仅仅是偶然留下的，根据克纳普和迈克尔斯的说法，在这种情况下，这些文字只是类似语言。它们实际上并不是语言，因为没有人写它们；没有任何东西写它们；它们并非由任何神灵或存在所书写，纯属偶然。因此，即便它们看起来像语言，我们也会突然意识到，认为它们有意义是多么愚蠢。有一首诗与我们眼前这堆符号完全吻合，那首诗有意义，但这堆符号却没有意义。

Knapp and Michaels’s point, which was the same point that you might make about a parrot saying, “My boss is a jerk,” for example–you know the parrot doesn’t mean that. The parrot is just making words. Somebody else meant it, maybe, but that’s just words for the parrot, okay? Or monkeys at typewriters writing Shakespeare. We are told that given eternity, this is a task that could be accomplished, always supposing somebody were there to whisk away the sheets whenever they wrote a word [laughs] and finally put it back together. All of these things are possibilities, but we suddenly realize that those texts, “My boss is a jerk” and “A slumber did my spirit seal,” written by chance by whatever it is–and already there is a sort of an intentionality entailed in the idea of writing “by” something–but just left by chance, we suddenly realize, according to Knapp and Michaels, that in that case those words are only like language. They are not actually language because nobody wrote them; nothing wrote them; no entity or being from God on down wrote them. They are just there by chance. Therefore, even though they look like language, we suddenly realize that it would be foolish to suppose that they have meaning. There is a poem that exactly resembles this bunch of marks that we see in front of us, and that poem has meaning, but this bunch of marks does not have meaning.

现在我想我们大多数人——这也是为什么我觉得克纳普和迈克尔斯本可以选个更好的例子——都会抗拒“我们无法解读这堆符号”这种说法。它们和语言一样，我们可以自由解读。毕竟，谁也不知道这首诗到底是什么意思！几十年来，它一直是评论界争论的焦点。这也是克纳普和迈克尔斯选择它的原因之一，好吧，它就摆在那里。我也来试着解读一下。它肯定有某种含义，那就试试吧。于是，我们开始抗拒这种说法。

Now I think probably most of us–and that’s why I think in a way Knapp and Michaels could have chosen a better example–I think probably most of us would resist the idea that we can’t interpret the bunch of marks. They’re identical to language. We feel free to interpret them. After all, nobody knows what the poem means anyway! It’s been the subject of critical controversy for decades. That’s one of the reasons Knapp and Michaels choose it, and so okay, there it is on the beach. I’ll have my stab at it. It must mean something, so here goes. And so we resist that.

所以我才给你们举了另一个例子，因为在我看来，这个例子在某种程度上比克纳普和迈克尔斯的例子更有说服力。[指向讲义] 现在你们看，这两位女士正抬头看着树。上面的——你们管它们叫什么？树枝被锯掉后，最终形成一种疤痕，你们管它叫什么？

That’s why I gave you this other example, because it seems to me that in a way, the other example is more compelling than that of Knapp and Michaels. [Points to handout.] Now you see these two ladies looking up at the tree. The upper–what do you call them? What do you call it when the branches are sawed off and eventually there’s a kind of a scar formed?

学生：树瘤。

Student: A burl.

保罗·弗莱教授：树瘤？上面的树瘤看起来确实很像耶稣，[笑声] 大约十五年前，当这棵树瘤出现在米尔福德时，不仅是这两位女士，还有成百上千的人都来参观了。当然，他们相信树瘤是上帝放在那里的。因此，它具有意义。我们知道它是什么。它是耶稣脸的象征，人们能够知道它是什么，能够解读它，并把它当作某种事物的真实象征，这种感觉因此毋庸置疑。正如我们都会同意的那样，你接受了这个前提：上帝写下了它，或者我应该说，上帝把它放在那里。众所周知，上帝也用烤奶酪三明治和墨西哥卷饼做过同样的事情，这很常见，对吧？你接受了这个前提，一切就都说得通了。但假设你说：“不，不，不，不。上帝没有写下它。上帝没有把它放在那里。这只是个意外。”那么你难道不会说，“哦，因此它没有任何意义，它不代表任何东西，它只是看起来像某个东西”吗？

Professor Paul Fry: Burl? The upper burl certainly looks an awful lot like Jesus, [laughter] and when this appeared in Milford about fifteen years ago, not just these two ladies but hundreds and hundreds of people visited the site. Now they, of course, believed that that was on the tree because God put it there. Therefore, it had meaning. We knew what it was. It was a representation of the face of Jesus, and the feeling that one could know what it was, interpret it, and take it to be an actual representation of something was therefore unquestioned. As we would all agree, you accept the premise: God wrote it or I should say put it there. He’s been known to do the same thing with toasted cheese sandwiches and tacos, and it happens, right? You accept that premise and you’re all set. But suppose you say, “No, no, no, no. God didn’t write that. God didn’t put that there. It’s just an accident.” Wouldn’t you then say, “Oh, therefore it has no meaning, it’s not a representation of anything, it just looks like something”?

换句话说，无论你对《沉睡封印了我的灵魂》这首歌有何感想，你都会接受克纳普和迈克尔斯的论点。你会说：“这确实取决于对意图的推断。如果我推断不出任何意图，我就不会赋予它任何意义。如果我推断出一个意图，我就会赋予它意义。”所以，克纳普和迈克尔斯对《沉睡封印了我的灵魂》这首歌的论证其实是一样的，而且我认为这是一个非常有力的论证。一旦你意识到——或者更确切地说，一旦你接受了这个观点——意义就是意图，并从词源学的角度去思考它——当我说“我的意思是”的时候，它的意思恰恰就是“我打算”，对吧？并非所有语言都如此，但在英语中确实如此。值得注意的是，“意思”即“意图”——说意义就是意图，这很有道理。将意义和意图分开来看，或许有悖常理，比如说：“我能看到这句话，也大致明白它的意思，但我仍然不知道作者的意图是什么。”这种说法在克纳普和迈克尔斯看来是不可取的。当然，你知道作者的意图是什么。你只是赋予了这句话意义而已。

In other words, in this case–however you feel about “A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal”– in this case you would accept Knapp and Michaels’s argument. You would say, “It really does depend on the inference of an intention. If I infer no intention, I ascribe no meaning. If I infer an intention, I ascribe meaning.” So Knapp and Michaels are simply making the same argument about “A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal,” and I think it’s a very strong argument. Once you realize–or once, I should say, you accept the idea–that meaning just is intention and think about it etymologically–when I say “I mean,” that precisely means “I intend,” right? It doesn’t quite work that way in all languages, but it certainly works that way in English, and it’s worth remembering to mean is “to intend” –it makes a lot of sense to say that a meaning just is an intention and that it’s perhaps against the grain of common sense to factor them apart, to say, “Well, I can see this sentence and I have a certain notion what it might mean, but I still don’t know what the author intended to say,” which is forbidden from the standpoint of Knapp and Michaels. Of course, you know what the author intended to say. You’ve just ascribed meaning to the sentence.

当然，你可能错了，但这并不意味着你的错误取决于你是否知道作者的意图。在某种意义上，克纳普和迈克尔斯与新批评家、福柯或其他任何人的观点完全一致，他们会说：“你永远无法知道作者的意图。”但这并非重点。句子的意义本身就蕴含着意图。如果一个句子不是由某个主体（无论是人还是其他生物）有意说出的，它就没有意义，因为它就不是语言。在某种意义上，这可以引出我们的第二个论点，因为他们已经充分证明，对于任何文本而言，文本的意义必然就是它的意图——换句话说，要想被理解为语言，再说一遍，要想被理解为语言，就必须推断出意图。这里的论点是，即使我们成功地没有推断出意图，我们也应该能够认识到，我们所看到的实际上并不是语言；它只是语言的模拟物，一种有效的语言复制品，例如鹦鹉的叫声或猴子用打字机打出的字等等。我们不应该从这种语言模拟物中推断出意图，更不应该推断出意义。把并非符号的标记当作语言来谈论是毫无意义的。

Now mind you, you may be wrong, but that isn’t to say that your being wrong hinges on knowing what the author intended. In a certain sense, Knapp and Michaels agree perfectly well with the New Critics and with Foucault or whoever it might be and say, “Well, you can never know what an author intended.” But that’s not the point. The meaning of the sentence in itself entails intention. If it weren’t a sentence spoken intentionally by an agent, human or otherwise, it wouldn’t have meaning because it wouldn’t be language. In a certain sense this, then, can carry us to our second argument because, having established in their own minds satisfactorily that for any text the meaning of the text must justbe its intention–in other words, to be understood as language at all, to repeat myself once again, and to be understood as language at all, an intention needs to be inferred. The argument here is that we ought to be able to recognize, supposing we succeed in not inferring an intention, that what we are looking at is actually not language; it’s just a simulacrum of language, an effective copy of language like, for example, the speech of a parrot or the words produced by monkeys on typewriters and so on. We should not from such simulacra of words infer not only intention but meaning as well. It is meaningless to speak of marks that are not signs as language.

第五章 言语中语言的发现

Chapter 5. The Discovery of Language in Speech

这就引出了“符号”的概念：对于C.S.皮尔斯而言，他实际上区分了数百种不同的符号，所有符号都是能动的——也就是说，它们具有能动性、目的性和功能。换句话说，皮尔斯并不像索绪尔那样将符号理解为差异性的。他也理解差异性，但对他而言，符号的核心在于符号的能动性。

Bringing us to the notion of “sign”: for C. S. Peirce, who actually discriminated among hundreds of different kinds of signs, all signs are active–that is to say, they have an agency, they have a purpose, they have a function. Peirce, in other words, does not understand them in the way that Saussure does as being differential. He understands that too, but for him the central point about a sign is the agency of the sign.

现在，这其中的含义显而易见，而这正是克纳普和迈克尔斯在论证中所依据的含义。他们的主张是，语言和言语之间没有区别。现在，让我们先来仔细思考一下他们​​的论证。我认为，当我们思考这个问题时——尤其是在我们接触过索绪尔，并且我希望我们已经接受了语言是一种虚拟的、共时性的、空间中呈现的实体，而言语则是一种源于语言、时间中呈现的实际的、历时性的实践这一观点之后——既然我们已经吸收了这些观点，而且如果我们是文学理论的学生，我们自然而然地会认为语言和言语之间存在区别：那么，当我们面对克纳普和迈克尔斯的这一主张时，我们该如何应对呢？

Now the implication of this is clear, and it’s the implication that Knapp and Michaels draw on in this argument. Their claim is that there is no distinction to be made between language and speech. Now let’s just pause over their argument. I would think the fact that as we think about that–especially since we have been exposed to Saussure and, I hope, have come to accept the idea that language is a virtual synchronic entity laid out in space, and speech is an actual diachronic performance derived from language laid out in time–since we have absorbed that and since we just have this sort of spontaneous belief, if we’re students of literary theory, that there is a distinction between language and speech: what do we do when we come face to face with this claim of Knapp and Michaels’s?

现在我认为他们最有力的论证体现在一个脚注中。这是本学期我要提请大家注意的最后一个脚注，而且和所有脚注一样，它或许是整篇文章中最具启发性的部分。它出现在复印中心资料包的第84页，脚注编号为12。我不会读完整篇，我只会读他们在第21页脚注12开头的一句话，他们说：“……[词典]是特定言语行为中常用词汇的索引，而不是抽象的、先于意图的可能性矩阵。”想想这句话。我们假设，语言除了是一套语法和句法规则之外，也是一套用于描述言语行为的定义。这是文学理论课程赋予我们的假设。

Now I think that they make their most effective case in a footnote. This is the last footnote I’ll be calling your attention to this semester, and it’s, like all footnotes, perhaps the most telling thing in the essay. It appears on page 084 in the copy center packet, footnote number twelve. I’m not going to read the whole thing. I’m just going to read a single sentence at the top their page twenty-one, footnote twelve, in which they say, “… [A] dictionary is an index of frequent usages in particular speech acts–not a matrix of abstract, pre-intentional possibilities.” Think about that. Language, we suppose, is, in addition to being a set of grammatical and syntactical rules, also a set of definitions made available for speech acts. That is the assumption that a course in literary theory provides for us.

克纳普和迈克尔斯在脚注中否认了这一点。他们认为，词典释义只不过是词语实际运用情况的总和，任何释义都指向一个本身就是一种言语行为的词语。你可以查阅一个词的全部十八个释义。它们都嵌入在句子（言语行为）之中，即使从句子中抽离出来，也能理解其作为言语行为的能动性。换句话说，根据克纳普和迈克尔斯的观点，词典中的任何词都是一个被执行过的词语，而词典中“化石化”的记录并非意义本身的记录，而是词语在言语和历史中运作方式的记录。词典只不过是言语行为的集合或总和。因此，将语言（作为行动前的存在）与言语（作为语言的实施）区分开来是错误的。语言，即便从它始终存在于我们面前的角度来看，也始终是活跃的。它是在我们作为说话者行动之前发生的那些行为的记录。我通过言语采取行动，与语言作为一种非行动的先存形式，两者之间并无区别。这一切都是持续不断的，构成了一个不断深化、扩展和自我复杂的行动记录，或者说是言语行动的记录。

Knapp and Michaels are denying that in this footnote. They are saying that dictionary definitions are just a sum total, as it were, of words in action, that any definition is of a word which is already a speech act. You go through all eighteen definitions of a word. They’re all of them embedded in sentences, speech acts, and can be taken out of sentences and still understood in their agency as performed. Any word in a dictionary, in other words, according to Knapp and Michaels, is a word performed, and the record fossilized, as it were, in the dictionary is a record not of meaning per sebut of performance, of the way in which the word works in speech, in history. A dictionary is nothing other than a composite or a sum total of speech acts. To distinguish, therefore, between language as something which is pre-action and speech as the implementation of language is a mistake. Language, even in the sense that it’s always there before us, is nevertheless always active. It is a record of those actions that have taken place before our own actions as speakers. There’s no difference between me acting through speech and language preexisting as something which is not action. It’s all continuous as an ever-deepening, broadening, and self-complicating record of action, or speech action.

这是一个非常有趣的想法，而且我认为，这个想法很有发展潜力。顺便说一句，我觉得应该为索绪尔辩护一下，因为他在某种程度上预见了这种观点。记得我之前说过，虽然为了学习，为了理解结构主义及其后续影响，我们通常只区分语言和言语，即“langue”和“parole”，但在索绪尔的理论中，实际上存在第三个范畴，一种中间范畴，他称之为“langage”（语言）。“langage”实际上是所有已知言语行为的总和。如果你能将所有曾经说过或写过的东西进行编码或量化，那就是“langage”。你可以看出它与“langue”的区别，“langue”未必曾经被说过。我稍后会再谈到这一点。换句话说，“langage”是“经验性的”，正如克纳普和迈克尔斯所说。如果我们有足够的信息，我们实际上可以将其编码到一个庞大的数据库中。它应该是所有言语行为的总和，而实际上，索绪尔所说的“语言”，与克纳普和迈克尔斯所说的“语言”并无太大区别。索绪尔意识到，人们可以像克纳普和迈克尔斯那样理解言语行为的总和，但他仍然坚持另一种范畴，即“语言”的概念，将其视为言语行为所源自的编码，一个独立于言语行为之外的概念。

Now this is a very interesting idea and I think, again, it’s an idea that one might well go a long way with. I think it should be said in defense of Saussure, by the way, that in a certain way he anticipates this position. Remember I told you that although for purposes of learning, to understand structuralism and its aftermath we only distinguish between language and speech, langue and parole, but in Saussure there’s actually a third category, a sort of intermediate category, which he calls langage. Langage is actually the sum total of all known speech acts. If you could codify or quantify everything that’s ever been said or written, that would be langage. You can see how it’s different from langue, which needn’t necessarily ever have been said at all. I’ll be coming back to that in a minute. Langage, in other words, is “empirical,” as Knapp and Michaels would say. It is something that, had we enough information, we could actually codify into a vast database. It would be the sum of all speech acts, and that actually, what Saussure calls langage, would be not unlike what Knapp and Michaels mean by language. Saussure is aware that you can think of the sum of speech acts in the way that Knapp and Michaels do, but he still holds out for this other category, this notion of langue as the code from which speech acts are derived, as a thing apart.

现在我认为，正如我所说，这是一个很有说服力的观点，因为归根结底，只要我们假设语言的存在是为了交流，假设它是互动的——只要我们接受（就像我们在课程中从巴赫金等人那里接受的那样）语言是社会性的，它的所有运用都是互动的，源于他人的言语行为，被使用者挪用为自己自己的一套言语行为，并作为一种言语行为影响他人——只要我们接受这一点，我们就会对自己说：“是的，把语言看作是言语不可分割的，把语言看作是所有能动性的总和，这样就不需要对这些能动性的总和与言语行为的个体能动性做出任何有意义的区分，这很有道理。”不过请注意——顺便说一句，接下来我要开始我的理论分析了，所以请各位做好准备！——请注意，我刚才那段话是以“只要我们假设语言的存在是为了交流”开头的。

Now I think, as I say, this is a persuasive position, because after all, as long as we suppose that language exists for communication, that it is interactive–as long as we accept, as we have accepted from Bakhtin and others during the course of the course–the idea that language is social, that all of its deployments are interactive, derived from the speech acts of others, appropriated for oneself as one’s own set of speech acts, and influential on yet other people as a speech act–as long as we accept this, we say to ourselves, “Yeah, it makes a lot of sense to think of language as inseparable from speech, to think of language simply as the sum of all agencies so that no meaningful distinction between that sum of agencies and the individual agency of a speech act needs to be made.” Notice though–and here, by the way, is where I’m going to make my turn and save theory, so sharpen your pencils!–notice that I began that last riff by saying “as long as we suppose language exists for communication.”

现在我们假设语言的存在是为了交流。除此之外，它还能为了什么而存在呢？除了交流，我们用语言还能做什么？你可能会说：“嗯，我们写涂鸦。我们在沙滩上留下毫无意义的痕迹。”我们或许会用语言做各种各样的事情，但说实话：我们并没有这么做，对吧？如果我真的在沙滩上留下了“沉睡封印了我的灵魂”这样的痕迹，那是因为我热爱华兹华斯，正如我所热爱的，我希望将这份热爱传递给全世界。这是一种言语行为。拜托，我不仅仅是在做标记。如果我想做标记，我会做一些更像标记的事情（做手势）。总之（笑声），我们生活在一个几乎不可能有人告诉我们“语言不是为了交流”的世界里。换句话说，克纳普和迈克尔斯的观点似乎完全正确。除此之外，它还能做什么呢？这就是我们使用语言的目的。我们已经将其完善为一种高效、灵活，有时甚至雄辩的沟通媒介。这就是语言的意义所在，也是它存在的意义。正如我所说，如果我们接受这个观点——这个观点似乎理所当然，因为谁还会想到其他观点呢？——如果我们接受这个观点，那么克纳普和迈克尔斯的观点就很有说服力。实际上，语言和言语之间并没有什么显著或重要的区别。

Now we do suppose language exists for communication. What else could it exist for? What do we do with language except to communicate? You could say, “Well, we write doodles. We make meaningless marks in the sand.” There are all kinds of things that maybe we do with language, but let’s face it: we don’t, right? If I do, in fact, make marks in the sand amounting to “A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal,” it’s because I love Wordsworth, as by the way I do, and I wish to communicate that love to the rest of the world. It’s a speech act. Come on, I’m not just making marks. If I wanted to make marks, I’d do something rather more mark-like [gesticulates]. Well, so [laughter] in any case, we certainly inhabit a life world in which it is almost inconceivable for anyone to come along and tell us, “Language is not for the purpose of communication.” In other words, Knapp and Michaels seem to be completely right. What else is it for? That’s what we use it for. We have refined it to a fare-thee-well as an efficient, flexible, sometimes even eloquent medium of communication. That’s what language is for, that’s what it exists for. As I’m saying, if we accept this idea–which seems simply to carry the day, because who could think anything else?–if we accept this idea, then there’s a very strong case for Knapp and Michaels being right. Really there’s no significant or important difference between language and speech.

第六章 理论的不切实际

Chapter 6. The Impracticality of Theory

但现在假设我们从一个——我不是说从经验的角度[笑]，而是从一个思辨的人类学的角度来探讨这个问题。假设我们用一些相当常识性的观点来看待它。我们说语言是为了交流；语言的目的是交流。我们这么说。尤其当我们回顾整个人类历史时，这是否意味着火的目的是烹饪？或者更贴近我们自身的例子，这是否意味着灵活的拇指的目的是抓握？这是否意味着洞穴，岩石上的洞，的目的是居住？不。在这些情况下，适应性使得火成为烹饪的好工具，灵活的拇指成为抓握的好工具，洞穴成为避难的好地方，但它们都以各自的方式存在于那里。显然，它们都有其他的，嗯，不是“目的”，因为仔细想想，目的只是我们强加于某物的东西；但它们的存在绝不是为了让我们去做我们后来觉得好做的事情。火会灼伤我们，但我们也可以用它来烹饪，等等。

But now suppose we approach the question from a–I don’t say from an empirical point of view [laughs] but from a speculative anthropological point of view. Suppose we approach it with some rather commonsense remarks. Now we say language is for communication; the purpose of language is for communication. We say that. Especially if we think of the whole history of mankind, does that mean that the purpose of fire is for cooking? Or to bring it a little bit closer to home, does it mean that the purpose of the prehensile thumb is for grasping? Does it mean that the purpose of a cave, a hole in the rock, is for dwelling? No. In those cases, adaptation is what makes fire a good thing to cook with, the prehensile thumb a good thing to grasp with, and a cave a good thing to take shelter in, but they all in their various ways are just there. Plainly, all of them have other, well, not “purposes,” because a purpose is, when you think about it, only something that we can impose on something; but they certainly are not there in any sense for us to do the thing that it turns out we’ve decided it’s a good idea to do with it. Fire burns us but we can cook with it, and so on.

就语言而言，我们必须承认，语言的出现方式，就像我们人类的拇指一样自然。当然，我们“发现了它的用途”，但这种说法未免有些滑稽。或许更准确的说法是，我们发现语言对我们而言具有交流的用途。一旦我们能够运用这种——无论它是什么，这种能够发出不同声音的奇特能力——一旦我们能够运用这种能力，语言便成为我们交流的工具。当然，我们成功地运用了语言，或者说，我们用它建造了一座巴别塔，无论你更倾向于哪种说法，但无论如何，我们拥有了语言，并且它在我们中间发展成为一种交流媒介。

Now in the case of language, we have to suppose as a matter of fact that language, as it were, appeared among us in the same way that the prehensile thumb did. Of course we “discovered its use,” but that’s a funny way to put it. It might be more circumspect to say that we discovered it had a use for us which was to communicate, and so once we were able to put this–whatever it was, this weird capacity to make differential sounds–once we put this weird capacity to make differential sounds to work, henceforth for us and for our purposes language was there to communicate. Of course we made an enormous success of it, or a tower of Babel of it, whichever you prefer to think, but in any case we have it, and it has developed among us as a means of a medium of communication.

但无论语言是通过何种变异产生的，假设情况确实如此——我在这里的论点与“智能设计”没有任何关系——假设语言是通过某种变异出现的，那么，当然，第二天就出现了雪崩式的传播：那么，我们这个物种（包括坐在这个房间里的所有人，以及我猜还有其他一些人）很可能是不会说话的。[笑] 它或许能以惊人的雄辩，甚至文学天赋，通过符号或其他方式进行交流——谁知道呢？或者，它的发展轨迹可能发生了某种转变，以至于交流方式不再具有任何人类特有的特征。所有有感知能力的生物都会交流，但这个特定的物种有可能在发展过程中发生了某种转变，之后它的交流方式就像老鼠、蚂蚁或其他生物之间的交流方式一样。

But by whatever mutancy language arose, supposing this to be the case–and I’m not making an argument that has anything to do with “intelligent design” one way or another–supposing that by whatever mutancy language appeared, then, of course, the next day there were an avalanche: then it might well be the case that this species consisting of all of us sitting in this room and I guess a few other people, [laughs] that this species might be mute. It might be communicating perhaps with incredible eloquence, perhaps even with literary genius, by means of signs or–who knows? Or for that matter it might have taken a detour in its development such that communication was not anything one could identify as specifically human. All sentient beings communicate, but it’s possible that this particular species could have taken a turn in its development after which communication was much as it is among mice or ants or whatever.

你看，这一切皆有可能，当我们从人类学的角度思考语言——一种我们拥有、操控并与之交流的属性时。语言的产生方式使得我认为，说它的目的是交流几乎无关紧要。它仅仅作为一种属性、一种特性而存在，是我们碰巧拥有的东西，是某人碰巧拥有的东西，然后人们发现了它的用途，就像火、灵活的拇指和洞穴一样。在我看来，洞穴和房屋之间的关系，为我们思考语言作为一系列差异和语言作为言语之间的关系提供了一个特别有趣的视角。

All of this is possible, you see, when we think about language–a property that we have and manipulate and communicate with–anthropologically. It comes into being in such a way that it is, I would think, scarcely relevant to say that its purpose is for communication. It comes into being simply as an attribute, a property, something we happen to have, something someone happens to have for which a use is then discovered, as for fire, for the prehensile thumb and for the cave. The relationship between the cave and the house, it seems to me, is a particularly interesting way of thinking about the relationship between language as a set of differentials and language as speech.

注意语言符号的一些特点——当然，这里我们也要提到索绪尔。索绪尔强调语言是由差异性和任意性的符号构成的。换句话说，索绪尔否认语言中存在所谓的自然符号。俄国形式主义者也持同样的观点。索绪尔和俄国形式主义者都告诫我们，不要相信拟声词——例如“哔哔哔”——之类的拟声词实际上是自然符号，也就是说，它们并非源自于它们通过声音所代表的现实世界。索绪尔提醒我们，这些拟声词是词源历史的偶然产物，也可以从适应性的角度来理解。拟声词之所以存在于语言中，是因为它有利于交流，而且交流起来也很有趣，但它并非作为自然符号进入语言的。它只是在某个词语的演变过程中，在声音与所代表事物之间的关系看似自然的时刻出现。

Notice something about the signs of language–and here of course we also invoke Saussure. Saussure lays every stress on the idea that language is made up of differential and arbitrary signs. In other words, Saussure denies that there is such a thing in language as a natural sign. The Russian formalists do this as well. Both Saussure and the Russian formalists warn us against believing that onomatopoetic devices–for example, “peep, peep, peep”–devices like that, are actually natural signs, that they are derived, in other words, from the thing in the world that they seem through their sound to represent. Saussure reminds us that these are accidents of etymological history which can also be understood in adaptive terms. Onomatopoeia exists in language because it’s good for communication and it’s fun to communicate with, but it doesn’t enter language as a natural sign. It only passes through moments–in the evolution of a given word–it only passes through moments in which the relationship between the sound and the thing represented seems to be natural.

索绪尔和俄国形式主义者都非常重视这一点。当你读到这些如此强调拟声的段落时，你可能会想：这未免太过分了。谁会在意拟声呢？然而，拟声恰恰是语言理念的核心，而语言理念的核心恰恰在于它并非言语。当我们说话时，我们不仅试图交流，也试图指称。换句话说，我们运用语言，并试图让它像哲学家所说的那样，与自然世界相联系。我们运用一套符号，一套本身并非自然、而是任意的符号系统，然后凭借意志力，尽我们所能地使这些符号与自然、与现实世界相联系。如此一来，我们便强化了语言是用来交流的观念——而我的论点是，语言并非用来交流的；言语才是。

This is a matter upon which great stress is laid both in Saussure and in the Russian formalists. When you read these passages in which such stress is laid on it you may have thought: well, that’s overkill. Who cares about onomatopoeia? Well, it anchors the entire idea about language, which is precisely that it is something other than speech. When we speak, we not only endeavor to communicate; we endeavor to refer. In other words, we take language and we try to make it, as the philosophers say, hook on to the natural world. We take a set of signs, a code which is not in itself natural, which is arbitrary, and through the sheer force of will, we make those signs as best we can hook on to the natural, to the actual world. In doing so, we reinforce the idea that language is for communication–whereas my argument is language isn’t for communication; speech is.

我们说话，完全、仅仅、没有任何其他动机，都是为了交流，但有一点例外，这一点尤其受到俄国形式主义者的关注。我们的语言中存在一些有趣的现象——头韵、不必要的或不简洁的重复——这些怪异的现象似乎与交流无关。事实上，它们似乎反而阻碍了交流。当我开始故意破坏语言时——例如，在刘易斯·卡罗尔的诗句“'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves / did gyre and gimble in the wabe”中——我就是在阻碍交流，因为我强调了节奏、模式和声音重复等元素，而这些元素与交流本身并没有直接关系。

When we speak, that is–entirely and exclusively and without any other motive–for communication, except for one thing that the Russian formalists in particular took note of. There are funny things going on in our speech–alliteration, unnecessary or uneconomical forms of repetition–weird things going on in our speech which don’t seem to have the purpose of communication. As a matter of fact, they actually seem to impede communication. When I really start messing language up–for example, in Lewis Carroll’s “’Twas brillig, and the slithy toves / did gyre and gimble in the wabe”–I am impeding communication because I am laying stress on elements of rhythm, pattern, and sound recurrence which cannot be said to have any direct bearing on communication.

当然，这正是我们反复研究的内容，而且我必须说，我们是通过实证研究得出的结论（笑），因为正如俄国形式主义者所坚持的那样，这些都是关于语言的经验事实。我们反复研究的是语言在言语中如何冒出其丑陋的一面，换句话说，语言不会仅仅被压制为一种交流手段，言语中包含着一些不断涌现并彰显自身存在的元素，而这些元素奇怪的是，实际上并不能说它们有助于交流。那些涌现出来的事物，那些浮出水面的元素，恰恰是语言存在的证据，正如弗洛伊德所说的弗洛伊德式口误——即我无法完整地说完一句话而不犯错，而且往往是令人尴尬的错误——被理解为一种意识层面的努力，试图表达那些语言无法控制的事物，也就是弗洛伊德所说的“无意识”。顺便说一句，如果没有弗洛伊德式口误，我们根本无法意识到无意识的存在。换句话说，正如弗洛伊德在学期初我发给你们的第一份讲义中所说，我们之所以从意识的行为推断无意识，是因为鉴于意识行为的反复无常，这样做似乎是必要的。

This, of course, is what we’ve studied recurrently and, I have to say, empirically [laughs] because these are all empirical facts about language, as the Russian formalists insisted. What we have studied recurrently is the way in which language rears its ugly head in speech, the way in which, in other words, language won’t be repressed as mere communication, the way in which speech entails elements that keep bubbling up to the surface and asserting themselves, which oddly enough really can’t be said to conduce to communication. Those things, those elements that bubble up to the surface, are nothing other than evidence of the presence of language, precisely in the way that in Freud the Freudian slip–the fact that I can’t get through a sentence without making some kind of blunder, very often an embarrassing blunder–is understood as the bubbling up into the conscious effort to speak of that which speech can’t control, of that which Freud calls “the unconscious” and which, by the way, we would have no idea of the existence of if it weren’t for the Freudian slip. In other words, as Freud said in the first handout that I gave you at the beginning of the semester, we infer the unconscious from the behavior of consciousness because, given the erratic nature of the behavior of consciousness, it seems necessary to do so.

以此类推，我们可以——而且我认为我们应该说——从言语行为的复合或总和中推断出语言是某种其他的东西。我们从言语行为的不规则性中推断出语言，因为似乎没有其他方法可以解释言语行为的不规则性。这种语言感——我将在周四更详细地讨论——在言语中自下而上地涌现，并证明其存在并非仅仅是所有言语行为的复合记录。正是这种语言感让我们觉得，克纳普和迈克尔斯关于语言和言语之间实际上没有区别的说法并不完全正确；如果语言和言语之间确实存在区别，正如我所主张的那样，而且如果这种区别正如索绪尔及其后继者直至解构主义所教导我们的那样——如果确实存在这样的区别，那么猜猜会发生什么？文学理论又重新焕发了生机，我们不再需要说它应该从我们对文学的思考中被抛弃。文学理论对我们有实际用途。

By precisely the same token, we can and, I think we should say, we do infer language as something else from the composite or sum total of speech acts. We infer language from the erratic behavior of speech because it seems there is no other way to account for the erratic behavior of speech. That sense of language, which I’m going to be talking a lot more about on Thursday, sort of bubbling up and from below in speech, and proving its existence as something other than a composite record of all speeches, is what suggests to us that Knapp and Michaels are not quite right in saying there is really no difference between language and speech; that if there is a difference between language and speech, as I am claiming, and if the difference between language and speech is much as we have been taught to think of it by Saussure and his successors down through deconstruction–if there is such a difference, then guess what? We have literary theory back in the fold, alive and well, and we no longer have to say that it should be jettisoned from our thinking about literature. We have a real use for literary theory.

但克纳普和迈克尔斯的情况恰恰相反，假设他们在这里，而我成功说服了他们——顺便说一句，我认识他们俩。你根本说服不了他们，但这并不奇怪。你可能也说服不了我——假设我们把他们叫来，而我成功说服了他们。他们会说：“好吧，这难道不可惜吗？因为你比我们更清楚地证明了文学理论毫无用处。我们为什么要费心去管这些与交流毫无关系的东西呢？毕竟，我们来到这个世界是为了交流，不是吗？我们一开始就说过，我们的生活世界正是由语言的运用构成的，而现在这个人却说有这些东西冒出来，使交流变得困难。这有什么用呢？”克纳普和迈克尔斯可能会这么说。你看，他们是实用主义者，不是吗？他们是实用主义者，或者说，他们关注的是实用性。他们对意义和诠释的兴趣，或者说他们感兴趣的原因，完全出于对交流的理解和促进交流的实践目的；而我保留下来的理论，似乎也付出了相当大的代价，因为我曾提出理论本身是完全不切实际的。我已经提出了这个观点，我们下次再来讨论。这就是周四讲座的主题。

But that’s exactly where Knapp and Michaels, supposing they were here and I’d convinced them–by the way, I know them both. You can’t convince them of anything, but that’s not unusual. You probably can’t convince me of anything either–suppose we had them here and I had succeeded in convincing them. They would say, “Well, okay, but isn’t it a pity? Because you have proved better than we did that literary theory has no purpose. Why on earth should we worry about all this bubbling up of stuff that has nothing to do with communication? After all, we’re here to communicate, aren’t we? We’ve begun by saying that our life world consists precisely in the deployment of language for communication, and here is this person saying there is this stuff bubbling up, which makes communication difficult. What use is that?” Knapp and Michaels might say. You see, they are pragmatists, aren’t they? They are pragmatists, or they are concerned with practicality. Their interest, their reason for being interested in meaning and interpretation, is a practical reason entirely entailed in the understanding of communication and the furtherance of communication; whereas theory, which I have saved, I nevertheless seem to have saved at a pretty considerable cost because I have suggested that theory itself is completely impractical. I have suggested it, and we’re going to get back to that next time. That’s what the Thursday lecture is going to be about.

与此同时，你可能会对自己说：“好吧，没问题。我们有了理论，但也已经证明它实际上毫无用处，所以或许我们应该假设克纳普和迈克尔斯是对的​​，然后像抛弃理论一样继续前进。” 最后再补充一点，回到意义和意图的区别：注意这个双管齐下的论点。一方面，像E·D·赫希这样的人认为，你可以通过援引作者的意图来确定意义——一方面是这样的人；另一方面，一些解构主义者则认为，由于不存在可推断的意图，文本本身就没有意义。但这并不完全正确，因为这并非解构主义的真正含义。解构主义并没有说文本没有意义。解构主义甚至没有说你无法确切地知道文本的意义是什么。解构主义认为，你无法将文本的意义界定起来。文本蕴含的意义太多了。文本的意义如同爆炸般涌现。你无法控制文本产生意义的方式。你无法通过推断意图来控制它。你也无法通过采取特定的解释路径来控制它。意义在文本中就是如此奔涌而出。

In the meantime you say to yourself, “Okay, fine. We’ve got theory, but we have also been shown that you can’t really do anything with it, and so it might just as well suit us to suppose that Knapp and Michaels are right and to proceed as though theory could be jettisoned.” One last quick point, going back to the distinction between meaning and intention: notice the two-pronged argument. On the one hand, there are people like E. D. Hirsch who believe that you can invoke an author’s intention in order to pin down a meaning–on the one hand, you have people like that and, on the other hand, you have people doing deconstruction who say that because there is no inferable intention, texts themselves have no meaning. But that’s not quite right, because that’s not really what deconstruction says. Deconstruction doesn’t say texts have no meaning. Deconstruction doesn’t even say that you can’t know what the meaning of a text is, exactly. What deconstruction says is that you can’t rope off meaning in a text. Texts have too much meaning. Texts explode with meaning. You can’t corral the way in which texts produce meaning. You can’t corral it by inferring an intention. You can’t corral it by taking a particular interpretive path. Meaning just explodes in texts.

这与克纳普和迈克尔斯所声称的“解构主义思维中文本没有意义”完全是两码事——这完全是两个截然不同的观点。我认为这或许暗示你，意图与意义之间的关系并非解构主义的核心所在。文本是有意图的，或者你可以说，“嗯，它可能是有意的，毫无疑问它是有意的”——各种各样的说法都有，但这真的是重点吗？在我看来，文本就是文本，正如我所说，文本本身就蕴含着丰富的意义，而这恰恰是关键所在。你无法控制它。这并非克纳普和迈克尔斯想要让你认为的反面——也并非赫希的追随者们所认为的“为了理解意义，你必须能够推断作者意图”这一观点的反面。那里存在不对称性，而且，正如我所说，我不确定解构主义，无论它声称什么，无论它有多么完美和不完美——我不确定解构主义是否真的以某种方式将意图与意义的关系问题放在了核心位置。

That’s not at all the same thing as to say, according to the claim of Knapp and Michaels, that in deconstructive thinking texts have no meaning–a very, very different proposition altogether. I think it might suggest to you that the relationship between intention and meaning isn’t really what’s at stake in deconstruction. A text is intended, or you can say, “Well, it may be intended, no doubt it’s intended”–all sorts of ways of putting it, but is that really the point? The text is the text on my view, and the text, just as I say, fairly bristles with meaning, that being precisely the point. You can’t rein it in. That’s not really the flip side–as Knapp and Michaels would want to make you think–that’s not really the flip side of the idea of the followers of Hirsch that in order to know a meaning, you have to be able to infer an authorial intention. There is nosymmetry there and, as I say, I’m not sure that deconstruction, whatever its claims, whatever its perfections and imperfections–I am not sure that really deconstruction has the question of intention in relation to meaning very much at heart one way or another.

抱歉耽搁了您。我们周四见。

Sorry to have kept you. We’ll see you Thursday.

第26讲——反思；现在谁不讨厌理论了？

Lecture 26 - Reflections; Who Doesn’t Hate Theory Now?

第一章 什么是理论？

Chapter 1. What Is Theory?

保罗·弗莱教授：上次我们把理论从克纳普和迈克尔斯的掌控中拯救了出来，我们通过指出语言和言语之间确实存在区别做到了这一点。在今天的总结讲座中，我将继续探讨这个观点。但与此同时，当我提到我们拯救了理论时，你们或许会问：“好吧，你们拯救了它，但是为了什么？为什么？”上次我们开始提出，在某种意义上，尤其考虑到新实用主义者关于语言和言语（被理解为同一事物）能动性的论断，鉴于这类论断，我们是否必须得出理论是不切实际的结论？也就是说，它与实用主义的目标毫无关系？这也是我今天想稍微探讨一下的问题。我们为什么要费心拯救文学理论？嗯，这显然与交流有关。

Professor Paul Fry: Well, last time we saved theory from the clutches of Knapp and Michaels, and we did so by saying that there really is a difference between language and speech. That’s a claim that I want to continue investigating in today’s concluding lecture, but in the meantime when I say we saved theory, you may well be asking by this time, “Well, okay, so you saved it, but for what? Why?” We began to suggest last time that in a certain sense, especially in view of neo-pragmatists’ claims about the agency of language and speech–understood to be one and the same thing–in view of claims of this kind, do we have to conclude that theory is impractical? That is, that it can’t have anything to do with pragmatist objectives? That, too, is something I want to worry a little bit about today. Why do we bother to save literary theory? Well, it has something to do plainly with communication.

正如我们上次所说，语言毫无疑问是为了沟通——也就是说，我们创造语言就是为了沟通。所以，那个老生常谈、说实话已经让人厌烦透顶的问题——“我们彼此沟通得如何？”——在某种程度上，与我们想要探讨的主题并非毫无关联。我想谈谈法国人在存在主义时期所说的“沟通缺失”（la manque de la communication）。某种程度上，这两者之间并没有真正的联系。首先，我想说，我们实际上沟通得相当不错。换句话说，恭喜我们！我认为，人们常常担忧我们是否能够互相理解——很多时候，这种担忧其实有些夸大其词。我个人的感觉是，或许很多时候我们对彼此的理解太透彻了，（笑）如果我们对彼此的立场没有那么敏锐的感知，或许会更好。这或许会改善人际关系，而不是适得其反，而这可能与我们试图聚在一起提升彼此意识的方式中存在的某种程度的不真诚有关。我们认为，问题的根源在于我们沟通不够顺畅，对彼此的立场理解不够透彻。

Speech, as we said last time, is unquestionably for–that is to say we have made it for–communication. So the old, frankly incredibly tired question, “How well do we communicate with each other?” is unfortunately, in a way, not irrelevant to what we’re trying to get at here. I want to say a couple of things about what the French during the existentialist period called la manque de la communication. In a way, they’re not really connected. First of all, I want to say that we actually communicate rather well. Congratulations to us, in other words! I think that many of the conventional ways in which people worry about whether or not we can understand each other–many of those ways of thinking about the problem are actually exaggerated. My own feeling is that perhaps a good deal of the time we understand each other all too well, and [laughs] that it might be better, in a way, if we didn’t have quite such an acute sense of where each of us are coming from. It probably would improve human relations rather than otherwise, and this may have something to do with what I take to be a certain measure of bad faith in the ways in which we try to get together and raise each other’s consciousness. Our supposition is that the whole problem is that we don’t communicate well enough, and we don’t understand each other’s subject positions well enough.

正如我所说，我对此并不完全信服，所以从某种意义上说，我会说：“嘿，口语很棒。它运行良好。别担心。我们的沟通非常顺畅，甚至可能太顺畅了。”那么，理论究竟为何要跳出来说：“嗯，沟通似乎存在一些问题”呢？问题在于语言这个令人烦恼的存在，它不断地在沟通过程中出现，阻碍沟通，正如俄国形式主义者所指出的那样——在他们看来，这完全是好事——语言确实会阻碍沟通。这为什么重要？究竟有什么利害关系？正如克纳普和迈克尔斯可能会说的那样，指出语言阻碍沟通的方式究竟有什么利害关系？换句话说，我们的沟通很好，但我们真正想表达的是，我们在日常沟通中表现良好。口语具有一种粗略而有效的特性，任何否认这一点的人，正如我所说，只是夸大了可能存在的问题，而这些问题并非源于沟通的困难。所以，口语在某种程度上确实很好。

As I say, I’m not completely convinced of that, so there’s a certain sense in which I say, “Hey, speech is great. It’s doing just fine. Don’t worry. We’re communicating perfectly well, possibly too well.” So why on earth should theory come along and say, “Well, there’s sort of a problem with communication”? The problem is this nagging entity called language which keeps poking up through the communication process, getting in its way, impeding communication, as the Russian formalists suggested–all for the better, as they saw it–that language does. Why should it matter? What’s at stake? As Knapp and Michaels might say, what’s at stake in calling attention to the way in which language does impede communication? In other words, we communicate fine, but what we really mean in saying that is, we communicate fine for everyday purposes. Speech has a rough and ready efficacy, and anybody who denies that, as I say, is simply exaggerating problems that may exist on grounds other than difficulty of communication. So speech is really fine up to a point.

理论的部分功能恰恰在于探究言语在不受阻碍的情况下究竟能达到怎样的沟通效果，以及言语沟通所能达到的准确性和细节程度。这些都是我们期望理论提出的问题。如果你说：“嗯，我仍然不太相信这是个人学术生活的重要组成部分”，我不会责怪你。我希望在接下来的四十五分钟左右的时间里，能够让你相信它在很多方面都非常重要，值得我们铭记于心。

Part of the function of theory is precisely to interrogate the degree to which speech in an unimpeded way communicates and the level of accuracy and detail at which speech can ever be expected to communicate. These are the sorts of questions that we might expect theory to ask, and if you say, “Well, I’m still not very convinced that that’s an important aspect of one’s intellectual life,” I don’t blame you. I hope to have convinced you over the next forty-five minutes or so that it’s pretty important in a variety of ways and that it’s worth keeping in mind.

与此同时，为了初步探讨这个问题，我们可以先理解理论——当然，我们这学期伊始就对理论进行了定义，试图区分理论与哲学、理论与方法论，甚至包括克纳普和迈克尔斯称之为“诗学”的文学研究方法；或许还可以区分理论与诠释学，毕竟，诠释学的全部动力和功能在于发现意义。正如我们遗憾地意识到，在某种程度上，理论更关注意义受阻的方式，因此——正如我们在课程伊始所指出的——如果我们想要真正理解理论，就必须牢记它并非哲学。

In the meantime, just to start on this issue tentatively, we can understand theory–and of course, we began the semester by defining it, by trying to distinguish between theory and philosophy; theory and methodology; perhaps even those sorts of approaches to literature that Knapp and Michaels call “poetics”; maybe even to distinguish between theory and hermeneutics, because after all, the whole drive and function of hermeneutics is to discover meaning. There is a certain sense, as we have come sadly to realize, in which theory is more interested in the way in which meaning is impeded, so it may be–as we suggested, as I say, at the beginning of the course–that as to theory, if we’re to get comfortable with it at all, we have to keep in mind that it’s not philosophy.

也就是说，即便你精通理论，理解理论的目的，你仍然可以成为系统构建者。也就是说，你仍然可以理解哲学若要发挥其应有的作用，或者说哲学本应发挥的作用，就需要解释所有事物的整体性。你仍然可以像克纳普和迈克尔斯所说的那样，以经验的方式探讨文学数据的问题，并将这些数据概括成我们所谓的“诗学”。你可以做所有这些事情，而不必觉得理论总是站在一旁，对你指手画脚、摇头晃脑。理论不必被理解为一种监督者。至少在我看来（并非所有人都同意我的观点），理论实际上让我们自由地探索，它只是提醒我们，在思考阐释和意义的问题时，有一些需要牢记的界限或保留意见，而牢记这些界限或保留意见或许是最明智的做法。

That is to say, even though you’re good at theory and you understand the purpose of theory, you can still be a system builder. That is to say, you can still have a sense of explaining the totality of things that philosophy needs if it’s going to function as philosophy or as philosophy properly should. You can still, as Knapp and Michaels say, engage empirically with questions of literary data summarized in such a way as to amount to what we call “poetics.” You can do all these things, and you don’t really have to feel as though theory is somehow or another standing on the sidelines sort of shaking its fist at you and wagging its finger. Theory doesn’t have to be understood as a watchdog. At least in my opinion, and not everyone agrees with me, theory really lets us go our own way and simply reminds us that there are certain limits or reservations that need to be kept in mind, that one is perhaps wisest to keep in mind, as we think through problems of interpretation and meaning.

因此，我将理论定义为——我多次使用了“否定”这个词——一种消极的思维运动，它描绘了理论合法性的种种方式——与我之前提出的那些可能不合法的方式相对——同时也描绘了对交流抱持怀疑态度的合理方式。理论是对那些通常被认为是真理、被假定为真理，以及——当然，这里就引出了关键点——被宣扬为真理的事物的一种反制力量：被阐明、被表达、被宣扬为真理。那么，如果真是如此，为什么还要纠结于语言呢？为什么我们如此迅速地将问题缩小到语言层面呢？

So theory I would define as–and I’ve used this word “negation” a lot–I would define theory as a negative movement of thought mapping the ways in which it is legitimate–as opposed to the ways in which I have suggested it’s perhaps not legitimate–but mapping the ways in which it is legitimate to be suspicious of communication. Theory is an antithetical counterforce to that which is commonly supposed to be true, posited as true, and–here of course one comes to the point–spoken as true: enounced, articulated, spoken as true. So if that’s the case, why the fuss about language? Why do we so quickly narrow the issue down to language?

第二章 语言阻碍言语的三种方式

Chapter 2. Three Ways That Language Impedes Speech

我上次关于语言以及语言与言语之间关系的论述可能因为过于狭隘而显得不够令人信服。今天，我想拓宽，大幅拓宽我对“语言”一词的理解。在我看来，理论在三个方面助长了人们对言语效力，也就是那些被认为是真理的话语的怀疑。

What I said last time about language and the relationship between language and speech may have seemed unconvincing to you because it was so narrow. I want to broaden today, considerably broaden, the sense of what I mean by “language.” It seems to me that theory encourages a measure of suspicion about the efficacy of speech, that which is spoken as true, in three ways.

上次我提到了一点，这次我想强调三点。第一点，也是我上次提到的，是语言以声音的形式介入的方式。换句话说，如果我们思考言语作为一种交流媒介的效率或功能，我们就不得不问自己，即便在我们说话的时候，言语为何会背负如此多的负担，而这些负担在大多数情况下对我们毫无用处。当然，有时它们确实有用。上次有个大一新生问我：“声音难道不是对意义的强化吗？” 我之前告诉过你们，我们学习新批评的时候，你们高中都学过新批评。你们就是通过新批评学习文学阐释的。嗯，这完美地体现了一个刚从高中毕业的聪明人会说：“阐释就是新批评，我学过声音强化意义。佩林的诗歌理解手册里也是这么说的。声音强化意义。”当然，这种情况经常发生，在这些情况下，我们可以尽情享受通过声音模式的使用方式而增强的有意含义或有意结构的复杂性。

Last time I mentioned one, but now let me emphasize three. The first and the one I did mention last time is the way in which language obtrudes itself as sound. In other words, if we think of the efficiency or functionality of speech as a medium of communication, we’re forced to ask ourselves, even as we engage in speech, how and why it is that speech is so much burdened in ways that are of no use whatsoever to us for the most part. Sometimes they are of use. One of the pre-freshmen asked me last time, “Well, isn’t sound a reinforcement of meaning?” I told you when we did the New Criticism that all of you had done the New Criticism in high school. That’s the way you learned literary interpretation. Well, this was a perfect embodiment of a bright person coming out of high school saying, “Interpretation just is the New Criticism and I’ve been taught that sound reinforces sense. That’s what it says in Perrine’s handbook about understanding poetry. Sound reinforces sense.” Well, it often does, of course, and on those occasions we can revel in the complexity of an intentional meaning or intentional structure that is augmented by the way in which sound patterns are used.

与此同时，正如俄国形式主义者所发现的那样，他们研究的材料或许并非像约翰·邓恩的《封圣》或某种程度上易于被新批评所接受的那种文本，而是俄罗斯传统中的头韵诗、民间传说和民间诗歌，以及蕴含谚语的诗歌——他们在研究这些材料时注意到，在这些材料所涉及的音韵元素中，根本无法把握语义目的，即与意义相关的目的。我认为，当我们意识到自发性言语中存在一种奇特的、趋向于声音重复的倾向时，这不仅仅是因为我们都在不知不觉中说着抑扬格五音步——顺便说一句，这在很大程度上是事实。不仅如此，更重要的是，我们所说的话中存在着大量的头韵和节奏规律。

At the same time, as the Russian formalists discovered, working through materials that weren’t perhaps so much materials like John Donne’s “The Canonization” or texts of the kind that lent themselves, to a degree, readily to the New Criticism; but rather alliterative verse, folklore and folk verse in the Russian tradition, verse embodying proverbs–what they noticed in studying these materials is that there is simply no way of grasping a semantic purpose, a purpose having to do with meaning, in the sound elements that are involved. I think that as we recognize the way in which there is a strange pull in our spontaneous speaking toward repetitiousness of sound, it’s not just that we all speak iambic pentameter without knowing it–which, by the way, is by and large and true. It’s not just that. It’s that there is an extraordinary amount of alliteration and rhythmic determination in what we say.

雅各布森在《语言学与诗学》中提出了一个有趣的观点，即当我们身处事故附近时，或者类似的事情发生时，我们往往会这样理解。他实际上是说：“你可以用任何词来称呼处于那种境地的人，但我们称他为无辜的旁观者，而我们这样做的原因在于度量标准。”之所以称某人为无辜的旁观者，并非因为这个表达方式与其他表达方式相比具有任何特定的含义或语义价值，而是因为它朗朗上口，因为它容易被记住，或许是出于记忆技巧的原因。艾森豪威尔之所以能击败史蒂文森赢得大选，是因为“我喜欢艾克”比“疯狂地支持阿德莱”更能有效地利用声音的重复。雅各布森没有深入探讨这一点，但我认为，正如我所说，“我喜欢艾克”的更有效性可以进行有趣的政治分析。所有这些声音的功能，或者更确切地说，声音在言语中的呈现方式，在经济学家看来或许是非理性的。它们就在那里，它们在发挥作用，但这并非我们通常意义上所说的沟通作用。它们所发挥的作用，某种程度上是语言自由发挥的产物。它们只是以一种任意的方式与言语的语义模式联系在一起。

Jakobson has an interesting point in “Linguistics and Poetics” about that moment when we’re nearby and an accident takes place or something like that. He says in effect, “You could call a person in a situation like that anything, but we call that person an innocent bystander, and the reason we do so is metric.” A person is an innocent bystander not because that expression has any particular meaning or semantic valence as over against other expressions but because it’s catchy, because it sort of sticks in our mind, perhaps for mnemotechnical reasons, as catchy. Eisenhower won the election against Stevenson because “I like Ike” is a more efficient sort of way of engaging with the repetition of sound than “Madly for Adlai.” Jakobson doesn’t go into that, but I think an interesting political analysis could be made of, as I say, the greater efficacy of “I like Ike.” All of these functions of sound or, I should say, appearances of sound in speech are what an economist might call irrational. They’re there, they’re doing a job, but it’s not really a job of anything that we could call communication. The job they’re doing is sort of free spirited on the part of language. It’s just there in an arbitrary relation with the semantic pattern of speech.

以上便是关于声音的部分，但文学理论远不止于此。如果仅仅如此，如果文学理论仅仅局限于俄国形式主义者最初两三年的研究成果，我们或许就不会开设这门学科的入门概览课程了。语言还会以其他两种方式阻碍言语表达。首先——或者更准确地说，是其次——言语表达会受到语言本身的一种干扰，即语言会在所说的话中产生一种无法控制的语义漂移。我就是想这样称呼它。换句话说，话语的语言是经过精心设计的，旨在表达某种特定的含义。事实上，索绪尔在他一部不如《普通语言学教程》那样广为人知的著作中，发表了一篇专著，探讨了如何在拉丁诗歌中发现各种隐藏或嵌入的缩略语。换句话说，意义之中蕴含着意义，这些意义不可能是人为植入的，然而，奇迹般地，你却能从中找到它们。你可以背诵一首著名的诗——就是我们上次讲的那首，因为它是克纳普和迈克尔斯在《反对理论》一书中举的例子——你可以一边读黑板上的内容一边背诵这首诗：[指着黑板上写的内容：

So much then for sound, but it’s not only that. If it were only that, if literary theory were only about the first two or three years’ worth of research performed by the Russian formalists, we probably wouldn’t be having an introductory survey course in the subject. Speech is impeded by language in two other ways. First of all– second of all, I should say, I suppose–speech is disturbed by the way in which language produces in what’s being said an uncontrollable semantic drift. That’s what I want to call it. In other words, the language of an utterance is crafted to say some particular thing. Actually, it was Saussure, in a work of his that’s less known than the Course in General Linguistics, who published a monograph on the way in which you can find acronyms of various kinds buried or embedded in Latin verse. In other words, there is meaning within meaning which can’t possibly have been planted there and yet, miraculously enough, you can find there. You can recite a well-known poem–the one that we took up last time because it was the example given in Knapp and Michaels’ “Against Theory”–you can recite a poem while reading this: [referring to what is written on the chalkboard:

啊，贫民窟每死一个，嗯，我用矛刺穿了海豹，眼睛补充道，知道休谟，而且凶猛！沙阿缝（呃！）很薄；蜱虫木结费用生病了：砰！翻过背耳。

Ah slum per dead, um, I spear’d seal, Eye add, know Hume, ’n fierce! Shah seam (duh!) thin; the tic wood-knot fee ill: Thud! A shover the lee ears.

不再！现在就避开哈希，不要四，嘘！膝盖后腿，北欧式轻松，角色溺水，受伤，死亡，骨灰瓮：所有尸体，牛去哪儿了？——嘶嘶！——负重条目。

No mo’! Shun hash e’en now, no fours, Shhh! Knee th’rears, Norse ease, Role drown, an’ hurts, die, urn: all corpse, Whither oxen?–ssst!-onus entries.]

沉睡封印了我的灵魂；我没有人类的恐惧：她似乎是一个感受不到尘世岁月痕迹的存在。

A slumber did my spirit seal; I had no human fears: She seem’d a thing that could not feel The touch of earthly years.

她现在没有动静，没有力量；她既听不见，也看不见；随着地球的昼夜循环，与岩石、石头和树木一起滚动。

No motion has she now, no force; She neither hears nor sees; Roll’d ’round in earth’s diurnal course With rocks, and stones, and trees.

现在你可以看出，这样写诗实际上是一种练习，而这种练习本质上与乔伊斯在《芬尼根守灵夜》中所做的练习如出一辙。事实上，当我把这首诗从笔记中誊写出来时（你看，我已经誊写了），我一直在对自己说：“你知道吗？这完全可以放在《芬尼根守灵夜》里。” 你可以想象，我当时对自己相当满意。[笑声][大笑] 注意，我用了所有单词。这八行诗里没有一个不是单词的。我当然运用了一些时代错置，但我也使用了标点符号，并且想办法让这段文字有意义。我本来可以把它写成胡言乱语——就像刘易斯·卡罗尔的“时值薄暮，滑溜溜的托夫斯/在波浪中旋转翻滚……”那样——这也是语言受到不可控的语义漂移影响的另一种方式。刘易斯·卡罗尔那首著名的无厘头诗的妙处在于，我们都以为自己知道它的意思：“风很大，黏糊糊的蟾蜍在波浪中跳跃嬉戏。”我们认为它的意思大概就是这样，但语义漂移——这正是刘易斯·卡罗尔刻意引入的——使我们无法得出任何确切的结论。

Now you can see that to write the poem in this way is to perform an exercise which is essentially what Joyce is doing inFinnegan’s Wake. As a matter of fact, as I transcribed the poem out of my notes [gestures to board]–as you can see, I transcribed it–I kept saying to myself, “You know what? This could be in Finnegan’s Wake.” I was actually quite pleased with myself, as you can imagine. [laughter] [laughs] Notice that I have used all words. There’s nothing in these eight lines which is not a word. I have certainly engaged in a certain amount of anachronism, but I have also used punctuation, and I have worked out ways in which this discourse makes sense. I could have just left it at nonsense–like Lewis Carroll’s “’Twas brillig, and the slithy toves / did gyre and gimble in the wabe…”–which is another way in which language is affected by uncontrollable semantic drift. The point of Lewis Carroll’s famous nonsense verse is that we all think we know what it means: “’Twas blusterous and the slimy toads did leap and frolic in the waves.” We think that it means something like that, but semantic drift–which is what Lewis Carroll deliberately introduces to it–prevents us from in any secure way drawing any conclusions about that.

当然，我丝毫没有声称自己对华兹华斯《沉睡封印我的灵魂》的转录有任何独到之处，但这或许能让我们了解语义漂移是如何发生的。假设你并不真正属于我们这些其他人所处的阐释共同体（正如斯坦利·菲什所说），你甚至不了解诗歌究竟是什么。有人在你面前朗诵了我刚才朗诵的内容。如果你书写迅速，并将其记录下来，你很可能会写出类似这样的内容（指向黑板）。换句话说，你不会自然而然地意识到华兹华斯所写的正是你听到的内容，这是因为我所说的这种语义漂移，实际上无可避免地存在于我们所做的任何言语表达之中。

I, of course, am making no claims for this transcription of Wordsworth’s “A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal” at all, but maybe this can show us the ways in which there is semantic drift. Let’s say that you were a person not really, as Stanley Fish would put it, in the interpretive community to which all the rest of us belong, and you don’t really know what a poem is. Somebody recites in your presence what I just recited to you. Well, if you were quick at writing and you transcribed the thing, you might very well produce something like that [points to board]. In other words, it wouldn’t just spontaneously occur to you that what Wordsworth wrote was what you were hearing, and that’s because the kind of semantic drift that I’m talking about really is inescapably present in any utterance that we make.

之所以很少出错，是因为我们其实很擅长理解语境。这也是所谓的沟通问题并没有人们有时说的那么严重的原因之一。我们真的很擅长理解语境。因此，我们不太可能犯下严重的错误，但当然，也确实存在犯错的情况。众所周知，拼写检查最令人恼火的地方就在于此。你打开拼写检查，写完论文，懒得修改就交上去了。结果论文里满是低级错误，因为语言中充满了同音异义词，而拼写检查总是给出错误的单词。坦白说，你这下可惨了，因为你的老师读着读着肯定会拍着腿哈哈大笑。[笑][笑声] 总之，别用拼写检查，但拼写检查本身[笑声]却揭示了语义漂移是如何渗透到语言中的。

The utterance is not often mistaken because we’re really actually good at understanding context. That’s one of the reasons why the so-called problem of communication isn’t as great as people sometimes claim it is. We’re really good at understanding context. Hence, we’re not likely to go badly wrong, but certainly there are occasions on which we go badly wrong. As we all know, that’s the irritating thing about spell check. You put on spell check, you write your term paper, you don’t bother to edit it, and you turn it in. It’s full of howlers because, of course, the language is full of homonyms, and spell check always gives the wrong word. You’re in the soup, frankly because, of course, your teacher is just kind of slapping his knee and guffawing while reading it. [laughs] [laughter] In short, don’t use spell check, but spell check is [laughter] a phenomenon that shows you the way in which semantic drift permeates language.

但这还不是全部。语言阻碍言语还有第三种方式。索绪尔从未明确指出这一点，但这无疑是他所说的“语言”（langue）的含义。还记得我说过语言（langue）是一种虚拟实体吗？因为我们永远无法以任何成文形式找到它。没错，字典、词汇表，对吧？但这只是其中的一部分。到目前为止，请注意，我们在讨论语义漂移时只谈到了词汇表，但除了词汇表之外，语言（langue）还是一套规则——语法和句法规则，正是通过这些规则，言语才能有意义。换句话说，语言对我们在言语表达时所做的选择有着这样的影响。

But it’s not just that either. There’s a third way in which language impedes speech. Saussure never says this in so many words, but this is definitely what he means by langue. Remember I said that language, langue, is a virtual entity because we could never actually encounter it written down in any codified form. Yes, it is: the dictionary, the lexicon, right? But that’s only part of it. So far, notice that we’ve only been talking about the lexicon when we talk about semantic drift, but in addition to the lexicon, language, langue, is a set of rules–rules of grammar and syntax, rules by means of which, and only by means of which, speech can make sense. In other words, language has this sort of bearing on the choices that we can make while producing speech.

不幸的是，这些规则有时确实有点模糊不清。当我们以“It is raining”这个看似无害的表达来阐释雅各布森的六组信息时，我们却被“It is raining”的元语言功能弄得措手不及。我们不禁自问：“‘It’到底是什么？”换句话说，“It is raining”这个表达显然在语法和句法上是允许的，但同时我们又真的不知道它究竟是什么。这个“It”可以把我们引向各种奇特的方向：木星普鲁维乌斯、上帝、宇宙、云朵。有些解释似乎合情合理，但没有一个是确定的。我们意识到，“It”在这个句子中只是一个占位符，它并没有发挥应有的作用，而且，相信我，这种情况并非英语独有。正如我之前所说，这种现象在任何语言中都能找到，甚至在“下雨了”这个表达中也是如此——il pleut、es regnet等等。在所有这些表达中，“它”并没有起到应有的作用，所以如果我们依赖语言表达，就必须意识到，我们正处于经济学家所说的非理性状态之中。

Unfortunately those rules can be a little bit slippery. When we talked about the innocuous expression “It is raining” as an illustration of Jakobson’s six sets of the message, just as an example, we were brought up short by the meta-lingual function of “It is raining.” We suddenly asked ourselves, “What on earth is ‘it’?” In other words, there is a kind of grammatical and syntactical permissibility, obviously, in the expression “It is raining,” but at the same time we really have no idea. It can lead us in strange directions, this “it”: Jupiter Pluvius, God, the cosmos, the clouds. Some of it is plausible but none of it is definite. We realize that “it” is a kind of placeholder in the sentence that is not doing its job and, believe me, it’s not just in English. As I said before, it’s a phenomenon that you can find in any language, even in the expression “It is raining”– il pleut, es regnet, and so on. In all of those expressions, “it” is not doing its job, so that’s another way in which, if we lean on a speech, we have to realize that we’re in the presence of what the economists again would call irrationality.

这与谓词在语言中的运作方式有关。正如我之前所说，断言，或者说真理的陈述——任何类型的断言都是隐喻的表达，因为任何断言的深层结构都是“A是B”。这本身就是一个断言；但是——“A是B”，当然，当这种结构符合语法规则时——换句话说，当它构成语法学家所说的系词时——当这种结构符合语法规则时，那就没问题了，因为我们明白A和B之间的关系并非一种绝对的同一关系；而是一种联系的建立——例如，德曼会称之为转喻的联系——这种联系是通过谓词建立起来的。问题在于，任何以转喻方式（即作为语法命题）宣称A是B的句子，如果我们仅仅从句子本身（即隐喻）的角度来看待，它同时也是一种坚持A是B（以A是A的意义上来说）的隐喻——换句话说，它本身就是一个不完全成立的隐喻。任何隐喻都无法完全成立。它包含一种被称为误用（catachresis）的成分，因此在某种意义上，当我们解读这个句子时，它必然会破坏句子的语法结构。

That has to do with the way in which predication works in language. As I said before, an assertion, a statement of truth–an assertion of any kind is the utterance of a metaphor, because the deep structure of any assertion is that A is B. That is an assertion by definition; but–“A is B,” and of course when that construction is grammatical–in other words, when it makes what the grammarians call a copula–when the construction is grammatical, well, that’s fine because we understand that the relationship between A and B is not a relationship that’s insistently one of identity; that a connection is being made–a connection which de Man, for example, would call metonymic–in predication. The problem is that any sentence which declares that A is B metonymically–that is to say, as a grammatical proposition–is at the same time, if we simply look at the sentence for what it is, which is a metaphor, an insistence that A is B in the sense that A is A–is a metaphor, in other words which doesn’t stand on all fours. No metaphor does. It has an element of what’s called catachresis in it, and therefore in a certain sense, as we read the sentence, necessarily undermines the sentence’s grammatical structure.

德曼在《符号学与修辞学》中提出的观点正是如此：任何话语中都存在着语法与修辞之间的永恒张力。没有哪句话是完全不符合语法的，也没有哪句话是完全不符合修辞的，但遗憾的是，语法与修辞总是或明或暗地相互冲突，正如隐喻与谓词必然相互冲突一样。换句话说，没有哪句话的语法和句法规则不会微妙地干扰我们所谓的修辞规则——也就是修辞格的运用方式，而这些方式最终可以归结为我们理解隐喻的过程。

This is the point that de Man is making in “Semiology and Rhetoric,” that there is a perpetual tension in any utterance between grammar and rhetoric. There is no utterance that’s not grammatical, there’s no utterance that’s not rhetorical, but unfortunately grammar and rhetoric are always rather openly or subtly at odds with each other, just in the way that metaphor and predication really have to be at odds with each other. In other words, there isn’t a sentence in which the rules of grammar and syntax are not subtly interfering with what you might call the rules of rhetoric–the ways in which tropes, in other words, deploy themselves, ways which can be distilled in an understanding of what we call metaphor.

第三章 语言表达

Chapter 3. Language Speaking Through Speech

所以，正如我所说，每个句子不仅受制于声音的变幻莫测，不仅受制于语义的漂移，还受制于语法和修辞的不相容性，而所有这些都隐含在索绪尔及其传统所称的语言之中。换句话说，如果我可以这样说的话，这就是语言通过言语表达的方式，这就是我们在任何场合所说的任何话都被另一种声音所笼罩的方式。我们从社会学的角度将其理解为巴赫金的多语现象。我们从精神分析的角度将其理解为无意识他者的话语。我们从纯粹的语言学的角度将其理解为语言，但我认为，现在我们可以用比喻的方式来理解它，把它理解为一种言语。语言是一种无意识的言语。语言正是那种我们——通过我一直在尝试的那种分析——所认识到的，不受意图支配的言语。

So every sentence, as I say, is shadowed not just by the vagaries of sound, not just by semantic drift, but by the incompatibility of grammar and rhetoric, and all of that is implicit in what Saussure and his tradition call language. Those are the ways, in other words, in which language, if I can put it this way, speaks through speech, the ways in which anything that we say on any occasion is shadowed by another voice. We’ve understood this in social terms as Bakhtinian polyglossia. We have understood this in psychoanalytic terms as the discourse of the otherness of the unconscious. We have understood this in purely linguistic terms as language, but we can, I think, metaphorically speaking, understand it now as well as a kind of speech. Language is an unintentional speech. Language is just that speech which, we recognize–having gone through the sort of analysis that I’ve been attempting–is not governed by intention.

请记住：没有人——任何理论家，任何头脑清醒的人——会试图反驳“言语是有意图的”这一论断，即我们说话是有意图的。克纳普和迈克尔斯的观点正是如此，他们也给我们敲响了警钟，提醒我们有些怀疑是错误的。认为言语并非出于意图——这究竟意味着什么？言语本身就是一种意图，但我一直试图论证，存在一种言语，即“语言的言语”，它是无意图的，它就在那里。它无法被排除在外。它可以被置于括号中，但不能被搁置一旁，仿佛它不存在一样。它总会再次出现。如果我们足够认真地对待诠释的艺术，那么在某个时候，它总会与我们对抗——换句话说，如果我们真的对人们所说的话施加一些压力：不仅仅是实用主义的压力（我认为实用主义对我们大多数人来说已经足够好了），而是超越实用主义的压力，注意到句子中真正包含的内容，任何人的话语中真正包含的内容。

Keep in mind: nobody–no theorist, nobody in his right mind–would ever try to resist the claim that speech is intentional, that we intend what we say. That’s the way in which Knapp and Michaels are right and give us a bracing reminder about things where our skepticism is misplaced. The idea that speech is somehow not intended–what could that mean? Speech just is intention, but I’ve been trying to argue that there is a speech, the “speech of language,” which is unintentional, which is just there. It can’t be factored out. It can be bracketed, but it can’t be set aside as though it were not there. It will always come back. It will always confront us at some point if we take the arts of interpretation seriously enough–if, in other words, we really do bring some pressure to bear on the things that people say: not just a pragmatic pressure, which I think works just fine for most of us, but a pressure that goes beyond the pragmatic and notices what’s really in a sentence, what’s really in anybody’s utterance.

语言通过言语表达，部分原因在于它的起源。换句话说，语言融入你我所说的话的方式，提醒我们所说的话并非空穴来风。它有其起源，而它的起源恰恰就是语言本身。语言不断地说着：“哦，哦，我在这里”，这就是你的起源，对吧？换句话说，这就是你正在做的事情的诞生，早在你发现语言的用途之前就已经存在了。还记得我们上次说过什么吗？你必须发现火可以用来烹饪。火并非“用来”烹饪的。山洞并非用来居住的。灵巧的拇指并非用来抓握的。你必须发现其中的缘由。语言存在于我们所说的话中，提醒我们并非一直如此，提醒我们它仅仅是有意识表达历史的起源，在这个历史进程中，我们开始了永无止境的语言驾驭之旅。当然，这就是写作的意义所在。你试图驾驭语言，使其臣服。这是我们所有人的共同目标，无论我们是在创作伟大的美国小说，还是在修改一篇学期论文。我们都在与语言搏斗，试图驾驭它，而我们都知道这并不容易。我只是想解释一下为什么这不容易。

Language speaks through speech partly as its origin. In other words, the way language gets into something that you or I might say is a reminder to us that what we say comes from someplace. It has an origin and its origin is precisely language. Language keeps saying, “Oh, oh, here I am,” your origin, right? The birth of what you’re doing, in other words, way back before you discovered that language was useful for something. Remember what we said about that last time: you have to discover that fire is useful for cooking. Fire is not “for” cooking. A cave is not for dwelling. A prehensile thumb is not for grasping. You have to discover the ways in which this is the case. Language is there in what we say to remind us that it wasn’t always the case, to remind us that it’s just the origin of a history of conscious expression during the course of which we began the never-ending process of trying to master language. That’s, of course, what it is to be a writer. You try to wrestle language into submission. That’s the ambition of all of us, whether we’re writing the great American novel or revising a term paper. We’re wrestling language into submission, and we all know it’s not easy. I’m just trying to explain some of the reasons why it’s not easy.

第四章 墓志铭研究

Chapter 4. A Study of Epitaphs

因此，语言既是言语的起源，也是言语的终结。换句话说，语言标志着言语的主动性最终受到质疑，某种程度上被削弱。我认为，将语言——再次以比喻的方式——称为言语的墓志铭是恰当的，也是公平的，因为在任何特定的言语中，其主动性的终结，即便仍在继续，也已铭刻其中。

So language speaks through us as the origin of speech, but it also speaks as the death of speech. It speaks, in other words, as the moment in which the purposeful agency of speech is finally called into question, in a certain sense undermined. I think it’s appropriate, I think it’s fair, to call language–again metaphorically–the epitaph of speech, the way in which in any given speech the end of its own agency is inscribed even as that agency is going forward.

现在我想测试一下这个例子，也想更详细地向你们展示一下语义漂移的原理——更重要的是，我想深入探讨语法、句法和修辞之间微妙而复杂的关系。我想实际地给你们演示几句墓志铭。如果语言是言语的墓志铭，那么为什么不简单谈谈墓志铭呢？

Now I want to test this example and also show you a little bit more about the way semantic drift–but even more than that about the way the perilous relationship between grammar and syntax and rhetoric works. I want to actually try out on you a couple of epitaphs. If language is the epitaph of speech, why not talk for a little bit about epitaphs?

现在说说我最喜欢的墓志铭：大概——好吧，我们就不去猜测这种墓志铭会出现在哪里了，但如果你在墓园里偶然看到它，很可能会忍不住笑出声来。墓碑上写着：“我早就告诉过你我病了。”[笑声] 这句话很有意思，原因有很多。首先，这一点值得深思，它暗示着说话者们都在有效地表达自己的想法，而且不止一个人。艾米莉·狄金森和其他作家的作品中有很多这样的例子。最明显的说话者是死者本人，仿佛在从坟墓里说话：“这些年来，我一直坐在角落里，告诉你我头疼。你却从来没听我的。”等等。

Now my favorite epitaph by far: probably–well, we won’t speculate about where such an epitaph might be found, but if and when you come across it walking through a cemetery, it’ll probably elicit a chuckle. On the gravestone it says, “I told you I was sick.” [laughter] Now this is a very interesting expression for a number of reasons. For one thing, and one should pause over this, one can infer speakers speaking efficaciously, not just one but many. There’s plenty of precedent for this in Emily Dickinson and in other writers. The most obvious speaker is the dead person speaking from the grave: “there I was, sitting in the corner all those years telling you I had a headache. You never listened to me” and so on.

这是最显而易见的辨认说话者的方式，但说话者当然也可能是其他人，我这么说并非出于怀疑。当我们假设某种意图时，我们只需判断说话者是谁即可。说话者可能是某个道歉的亲戚，承认自己没听进去，但又带着幽默感，于是用死者的口吻抱怨道：“我早就告诉过你我生病了”，以此作为一种道歉：“是的，我知道你说了，但很不幸，我不得不去趟超市。”[笑声] 这也有可能是说话者。

That is the most obvious identification of a speaker, but of course the speaker could be somebody else, and I’m notintroducing a measure of skepticism in saying this. When we posit an intention, we just decide which of these speakers it is. The speaker could be an apologetic relative, someone acknowledging that they hadn’t listened, but with a sense of humor, and so putting in the voice of the dead person the complaint, “I told you I was sick” as a form of apology: “Yes, I know you did, and unfortunately I had to go to the grocery store.” [laughter] That, too, can be the speaker.

另一方面，也可能只是有人在墓前说教，这在十八世纪很常见——那也是我研究的时期之一，所以我很熟悉。也可能是一位哲学家——对吧？——说：“嗯，这就是人类的境况，[笑] 我一直跟你们说。我出版了十三本书，它们的全部主旨就是‘我病了’。我是陀思妥耶夫斯基笔下的地下室人。我病了。我病得很重。好吧，那就让它更糟吧。” 哲学家可能就是以这种方式在墓前说教，或者也可能是一位文化评论家。也可能是有人带着某种寓言式的口吻，在墓碑上刻下文化的死亡。文明早已每况愈下，如今终于走到了尽头。那么，表达这个意思的方式就是：“我告诉过你我生病了：文明有办法让我们知道它出了问题：我们没有重视，这就是结果。”

Well, on the other hand, it could be someone simply moralizing over the grave, which is a frequent habit of the eighteenth century–one of my periods, so I’m familiar with it. It could be a philosopher–right?–saying, “Well, this is the human condition, [laughs] as I kept telling you. I published thirteen books, the whole purport of which was ‘I am sick.’ I’m Dostoevsky’s Underground Man. I am a sick man. I am a very sick man. Well, let it get worse.” It could be in this mode that a philosopher is moralizing over the grave, or again it could be a cultural critic. It could be someone in a kind of an allegorical mood inscribing on the gravestone the death of culture. Civilization has been in a bad way for a long time and here finally it lies. The way to communicate this would then be, “I told you I was sick: civilization has ways of letting us know that all is not well with it: we didn’t pay any attention, and here is the result.”

我认为所有这些解读墓志铭的方式都符合诠释学。它们与我们试图理解说话者意图的方式相符；但假设我们说，“语言”必然像其他任何话语一样，在这段话语中显露出来。那会是什么呢？你看，这不仅仅是声音的问题。在这种情况下，甚至也不是语义漂移的问题。而是我们突然以一种或许任何说话者都不愿赋予的方式理解这句话的问题。确切地说，这是一个由语言巧妙引入的寓言，讲述了言语的无力。这正是言语的问题所在，不是吗？“我一遍又一遍地告诉你，你就是不听”——这就是当讲师的问题，[笑] 那种“我告诉过你我病了，你——”“哦，好吧。他只是在开玩笑。”

I would say that all of those ways of reading the epitaph are consistent with hermeneutics. They are consistent with the way in which we can try to come to terms with the intention of a speaker; but suppose we say that “language” must be obtruding itself in this utterance like any other. What would that be? You see, that isn’t just a question of sound. It isn’t even a question of semantic drift, in this case. It’s a question of our suddenly coming to understand the sentence in a way that perhaps no individual speaker would want to give it. It’s an allegory, precisely, cleverly introduced by language, about the inefficacy of speech. That’s just the problem with speech, isn’t it? “Again and again and again I tell you something and you don’t listen”–that’s the problem with being a lecturer, [laughs] that sort of “I told you I was sick and you–” “Oh, well. He’s just joking.”

所以，根据语言以牺牲言语为代价而引入的寓言，言语本身也是如此。这是一个关于沟通局限性的寓言，因为归根结底，这正是说话者——如果真有说话者在墓碑上刻下这段话的话——所关心的。这个坐在角落里，愤愤不平地抱怨没人听她或他说话的人，实际上是一位寓言家，他在告诉我们，言语就是这样。换句话说，言语是有局限性的。从某种意义上说，当我说语言是言语的墓志铭时，我们意识到，如果我们把这句话理解为一个寓言，那么躺在这里的正是言语——正如我所暗示的，这是言语所宣告或宣告的沟通能力的终结。

So it is–according to the allegory introduced by language at the expense of speech–with speech in general. It’s an allegory about the limits of communication because that’s, after all, what the speaker–insofar as there is a speaker inscribing this expression on the gravestone–is concerned about. This person sitting in the corner, complaining bitterly about nobody ever listening to her or to him, is actually an allegorist telling us that that’s the way speech is. Speech, in other words, has its limits. In a sense then, when I say language is the epitaph of speech, we realize that if we understand this utterance as an allegory, it is precisely speech that’s lying here–the end, as I suggested, of speech’s powers of communication as announced or declared by language.

好，我们再举一个例子：“约翰·多伊长眠于此”，这大概是墓志铭的雏形。换成你自己的名字：“约翰·多伊长眠于此”。好吧，我们甚至都不用在说话者身上。让我们直接探讨语言带来的问题。首先，约翰·多伊显然并不正好长眠于“此处”，对吧？事实上，仔细想想，约翰·多伊完全有可能在任何地方，唯独不在“此处”，因为在这句话出现的地方，我们知道约翰·多伊并不在那里。正如我所说，他可能在其他任何地方。因此，任何墓志铭都是一种自我宣称的衣冠冢，是在尸体不在的地方刻下的铭文，这当然也告诉我们很多关于语言任意性的信息。语言并不依附于现实世界。它并不依附于身体。语言唯一不在的地方就是身体上。语言唯一不在的地方就是事物上。言语存在于事物上。言语可以被铭刻在一块石头上。

Well, let’s try another one: “Here lies John Doe,” probably the Ur-epitaph. Supply your own name: “Here lies John Doe.” Well, let’s not even pause over the speaker there. Let’s get immediately to the problems posed by language. In the first place, John Doe obviously does not lie precisely “here,” right? In fact, if you think about it, it’s altogether possible that John Doe could be absolutely anywhere except precisely “here,” because where the sentence is we know John Doe not to be. He could be anyplace else, as I say. So any epitaph is therefore a self-declared cenotaph, an inscription on a place where the body isn’t, which of course tells us a lot, too, about the arbitrary nature of language. Language does not hook on to the real world. It doesn’t hook on to the body. The one place where language is not is on the body. The one place where language is not is on things. Speech is on things. Speech can be inscribed on a piece of rock.

所以，这句话是“约翰·多伊长眠于此”，但并非长眠于此，而是长眠于任何地方，唯独不在此——当然，这正是“谎言”这个词如此引人入胜的原因。[笑] 这句话本身是谎言，但说谎的并非约翰·多伊。可怜的约翰·多伊只是躺在某个地方而已。约翰·多伊并没有说谎，对吧？是语言[笑]让言语说谎，而且正如我们所见，它在各个层面上都发挥着作用。墓志铭的奇妙之处在于，一些秉承我们姑且称之为“解构主义”传统的作家也注意到了这一点：墓志铭是研究语言如何挑战、削弱和取代言语的绝佳切入点，正如我所说，这两个例子或多或少地展现了这种运作方式。

So “Here lies John Doe,” except not here, anyplace but here–which is why, of course, the interest of the word “lies” is so interesting. [laughs] The utterance is a lie, but it’s not John Doe who lies. Poor John Doe is just lying someplace. John Doe is not lying, right? It’s language [laughs] that’s making speech lie, and it’s doing it on any number of levels, as we’ve seen. It’s a funny thing about epitaphs, and this has been noted by certain authors writing in the tradition of what we loosely call “deconstruction”: the epitaph is a particularly fruitful locus for the study of the ways in which language challenges, undermines, and displaces speech, and as I say, these two examples show more or less the way that works.

所以，言语无处不在，唯独这里例外——我指的不是这里！——言语之所以会“撒谎”，是因为它永远无法摆脱语言的本质，因此我们永远不可能真正表达我们所说的确切含义。我们可以表达我们所说的含义，但我们无法表达我们所说的确切含义。这或许是最符合常理的表述方式。斯坦利·卡维尔在他的一本书的标题《我们必须表达我们所说的含义吗？》（Must We Mean What We Say?）中提出了这个问题[笑声]，他实际上是在告诉我们，也许言语并非如此简单[笑声]，言语行为的本质远比这复杂。当然，我们都以表达我们所说的含义为目标，但与此同时，正如新实用主义者所言，我们在说话的过程中也在表演，也在行动，我们在做着除了意义之外的各种事情。这一点确实需要被考虑在内，即便是在理解言语能做什么的时候，更不用说理解言语不能做什么的时候了。所以可以说，是的，我们可以言行一致；但是，我们能否言行一致，这是一个问题——实际上，这是一个非常紧迫的问题。

So speech lies everywhere except here–I don’t mean here!–speech lies because it can never stop being language, and therefore we can never really possibly mean exactly what we say. We can mean what we say, but we can’t mean exactly what we say. That’s probably the most commonsensical way of putting the matter. When Stanley Cavell poses the question in the title of one of his books, Must We Mean What We Say? [laughter] he is actually offering us the possibility that maybe that’s not the be all and end all of speaking, [laughs] that the speech-act situation is more complicated than that. Sure, we all have it at heart as an objective to mean what we say, but at the same time in speaking we are performing, we’re acting, as the neo-pragmatist would suggest, and we’re doing all kinds of things besides meaning. That really needs to be taken into account, even in understanding what speech can do, let alone in understanding what speech can’t do. So it’s plausible to say that yes, we can mean what we say; but it’s a question–indeed, it’s a very insistent question–whether we can mean exactly what we say.

第五章 关于拖车托尼的最后反思

Chapter 5. Final Reflections on Tony the Tow Truck

现在你问——你必须问，毕竟它一直是我们的指路明灯——你问：“托尼拖车会说话吗？”我知道你一直在思考这个问题，所以我们当然要讨论一下。我认为关于这个问题有一些有趣的地方可以探讨。这学期早些时候，我谈到了纵轴上的游行，也就是那个被称为“我”的纵轴。当你阅读文本时，你会发现，[笑]无论你从哪个角度来看，它都带有拉康的色彩，带有拉康式女性主义的色彩：阳具中心就在那里，“我”。但是，“我”绝不是婴儿说的第一个词。这是拉康的另一个教训。 “我”是你必须学会​​如何成为的——也许用朱迪斯·巴特勒的话来说——因此，“我”就像《拖车托尼》中一根不可思议的直立支柱，一句接一句地贯穿全书，它恰恰是对能动性的承诺：是对那种能够直立的身份的承诺，它是对镜中所见之物的成功模仿，然后发展成弗洛伊德所说的“自我之威严”，指的是婴儿开始在世界上获得自己想要的东西。

Now you ask–you must ask, because after all it’s been our constant guide–you ask, “Does language speak in Tony the Tow Truck?” I know this has been on your mind, and so of course we have to address it. I think there are a few interesting things to be said about that. I spoke earlier in the semester about the parade on the vertical axis, of that vertical axis, called “I.” As you read the text, there it is, [laughs] sort of out of Lacan, out of Lacanian feminism, however you look: the phallogocenter right there, I. But now I is never the first word spoken by an infant. That’s another lesson of Lacan. I is what you have to learn how to be–maybe to put it in Judith Butler’s terms–so that I, insofar as it is this incredible upright pillar starting one sentence after another in Tony the Tow Truck, is a promise of, precisely, agency: the promise of the kind of identity which stands upright, which is a successful simulacrum of what is seen in the mirror, and which then develops into what Freud called, referring to the way in which infants begin to get their way in the world, “his majesty the ego.”

所以“我”确实有这个功能，但正如我所说，这是一个关于友谊的故事，“我”消失了。我认为，这一点也可以用一些在语言功能层面上不能称之为言语的方式来传达给婴儿。例如，Bumpy（发音：BUM-py）和Tony（发音：TO-ny）之间存在着友谊，哎呀：在婴儿学会说“我”之前很久，他就已经说了“哎呀”，而这个“哎呀”与Bumpy和Tony的友谊产生了共鸣。为什么是“哎呀”呢？因为Tony被困住了，而Tony被困住时的自然反应就是“哎呀”。这时Bumpy出现了——“哎呀”——他不仅发现了问题，还解决了问题。

So the I has that function, but as I’ve said, it’s a story about friendship, and the I disappears. This, too, I think, can be communicated as relevant to the infant in ways that at the functional level of language can’t really be called speech. For example, the friendship exists between Bumpy [pron. BUM-py] and Tony [pron.TO-ny], uh-oh: long before the baby says “I,” it says “uh-oh,” and that “uh-oh” resonates in the friendship of Bumpy and Tony. Why “uh-oh?” Because Tony is stuck and Tony’s natural response to being stuck would be, “Uh-oh.” Along comes Bumpy and–“uh-oh”–not only recognizes the problem but takes care of the problem.

另一方面，自我问题，也就是被困于这个垂直“我”之中的问题，对于婴儿来说，就如同意识到他者或异己之物一般凸显出来。那些无法被还原为自我的事物开始显现，而表达这种感受的一种方式就是发出“咿咿”的声音，这或许在某种程度上是“嘿嘿嘿嘿”的伪装或模仿。我认为，故事中的两个反派角色，那些无法被同化、不提供帮助的“他者”，之所以被称作“斯皮迪”（Speedy，发音为SPEE-dee）和“尼托”（Neato，发音为NEE-to），正是出于这个原因。换句话说，那种他者感——那种难以驾驭的、无法被有效还原为自我的事物——我认为正是通过“咿咿”这个声音表达出来的。换句话说，婴儿说的不是言语，对吗？那是语言。如果你想在言语中聆听语言，只需听听婴儿的声音。这就是为什么无厘头诗歌对幼儿如此具有吸引力。他们依然能听到语言。这就像华兹华斯的《暗示颂》一样。他们依然能听到奔腾不息的洪流。在我们所有人都能听到言语的地方，他们听到的是“唵”。

Now on the other hand, the problem of self, the problem that’s caught up in this vertical I, comes into focus for the infant as the awareness of otherness or that which is alien. That which is irreducible to the self begins to come into focus, and a way of expressing this is to say, “e-e-e-e,” which is perhaps in some way or another a mask or a simulacrum of “he-he-he-he.” I think it’s for that reason that the two antagonists of the story, the unassimilable others who do not help, are called Speedy [pron. SPEE-dee] and Neato [pron. NEE-to]. In other words, that sense of otherness–of that which is intractable, that which cannot be reduced effectively to self–is I think articulated in “e-e-e.” In other words, what the infant speaks is not speech, is it? It’s language. If you want to hear language in speech, just listen to a baby. That’s why nonsense verse has such appeal to young children. They’re still hearing language. It’s a way of putting Wordsworth’s “Intimations Ode.” They’re still hearing the mighty waters rolling evermore. They’re hearing “ohm” where we’re all hearing speech.
